17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ satisfy the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=A\text{ }x(t)$ and ${x}_{p}(t)$ satisfy the inhomogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=A\text{ }x(t)+f(t).$ Which of the following is **always** a solution of the same inhomogeneous system? I. $2\cdot {x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)$ II. ${x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)$ III. $3\cdot {x}_{p}(t)$ Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${x}_{h}(t)$ satisfies a homogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution to an inhomogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t),$ then ${x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)$ is also a solution to the same inhomogeneous system. Additonally, the *linearity principle* for systems of linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) states that if ${x}_{1}(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t),…,{x}_{k}(t)$ are solutions to a homogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ then any linear combination $$ {c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)+⋯+{c}_{k}{x}_{k}(t) $$ with ${c}_{1},{c}_{2},…,{c}_{k}\in R$ is also a solution of the same homogeneous system. With that in mind, let's examine the given expression. - Option I is a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Indeed, notice that the linear combination $$ {x}_{h}(t)=2\cdot {x}_{1}(t) $$ is a solution to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ according to the linearity principle. Thus, $$ {{2\cdot {x}_{1}(t)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{h}(t)}+{x}_{p}(t) $$ is a solution to our inhomogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t).$ - Option II might be *not* a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Notice that ${x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)$ can't be written as $$ {x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t), $$ where ${x}_{h}(t)$ is a solution of the homogeneous system, because it lacks the particular solution term ${x}_{p}(t).$ - Option III might be *not* a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Notice that $3\cdot {x}_{p}(t)$ can't be written as $$ {x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t), $$ where ${x}_{h}(t)$ is a solution of the homogeneous system, because of the multiplier $3$ next to the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t).$ Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"."} {:db/id 17592186304815 :question/id #uuid "d7119481-1ac5-5669-b8e8-7afd953dbdf9" :question/math-academy-id "q-330309"} {:db/id 17592186379411 :question/id #uuid "ec98e74e-e68c-5045-a599-d3ec1260eaf6" :question/math-academy-id "q-330299"} {:db/id 17592186379418 :question/id #uuid "028e3468-5c29-5e67-a28b-97b2d534ac0d" :question/math-academy-id "q-330306"} {:db/id 17592186049852} {:db/id 17592186048395 :topic/difficulty 0.5681913796417801 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428988 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=3y(t)\end{aligned}\right. $$ Select the correct options below regarding the given decoupled system of linear differential equations. $\,$ The $x$-axis is a {{field-1}} line. $\,$ The $y$-axis is a {{field-2}} line. $\,$ The equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have $$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}x(t) $$ where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$ Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin. Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following: - Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form ${c}_{1}{e}^{5t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ lie on the $x$-axis and move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line. - Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form ${c}_{2}{e}^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ lie on the $y$-axis and also move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line. Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{an unstable node (source)}.$ **Note:** The phase portrait of the system looks as follows: :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$ f(\theta ,ϕ)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\text{_____},\,5\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩ $$ The vector-valued function $f(\theta ,ϕ)$ above parametrizes the ellipsoid defined in Cartesian coordinates as $\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+4{y}^{2}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{25}=1.$ What is the second component of $f?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we make the following substitution: $$ x=2X,\,y=\frac{1}{2}Y,\,z=5Z $$ Substituting the above into the Cartesian equation of our ellipsoid, we get $$ {X}^{2}+{Y}^{2}+{Z}^{2}=1, $$ which is the equation of a sphere of radius $1$ centered at the origin in $(X,Y,Z)$ coordinates. In spherical polar coordinates, this sphere has the equation $\rho =1.$ If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical polar coordinates of a point, then its $(X,Y,Z)$ coordinates can be found using the following formulas: $$ X=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,Y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,Z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ. $$ Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following: $$ \begin{aligned}f(\theta ,ϕ) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\ & =⟨2X,\frac{1}{2}Y,5Z⟩ \\ & =⟨2\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\frac{1}{2}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,5\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩ \\ & =⟨2\cdot 1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,5\cdot 1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩ \\ & =⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,5\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩\end{aligned} $$ where $\theta \in [0,2\pi )$ and $ϕ\in [-\pi ,\pi ].$ Therefore, the second component of $f$ is $\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$"} {:db/id 17592186241113 :question/id #uuid "246d3e23-2beb-5fb6-85c7-306f6b17e271" :question/math-academy-id "q-105686"} {:db/id 17592186241114 :question/id #uuid }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(y+x)\,i+x\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=4$ traversed from the point $A(-2,0)$ to the point $B(0,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula $$ {\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t. $$ First, we need to parameterize the curve. Notice that we can write its equation as $$ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}=1. $$ So, our curve is a part-ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $2$ and $1$ respectively. This curve can be parameterized as $$ r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}. $$ So, along the curve $C,$ we have $$ x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t. $$ As a result, $$ \begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(y+x)\,i+x\,j \\ & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned} $$ Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\ & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\ & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\ & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/de/de3e018fa1382ee2250d1b2e256e3b47cafef346852007f0e6afb84342d7cb04.png) Consider the vector field $F=3x\,i-2y\,j$ and a rectangle $C$ with base $4$ and height $6$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$ *Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by $$ {∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s, $$ where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have $$ {∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s, $$ where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below. ![](images/09/0950c559d5d6df93cf40afd8fdbd07f090f864fa462083bfd496246e7f2bded9.png) We compute this integral in two stages. - First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(3x\,i-2y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\ & =3{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned} $$ This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have $$ r(t)=2i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-3,3]. $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}3{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =3{\int }_{-3}^{3}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\ & =6{\int }_{-3}^{3}\text{d}t \\ & =6\cdot 6 \\ & =36.\end{aligned} $$ By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{3}$ must be the same. Therefore, $$ {\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=36. $$ - Next, we consider the side ${C}_{2}.$ We have that ${n}_{2}=j,$ and therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(3x\,i-2y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\ & =-2{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned} $$ This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{2},$ we have $$ r(t)=t\,i+3j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=i,\,t\in [-2,2]. $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}-2{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s & =-2{\int }_{-2}^{2}3\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\ & =-6{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\ & =(-6)\cdot 4 \\ & =-24.\end{aligned} $$ By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore, $$ {\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=-24. $$ Finally, then $$ {∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=2\cdot 36+2\cdot (-24)=24. $$"} {:db/id 17592186420916 :question/id #uuid "ab737fa4-bfd8-53e2-9695-4ad4cbdcb6c6" :question/math-academy-id "q-226136"} {:db/id 17592186421470 :question/id #uuid "f9f7d0a1-c461-5247-ab30-95b875686e93" :question/math-academy-id "q-226134"} {:db/id 17592186050793} {:db/id 17592186049462 :topic/difficulty 0.686470580486518 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186429230 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ and $\frac{dx}{d\theta }.$ To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use $$ x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $$ as parametric equations of a curve in terms of $\theta .$ Using the fact that $r=\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta ,$ we get $$ x=\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ,\,y=1. $$ Then, to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule $$ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}. $$ Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have $$ {x}^{′}(\theta )=-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=0. $$ Therefore, $$ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{0}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta }=0. $$ Finally, substituting into our formula for the second derivative, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(0)}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta } \\ & =\frac{0}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta } \\ & =0.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186188282 "![](images/49/49a3333a52a6b7d7451095dbc46ab1009df491c92726436929a6f93cff38db60.png) Notice that our solid can be written as the type I region $$ R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,\,0\le z\le 3-2x\}, $$ where $$ D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2\} $$ is the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below. ![](images/df/dfa0a80bc323401f050d1302dc42c92558d8b566d9b0f985e955d34eb5cc15bd.png) Hence, we can express the region $R$ as $$ R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 3-2x\} $$ As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain $$ {∭}_{R}2xz\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3-2x}2xz\,dz\,dy\,dx. $$ First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $x$ and $y$ as constants: $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3-2x}2xz\,dz\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{3-2x}2xz\,dz]dy\,dx \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}[x{z}^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=3-2x}\,dy\,dx \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}x(3-2x)^{2}\,dy\,dx \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(9x-12{x}^{2}+4{x}^{3})\,dy\,dx\end{aligned} $$ Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant: $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(9x-12{x}^{2}+4{x}^{3})\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{2}(9x-12{x}^{2}+4{x}^{3})\,dy]dx \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(9x-12{x}^{2}+4{x}^{3}){[y]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,dx \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2(9x-12{x}^{2}+4{x}^{3})\,dx \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(18x-24{x}^{2}+8{x}^{3})\,dx\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$ $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(18x-24{x}^{2}+8{x}^{3})\,dx & ={[9{x}^{2}-8{x}^{3}+2{x}^{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\ & =[9-8+2] \\ & =3.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186050165} {:db/id 17592186050524} {:db/id 17592186049016 :topic/id #uuid 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Change the order of integration in the integral $$ {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡y}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y. $$ so that it is integrated first with respect to $y,$ then $x,$ and then $z.$" :question/worked-solution "We wish to find limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,z),$ ${u}_{2}(x,z),$ ${v}_{1}(z),$ ${v}_{2}(z),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that $$ {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡y}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(z)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z. $$ From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type II region as follows: $$ R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{4},\,\,0\le z\le \frac{\pi }{4},\,\,0\le x\le \operatorname{tan}⁡y\} $$ Now, let's sketch the region. Since it is a type II region, we first sketch the projection onto the $yz$-plane, given by $$ E=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{4},\,\,0\le z\le \frac{\pi }{4}\}. $$ as shown below. ![](images/e3/e32a019900b77c0bb84b4599b8899e3d0d32ae07d9674da126db34394b97ea24.png) Then, the region $R$ is shown in the diagram below, where $0\le x\le \operatorname{tan}⁡y.$ ![](images/af/af629672ff2fd31eeae585ad4941fb8682941444cd34383392fb0a6bec24396e.png) To change the order of integration from $\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z,$ we write $R$ as a type III region and its projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane as a type II *plane* region. To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below. ![](images/04/04dc917237ab002263e35fb4a84c264fef240fefaa456c5249d6e24d0c8ebe28.png) The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary: - The left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x,z),$ is $$ x=\operatorname{tan}⁡y\,⟹\,y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x. $$ - The right boundary of the region is $$ y=\frac{\pi }{4}. $$ Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is $$ R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\le y\le \frac{\pi }{4}\}, $$ as shown in the diagram below. ![](images/b2/b2a6fc02441bb6013b6f54d49ceefafc1468b291ae4149847290135bbf2d2e56.png) We now consider the projection $D$ as a type II plane region in the $xz$-plane with the top curve given by $$ x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=1. $$ ![](images/b9/b942dbfba8276421620df6258c9951c2b91a5d2dea18c84260c90b6cbe6f760b.png) Hence, we have that $$ D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le \frac{\pi }{4}\}. $$ Therefore, by swapping the order of integration so that it is integrated first with respect to $y,$ then $x,$ then $z,$ we obtain $$ {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡y}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\operatorname{arctan}⁡x}^{\pi /4}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z. $$"} Recall that: - The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$ $$ max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}} $$ The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$ - The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$ $$ min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}} $$ The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$ First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form: $$ A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} $$ Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-2:$ $$ \begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}-(-2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$ Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get $$ {u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}. $$"} {:db/id 17592186198562 :question/id #uuid "48e09a9b-efe0-5a6d-96f4-c82dbcd33806" Recall that: - The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$ $$ max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}} $$ The maximum is attained on the corresponding attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$ First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form: $$ A=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 0 & -12 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -12 & 0 & 14\end{bmatrix} $$ Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$ $$ \begin{aligned}A-20I & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 0 & -12 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -12 & 0 & 14\end{bmatrix}-20\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-24 & 0 & -12 \\ 0 & -19 & 0 \\ -12 & 0 & -6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$ Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-20I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get $$ $Q(x)=3{x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $2.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: - The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$ $$ max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}} $$ The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$ - The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$ $$ min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}} $$ The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$ First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form: $$ A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix} $$ Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=2:$ $$ \begin{aligned}A-2I & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}-2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$ Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get $$ {u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}. $$"} {:db/id 17592186269174 :question/id #uuid & -8 \\ -8 & -4\end{aligned}] $$ Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows: $$ \frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}=1 $$ This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=5$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables $\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{5},$ the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$ So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix $$ P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}], $$ we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get $$ Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y). $$ As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is $$ \begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\ & =PAP \\ & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & -8 \\ -8 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -16 \\ -40 & -20\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}20 & -80 \\ -80 & -100\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following: $$ \begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}20-\lambda & -80 \\ -80 & -100-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (20-\lambda )(-100-\lambda )-6\,400 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+80\lambda -8\,400 & =0 \\ (\lambda -60)(\lambda +140) & =0 \\ \lambda & =60,\,-140\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we have $$ min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-140. $$"} {:db/id 17592186284641 :question/id #uuid "80991c77-0c00-52ac-bae2-41a3b83ff730" :question/math-academy-id "q-170515" {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $25.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form: $$ A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} $$ Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows: $$ \frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1 $$ This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables $\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$ the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$ So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix $$ P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}, $$ we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get $$ Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y). $$ As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is $$ \begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\ & =PAP \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have $$ max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25. $$ Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$ $$ \begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$ Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get $$ {u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}. $$ Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate system using the change-of-coordinates matrix: $$ \begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186492837 :question/id #uuid "1e463920-832a-54ce-b343-95505e40d97a" :question/math-academy-id "q-170527" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices Indeed, $Q({u}_{1})⊥Q({u}_{2})$ since $$ Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0. $$ - Statement III is true. Indeed, both $Q({u}_{1})$ and $Q({u}_{2})$ are unit vectors: $$ \begin{aligned}‖Q({u}_{1})‖ & =‖{u}_{1}‖=\sqrt{(\frac{4}{5})^{2}+(\frac{3}{5})^{2}}=1 \\ ‖Q({u}_{2})‖ & =‖{u}_{2}‖=\sqrt{(-\frac{3}{5})^{2}+(\frac{4}{5})^{2}}=1\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""} {:db/id 17592186284764 :question/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms: $$ \begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}\} \\ & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+L\{2t{e}^{2t}\} \\ & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+2L\{t{e}^{2t}\}\end{aligned} $$ We are given that, for $s>0,$ $$ \begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we have the following: $$ \begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}\end{aligned} $$ The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}L\{t{e}^{2t}\} & =\frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is $$ \begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+2L\{t{e}^{2t}\} \\ & =\frac{1}{s+2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}} \\ & =\frac{1}{s+2}+\frac{2}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned} $$ This transform is valid for $s>2.$"} {:db/id 17592186304984 :question/id #uuid "8e2260d5-2c33-5f8d-aede-72fd6d295719" :question/math-academy-id =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we have the following: $$ \begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{2}\} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\end{aligned} $$ The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\} & =\frac{2}{(s-5)^{3}}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is $$ \begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =2L\{{e}^{-3t}\}+7L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\} \\ & =2\cdot \frac{1}{s+3}+7\cdot \frac{2}{(s-5)^{3}} \\ & =\frac{2}{s+3}+\frac{14}{(s-5)^{3}}.\end{aligned} $$ This transform is valid for $s>5.$"} {:db/id =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we have the following: $$ \begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}} \\ L\{{t}^{3}\} & =\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}\end{aligned} $$ The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore, $$ L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\}=\frac{6}{(s-2)^{4}}. $$ Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is $$ \begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =6L\{t\}+4L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\} \\ & =6\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+4\cdot \frac{6}{(s-2)^{4}} \\ & =\frac{6}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{24}{(s-2)^{4}}.\end{aligned} $$ This transform is valid for $s>2.$"} {:db/id $y(1)$ and $y(2),$ rounded to two decimal places. $$ y(1)≈{{field-1}},\,y(2)≈{{field-2}} $$" :question/worked-solution "For an initial value problem $$ {y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c, $$ the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by $$ Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx, $$ with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values. First, note that we are given $y(0)$ and asked to find $y(2).$ The distance from $x=0$ to $x=2$ is $2,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be $$ Δx=\frac{2-0}{2}=1. $$ Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $Δy$ is given by $$ \begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\ & =\frac{1}{2}((x+y)+({x}_{\text{new}}+{y}_{\text{new}}))\cdot 1 \\ & =\frac{1}{2}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+y)+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}}.\end{aligned} $$ We substitute this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy:$ $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{2}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+y)+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+3y)+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}}\end{aligned} $$ Then, we solve for the general formula for ${y}_{\text{new}}:$ $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+3y) \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =x+{x}_{\text{new}}+3y\end{aligned} $$ We now proceed to calculate our approximations of $y(1)$ and $y(2).$ **Step 1**. From the initial conditions, we have $$ x=0,\,y=0. $$ Therefore, the new $x$ value is $$ {x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=0+1=1. $$ Hence, the new $y$ value is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =x+{x}_{\text{new}}+3y \\ & =0+1+3\cdot 0 \\ & =1.\end{aligned} $$ **Step 2**. From the previous step, we have $$ x=1,\,y=1. $$ Therefore, the new $x$ value is $$ {x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=1+1=2. $$ Hence, the new $y$ value is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =x+{x}_{\text{new}}+3y \\ & =1+2+3\cdot 1 \\ & =6.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we conclude that $$ y(1)≈1.00,\,y(2)≈6.00. $$"} {:db/id 17592186314870 :question/id #uuid y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+2y \\ -3x+{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.$ We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ In our case, we have the following: $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix} $$ First, we compute the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2y)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2y)=2 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3x+{y}^{2})=-3,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3x+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2x & 2 \\ -3 & 2y\end{bmatrix}. $$ Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}2(0) & 2 \\ -3 & 2(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}. $$ Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by $$ {u}^{′}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}u, $$ where the deviation vector is $$ u=x-{x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}. $$"} {:db/id 17592186368152 :question/id #uuid :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem: $$ {y}^{′}=2x-2y-3,\,y(0)=1 $$ To approximate the solution, one step of the Runge-Kutta method has already been computed, resulting in the following estimate: $$ y(1)≈0 $$ Use the $2$-Step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton Method with one step to approximate $y(2).$ *Hint: The corrector equation of the two-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method is defined as* $$ Δy=\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx $$ *where ${y}_{p}$ denotes the predictor at the current step, and ${y}_{-1}^{′}$ is the estimated slope at the previous point.*" :question/worked-solution "For an initial value problem $$ {y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c, $$ the $2$-Step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton (ABM $2$-step) Method with step size $Δx$ is given by $$ \begin{aligned}\text{Predictor} & : & Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx, \\ \text{Corrector} & : & Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx,\end{aligned} $$ where - ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the current point $(x,y),$ - ${y}_{-1}^{′}=f({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})$ is the estimated slope at the previous point (${x}_{-1},{y}_{-1}),$ and - ${y}_{p}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})$ is the estimated slope at the predicted new point $({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})=(x+Δx,y+Δ{y}_{p}).$ Before we start, let's add the initial condition data and Runge-Kutta step data to a table. | $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $0$ | $1$ | | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | | $1$ | $0$ | | | | | | Now, since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=2,$ we will use a step size of $$ Δx=2-1=1. $$ First, we compute the values of ${y}^{′}$ at each point according to the given rule: - The slope at the previous point $({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})=(0,1)$ is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{-1}^{′} & =2{x}_{-1}-2{y}_{-1}-3 \\ & =2\cdot 0-2\cdot 1-3 \\ & =-5.\end{aligned} $$ - The slope at the current point $(x,y)=(1,0)$ is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2x-2y-3 \\ & =2\cdot 1-2\cdot 0-3 \\ & =-1.\end{aligned} $$ We add these values to our table. | $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | | $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | | | | | Next, we compute $Δ{y}_{p}$ using the predictor equation: $$ \begin{aligned}Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\ & =\frac{1}{2}(3\cdot (-1)-(-5))\cdot 1 \\ & =1.\end{aligned} $$ We add this to our table. | $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | | $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | | | | So, the coordinates of the predicted new point are $$ \begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+1=2, \\ {y}_{p} & =y+Δ{y}_{p}=0+1=1.\end{aligned} $$ Let's add the second value to the table. | $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | | $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $1$ | | | Hence, the slope at this predicted point is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =2{x}_{\text{new}}-2{y}_{p}-3 \\ & =2\cdot 2-2\cdot 1-3 \\ & =-1.\end{aligned} $$ We can add this to our table. | $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | | $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-1$ | | Finally, we compute $Δy$ using the corrector equation: $$ \begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\ & =\frac{1}{12}(5\cdot (-1)+8\cdot (-1)-(-5))\cdot 1 \\ & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot (-8) \\ & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned} $$ We add this to our table. | $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | | $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-\frac{2}{3}$ | The value of $x$ in the next row is ${x}_{\text{new}}=2.$ To get the value of $y$ in the next row, we add $Δy$ to $y:$ $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ & =0+(-\frac{2}{3}) \\ & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned} $$ Adding these results to our table gives the following: | $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | | $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-\frac{2}{3}$ | | $2$ | $-\frac{2}{3}$ | | | | | | Therefore, we conclude that $y(2)≈-\frac{2}{3}.$"} {:db/id 17592186308490 :question/id #uuid "e92e1b49-1def-5e1c-b19c-ef83416fc895" :question/math-academy-id approximate the solution to an initial value problem. - With step size $Δx=0.08,$ the observed local truncation error is $τ(0.08)=0.13.$ - With step size $Δx=0.02,$ the observed local truncation error is $τ(0.02)=0.002.$ Estimate the order of the numerical method." :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies $$ τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0. $$ The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases. In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$ In our case, the step size decreases from $0.08$ to $0.02.$ So, it reduces by a factor of $$ k=\frac{0.08}{0.02}=4. $$ As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately $$ {k}^{p+1}={4}^{p+1}. $$ On the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.13$ to $0.002.$ So, it reduces by a factor of $$ \frac{0.13}{0.002}=65. $$ Comparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get $$ \begin{aligned}{4}^{p+1} & ≈65 \\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{4}⁡(65) \\ p+1 & ≈3.011… \\ p & ≈2.011….\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is $2.$"} {:db/id 17592186221987 :question/id #uuid "36473f35-3093-5439-832b-c821da150814" :question/math-academy-id "q-333706"} {:db/id 17592186308663 :question/id #uuid the method is approximately {{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies $$ τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0. $$ The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases. In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$ First, we compute the LTE for the given step sizes: - With step size $Δx=0.5,$ the LTE is $$ \begin{aligned}τ(0.5) & =8(0.5)^{5}+2(0.5)^{6} \\ & =8\cdot 0.031\,25+2\cdot 0.015\,625 \\ & =0.281\,25 \\ & ≈0.281.\end{aligned} $$ - With step size $Δx=0.2,$ the LTE is $$ \begin{aligned}τ(0.2) & =8(0.2)^{5}+2(0.2)^{6} \\ & =8\cdot 0.000\,32+2\cdot 0.000\,064 \\ & =0.002\,688 \\ & ≈0.003.\end{aligned} $$ Next, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.5$ to $0.2.$ So, it reduces by a factor of $$ k=\frac{0.5}{0.2}=2.5. $$ As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately $$ {k}^{p+1}={2.5}^{p+1}. $$ On the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.281\,25$ to $0.002\,688.$ So, it reduces by a factor of $$ \frac{0.281\,25}{0.002\,688}=104.631\,69…≈104.632. $$ Comparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get $$ \begin{aligned}{2.5}^{p+1} & ≈104.631\,69… \\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{2.5}⁡(104.631\,69…) \\ p+1 & ≈5.075… \\ p & ≈4.075….\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is $4.$ Indeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the LTE: $$ τ(Δx)=8(Δx)^{5}+2(Δx)^{6}\,⇒\,τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{5})=O\,((Δx)^{4+1}),\,Δx\to 0. $$ Hence, the order of the method is $4.$"} {:db/id 17592186443229 :question/id #uuid In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p}.$ In our case, the step size decreases from $0.2$ to $0.1.$ So, it reduces by a factor of $$ k=\frac{0.2}{0.1}=2. $$ Now, since the numerical method is of order $3,$ the error is expected to decrease by a factor of 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem: $$ {x}^{2}{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}-y=0,\,y(1)=-1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=2 $$ Use Euler's Method with two steps to approximate $y(2)$ and ${y}^{′}(2).$ $$ y(2)≈{{field-1}},\,{y}^{′}(2)≈{{field-2}} $$" :question/worked-solution "For a second-order initial value problem $$ {y}^{″}=f(x,y,{y}^{′}),\,y(a)=c,\,{y}^{′}(a)=d, $$ we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs, $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{′} &=f(x,y,z)\, && z(a)=d,\end{aligned}\right. $$ before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation. To apply Euler’s method, we first isolate ${y}^{″}$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z:$ $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}-y & =0 \\ {x}^{2}{y}^{″} & =y-4{y}^{′} \\ {y}^{″} & =\frac{y-4{y}^{′}}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned} $$ Then, we substitute our new variable $z={y}^{′},{z}^{′}={y}^{″}$ in the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives $$ {z}^{′}=\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}}. $$ Note that the initial value of $z$ is $z(1)={y}^{′}(1)=2.$ So, the initial value problem reduces to the following system of first-order ODEs: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(1)=-1, \\ {z}^{′} &=\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}},\, && z(1)=2\end{aligned}\right. $$ Now, we can proceed with Euler's method by applying the update rule component-wise. First, note that we are given the values of $y$ and $z={y}^{′}$ at $x=1$ and asked to find their values at $x=2.$ The distance from $x=1$ to $x=2$ is $1,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be $$ Δx=\frac{2-1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}. $$ Now, we'll start by creating a table that includes the initial condition data $y(1)=-1$ and $z(1)=2.$ | $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $1$ | $-1$ | | | $2$ | | | **Step 1**. We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the first row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method: $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=2 \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{-1-4\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}}=-9 \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=2\cdot \frac{1}{2}=1 \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=-9\cdot \frac{1}{2}=-\frac{9}{2} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=-1+1=0 \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=2-\frac{9}{2}=-\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned} $$ We add these values to our table. | $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $1$ | $-1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-9$ | $-\frac{9}{2}$ | | $\frac{3}{2}$ | $0$ | | | $-\frac{5}{2}$ | | | **Step 2**. We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the second row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method: $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=-\frac{5}{2} \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{0-4(-\frac{5}{2})}{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}}=\frac{10}{(\frac{9}{4})}=\frac{40}{9} \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=-\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}=-\frac{5}{4} \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=\frac{40}{9}\cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{20}{9} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=2 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=0-\frac{5}{4}=-\frac{5}{4} \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=-\frac{5}{2}+\frac{20}{9}=-\frac{5}{18}\end{aligned} $$ We add these values to our table. | $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $1$ | $-1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-9$ | $-\frac{9}{2}$ | | $\frac{3}{2}$ | $0$ | $-\frac{5}{2}$ | $-\frac{5}{4}$ | $-\frac{5}{2}$ | $\frac{40}{9}$ | $\frac{20}{9}$ | | $2$ | $-\frac{5}{4}$ | | | $-\frac{5}{18}$ | | | Therefore, we conclude that $y(2)≈-\frac{5}{4}$ and ${y}^{′}(2)=z(2)≈-\frac{5}{18}.$"} {:db/id 17592186308538 :question/id #uuid problem: $$ {y}^{′}=3x-{y}^{2},\,y(0)=1 $$ Use the implicit Euler method with one step and Newton's method to approximate $y(0.4).$ Round your answer to two decimal places. $y(0.4)≈$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For an initial value problem $$ {y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,{y}_{0}=y({x}_{0}), $$ the implicit Euler method with step size $Δx$ is given by $$ Δy={y}_{\text{new}}^{′}\cdot Δx, $$ with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values. Since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=0.4,$ we will use a step size of $$ Δx=0.4-0=0.4. $$ Now, let's proceed with the implicit Euler method. In general, $Δy$ is given by $$ \begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}_{\text{new}}^{′}\cdot Δx \\ & =(3({x}_{\text{new}})-({y}_{\text{new}})^{2})\cdot 0.4 \\ & =1.2({x}_{\text{new}})-0.4({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}.\end{aligned} $$ We substitute this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy$ and move all terms to the left-hand side and define the resulting expression as $g({y}_{\text{new}}):$ $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+1.2({x}_{\text{new}})-0.4({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}\end{aligned} $$ which gives the equation $$ 0.4({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-y-1.2({x}_{\text{new}})=0. $$ So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=0.4$ is $$ g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.4({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-y-1.2({x}_{\text{new}}). $$ Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is ${x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=0+0.4=0.4.$ Then, the function $g$ is $$ \begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & =0.4({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-1-1.2(0.4) \\ & =0.4({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-1.48.\end{aligned} $$ We use a root-finding method with starting point $y=1$ to solve $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.$ We'll use Newton's method. $$ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{g({y}_{\text{new}})}{{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})} $$ Note that the derivative of $g$ is $$ {g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})=0.8({y}_{\text{new}})+1. $$ Therefore, our Newton's method iterative scheme is as follows: $$ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{0.4(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{2}+({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-1.48}{0.8(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})+1} $$ Applying several iterations of Newton's method starting with $y(0)=1,$ we get the following: $$ \begin{aligned}({y}_{\text{new}})_{1} & =1 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{2} & =1.044444 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{3} & ≈1.044014 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{4} & ≈1.044014\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we conclude that $y(0.4)≈1.04,$ rounded to two decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186308430 :question/id #uuid "faf897e3-cf50-5b4e-b765-c864f4378034" {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L\{y(t)\}$ if $$ {y}^{″}+9y=5{u}_{3}(t)\cdot (t-3)^{2}\,,\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0, $$ where ${u}_{3}(t)=u(t-3)$ is the unit step function." :question/worked-solution "First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform: $$ \begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{″}+9y\} & =L\{5{u}_{3}(t)\cdot (t-3)^{2}\} \\ L\{{y}^{″}\}+9L\{y\} & =L\{5{u}_{3}(t)\cdot (t-3)^{2}\}\end{aligned} $$ To calculate $L\{{y}^{″}\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of the second derivative and the initial conditions $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=0:$ $$ L\{{y}^{″}\}={s}^{2}Y(s)-sy(0)-{y}^{′}(0)={s}^{2}Y(s) $$ To find the transform of the right-hand side, we note that the term $$ 5{u}_{3}(t)\cdot (t-3)^{2} $$ is in the form $u(t-a)\cdot f(t)$ where $a=3$ and $f(t)=5(t-3)^{2}.$ Now, recall that the second shifting theorem (time-shifting property) accumulation function $F(x)$ is defined as* > > > $$ > F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,\textrm d t, > $$ > > > *then the derivative of $F(x)$ is given by* > > > $$ > F'(x) = \dfrac {\textrm d} {\textrm dx} \int_a^x f(t) \,\textrm d t = f(x). > $$ Loosely speaking, taking the derivative "cancels out" the integral and leaves us with the integrand. This happens because the derivative and the integral are *opposite* operations. To demonstrate how this works, let's define the accumulation function $F(x)$ as $$ F(x)=\int^{x}_{2} \sin(t^2)\,\textrm d t. $$ Suppose that we want to differentiate this function to find $F'(x).$ Let's start by differentiating both sides with respect to $x,$ which gives $$ F'(x) = \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\int^{x}_{2} \sin(t^2)\,\textrm d t. $$ Evaluating the integral on the right-hand side is difficult. However, we can apply FTC II and get $$ \begin{aligned}{F}^{'}(x)=\operatorname{sin}({x}^{2}).\end{aligned} $$ And that's it! This theorem saves us a ton of work and is especially useful when the integral is hard to calculate. **Note:** To gain further intuition for FTC II, it helps to work out an example in a simple case. Let's define the accumulation function $F(x)$ as an integral that we can actually compute: $$ F(x)=\int^{x}_{2} t^2 \,\textrm d t $$ Computing the integral, we have $$ \begin{aligned}F(x) & ={\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}|}_{2}^{x}=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-\frac{8}{3},\end{aligned} $$ and taking the derivative, we get $$ \begin{aligned}{F}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-\frac{8}{3})={x}^{2},\end{aligned} $$ which matches up with the original integrand. "30fad2b1-33b1-5011-baca-2c53469ec04d" :question/math-academy-id "q-99827" :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions: $$ {f}_{1}(t)=1,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{f}_{3}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t $$ Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-\pi ,\pi ]$ of continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$ is defined as $$ ⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t, $$ which of the following statements are true? I. ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product II. ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product III. $S=\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product *Hint: $⟨{f}_{2},{f}_{3}⟩=0$* Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn. - Statement I is true. We have $$ \begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨1,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\ & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t{|}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\ & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi ) \\ & =0.\end{aligned} $$ This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product. - Statement II is true. :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186148455 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148756 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will solve first-order *initial value problems* using Laplace transforms. The key idea is that the Laplace transform converts derivatives into algebraic expressions involving the transform of the unknown function. If we write $$ Y(s) = \mathcal L\{y(t)\}, $$ then the initial condition appears automatically through the **derivative rule** $$ \mathcal L\{y'\} = sY(s) - y(0). $$ So, when we take the Laplace transform of a differential equation like $$ y' + ay = f(t), $$ we get an algebraic equation in $Y(s),$ which we can solve using standard algebra. In the first few problems, our goal will be to find an explicit formula for $Y(s).$ Later, we will finish the process by taking the inverse Laplace transform to recover $y(t).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "19b12099-79ea-57ad-8d49-b0ec631e099d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4111 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "ce168e7b-e179-5ef7-a408-d6641bda4d96" :step/math-academy-id 612632 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148456}} {:db/id 17592186148456 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148667 :tutorial/content "The **Laplace transform method** is a powerful tool that converts a differential equation (a calculus problem) into an algebraic equation, which is often much easier to solve. To solve a first-order initial value problem (IVP) of the form $$ y' + ay = f(t), \quad y(0)=y_0, $$ we follow a standard workflow. - First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides of the equation to obtain an algebraic equation in $Y(s)=\mathcal L\{y(t)\}.$ Using linearity and the derivative formula $$ \mathcal L\{y'\} = sY(s) - y(0), $$ we convert the IVP into an algebraic equation for the unknown transform, $Y(s).$ - After substituting the initial condition $y(0)=y_0$ and finding the transform of $f(t),$ we solve the resulting algebraic equation for $Y(s).$ The calculus portion of the problem is now complete. - Before applying the inverse transform, we rewrite $Y(s)$ as a sum of simpler expressions found in a standard table of Laplace transforms. This step often requires techniques like **partial fraction decomposition**. - Finally, we take the inverse Laplace transform, $\mathcal L^{-1},$ of each term in $Y(s)$ to find the solution $y(t)$ to the original initial value problem. Next, we consider the example of finding $Y(s)$ for the concrete initial value problem." :tutorial/id #uuid "2a58657b-748f-56e6-9ebc-7cb481b9bf57" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14889 :tutorial/title "Using Laplace Transforms to Solve First-Order IVPs"} :step/id #uuid "fa47c1d6-1923-5ff4-aafc-fbb54002fb57" :step/math-academy-id 612633 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148457}} {:db/id 17592186148457 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148668 :tutorial/content "Consider the following initial value problem. $$ \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t} + 4y = 2t-1, \qquad y(0)=0. $$ To find $Y(s) = \mathcal L \{y(t)\},$ we first take the Laplace transform of both sides of the differential equation. Using the linearity property, we have $$ \mathcal{L}\{y'\} + 4\mathcal{L}\{y\} = 2\mathcal{L}\{t\}-\mathcal{L}\{1\}. $$ To calculate $\mathcal L\left\{ y' \right\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=0{:}$ $$ \mathcal{L}\left\{y'\right\} = sY(s) - y(0) = sY(s). $$ So, the differential equation transforms to $$ sY(s) + 4Y(s) = 2\mathcal{L}\{t\}-\mathcal{L}\{1\}. $$ Now, we make use of the following result: $$ \mathcal L\{t^n\} = \dfrac{n!}{s^{n+1}}, \qquad s > 0, \quad n\in \mathbb{N}_0. $$ This gives $$ \begin{aligned}L{t} & =\frac{1!}{{s}^{1+1}}=\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}, \\ L{1} & =\frac{0!}{{s}^{0+1}}=\frac{1}{s}.\end{aligned} $$ Substituting these results into the transformed equation, we get $$ \begin{aligned}sY(s)+4Y(s) & =2\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}-\frac{1}{s} \\ (s+4)Y(s) & =\frac{2}{{s}^{2}}-\frac{1}{s} \\ (s+4)Y(s) & =\frac{2-s}{{s}^{2}}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, dividing by $(s+4),$ we obtain $$ Y(s) =\dfrac{2-s}{s^2(s + 4)}. $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fc740a47-119f-5fa2-bac2-018828c79406" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14890 :tutorial/title "Finding the Laplace Transform of the Unknown Function Satisfying the IVP"} :step/id #uuid "8da8db44-ae26-54f5-ba7f-f8256253813f" :step/math-academy-id 612634 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148458}} {:db/id 17592186148458 :step/content {:db/id 17592186147527 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186147362 :question/id #uuid "700f5e8f-33f6-568a-ad11-d2664336725d" :question/math-academy-id "e-6657"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b1417a42-f47a-5611-84be-f331c75287a9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048580} {:db/id 17592186049301} {:db/id 17592186050608}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186148146} {:db/id 17592186148153} {:db/id 17592186317269} {:db/id 17592186317332} {:db/id 17592186317357} {:db/id 17592186335707} {:db/id 17592186335708}] :knowledge-point/title "Laplace Transforms of First-Order Linear IVPs"} :step/id #uuid "451b2242-11ee-5088-a876-11e2c54ac097" :step/math-academy-id 612635 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148459}} {:db/id 17592186148459 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148665 :tutorial/content "Once we have solved for $Y(s)$, the final step is to compute the solution . The main idea is to rewrite $Y(s)$ as a sum of simpler terms whose inverse transforms are known from a table. **Step 1:** Look for standard inverse-transform patterns. The goal is to match terms in $Y(s)$ to known transform pairs. Common forms include: - $\mathcal{L}^{-1}\left\{\dfrac{1}{s-a}\right\} = e^{at}$ - $\mathcal{L}^{-1}\left\{\dfrac{1}{(s-a)^n}\right\} = \dfrac{t^{n-1}e^{at}}{(n-1)!}$ for integer $n \ge 1$ - $\mathcal{L}^{-1}\left\{\dfrac{s}{s^2+\omega^2}\right\} = \cos(\omega t)$ - $\mathcal{L}^{-1}\left\{\dfrac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2}\right\} = \sin(\omega t)$ **Step 2:** If $Y(s)$ is a rational function, use **partial fraction decomposition**. If the denominator has distinct linear factors, we write: $$ \dfrac{P(s)}{(s-a)(s-b)} = \dfrac{A}{s-a} + \dfrac{B}{s-b} $$ where $P(s)$ is a polynomial with $\deg (P) < 2$. If there is a repeated linear factor, we include a term for each power: $$ \dfrac{P(s)}{(s-a)^2} = \dfrac{A}{s-a} + \dfrac{B}{(s-a)^2} $$ where $P(s)$ is a polynomial with $\deg (P) < 2$. **Step 3:** Apply the inverse transform term-by-term. Because the inverse Laplace transform is **linear**, we can apply it to each term in the sum separately to find the final solution $y(t)$. Next, we will apply this method to a specific example." :tutorial/id #uuid "785dff4c-cd6a-5cdd-bbcf-7c6b0c82c077" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14742 :tutorial/title "Getting Ready for the Inverse Laplace Transform"} :step/id #uuid "d4f76515-92a2-55e5-b0c3-2c8b3edd59d2" :step/math-academy-id 612638 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148460}} {:db/id 17592186148460 :step/content {:db/id 17592186147528 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186147363 :question/id #uuid "409c5aa3-5c53-5ab4-b2f7-bcfe01a14914" :question/math-academy-id "e-6661"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5eae6b5d-adff-53b2-970d-f0dcee58365f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050050} {:db/id 17592186050768} {:db/id 17592186050964}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186147787} {:db/id 17592186147788} {:db/id 17592186317272} {:db/id 17592186317338} {:db/id 17592186317340} {:db/id 17592186391797} {:db/id 17592186391831}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving First-Order Initial Value Problems Using Laplace Transforms"} :step/id #uuid "71fe0cf6-2b8b-5473-b14f-c3ddf9ebb1d5" :step/math-academy-id 612639 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148461}} {:db/id 17592186148461 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148666 :tutorial/content "When $Y(s)$ is a rational function, we often use partial fractions to rewrite it in a form where we can apply $\mathcal L^{-1}.$ Sometimes the denominator contains an *irreducible quadratic factor*, such as $s^2+\omega^2.$ In that case, the partial fraction term must have a linear numerator. **Step 1:** Write the correct decomposition form. For example, if $$ Y(s)=\dfrac{P(s)}{(s-a)(s^2+\omega^2)}, $$ then we decompose it as $$ \dfrac{P(s)}{(s-a)(s^2+\omega^2)} = \dfrac{A}{s-a} + \dfrac{Bs+C}{s^2+\omega^2}. $$ **Step 2:** Multiply both sides by the denominator. Clearing denominators gives an identity in $s{:}$ $$ P(s)=A(s^2+\omega^2) + (Bs+C)(s-a). $$ **Step 3:** Solve for the constants. We can find $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ by expanding the right-hand side and matching coefficients of powers of $s.$ **Step 4:** Take the inverse Laplace transform. y(0) = sY(s). $$ So, the differential equation transforms to $$ sY(s) + 4Y(s) = 2\mathcal{L}\{t\}-\mathcal{L}\{1\}. $$ Now, we make use of the following result: $$ \mathcal L\{t^n\} = \dfrac{n!}{s^{n+1}}, \qquad s > 0, \quad n\in \mathbb{N}_0. $$ This gives $$ \begin{aligned}L{t} & =\frac{1!}{{s}^{1+1}}=\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}, \\ L{1} & =\frac{0!}{{s}^{0+1}}=\frac{1}{s}.\end{aligned} $$ Substituting these results into the transformed equation, we get $$ \begin{aligned}sY(s)+4Y(s) & =2\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}-\frac{1}{s} \\ (s+4)Y(s) & =\frac{2}{{s}^{2}}-\frac{1}{s} \\ (s+4)Y(s) & =\frac{2-s}{{s}^{2}}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, dividing by $(s+4),$ we obtain $$ Y(s) =\dfrac{2-s}{s^2(s + 4)}. $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fc740a47-119f-5fa2-bac2-018828c79406" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14890 :tutorial/title "Finding the Laplace Transform of the Unknown Function Satisfying the IVP"} {:db/id 17592186148458 :step/content {:db/id 17592186147527 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186147362 :question/id #uuid "700f5e8f-33f6-568a-ad11-d2664336725d" :question/math-academy-id "e-6657"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b1417a42-f47a-5611-84be-f331c75287a9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048580} {:db/id 17592186049301} {:db/id 17592186050608}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186148146} {:db/id 17592186148153} {:db/id 17592186317269} {:db/id 17592186317332} {:db/id 17592186317357} {:db/id 17592186335707} {:db/id 17592186335708}] :knowledge-point/title "Laplace Transforms of First-Order Linear IVPs"} :step/id #uuid "451b2242-11ee-5088-a876-11e2c54ac097" :step/math-academy-id 612635 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148459}} {:db/id 17592186148459 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148665 :tutorial/content "Once we have solved for $Y(s)$, the final step is to compute the solution . The main idea is to rewrite $Y(s)$ as a sum of simpler terms whose inverse transforms are known from a table. **Step 1:** Look for standard inverse-transform patterns. The goal is to match terms in $Y(s)$ to known transform pairs. Common forms include: - $\mathcal{L}^{-1}\left\{\dfrac{1}{s-a}\right\} = e^{at}$ - $\mathcal{L}^{-1}\left\{\dfrac{1}{(s-a)^n}\right\} = \dfrac{t^{n-1}e^{at}}{(n-1)!}$ for integer $n \ge 1$ - $\mathcal{L}^{-1}\left\{\dfrac{s}{s^2+\omega^2}\right\} = \cos(\omega t)$ - $\mathcal{L}^{-1}\left\{\dfrac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2}\right\} = \sin(\omega t)$ **Step 2:** If $Y(s)$ is a rational function, use **partial fraction decomposition**. If the denominator has distinct linear factors, we write: $$ \dfrac{P(s)}{(s-a)(s-b)} = \dfrac{A}{s-a} + \dfrac{B}{s-b} $$ where $P(s)$ is a polynomial with $\deg (P) < 2$. If there is a repeated linear factor, we include a term for each power: $$ \dfrac{P(s)}{(s-a)^2} = \dfrac{A}{s-a} + \dfrac{B}{(s-a)^2} $$ where $P(s)$ is a polynomial with $\deg (P) < 2$. **Step 3:** Apply the inverse transform term-by-term. Because the inverse Laplace transform is **linear**, we can apply it to each term in the sum separately to find the final solution $y(t)$. Next, we will apply this method to a specific example." :tutorial/id #uuid "785dff4c-cd6a-5cdd-bbcf-7c6b0c82c077" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14742 :tutorial/title "Getting Ready for the Inverse Laplace Transform"} :step/id #uuid "d4f76515-92a2-55e5-b0c3-2c8b3edd59d2" :step/math-academy-id 612638 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148460}} {:db/id 17592186148665 :tutorial/content "Once we have solved for $Y(s)$, the final step is to compute the solution . For example, if $$ Y(s)=\dfrac{P(s)}{(s-a)(s^2+\omega^2)}, $$ then we decompose it as $$ \dfrac{P(s)}{(s-a)(s^2+\omega^2)} = \dfrac{A}{s-a} + \dfrac{Bs+C}{s^2+\omega^2}. $$ **Step 2:** Multiply both sides by the denominator. Clearing denominators gives an identity in $s{:}$ $$ P(s)=A(s^2+\omega^2) + (Bs+C)(s-a). $$ **Step 3:** Solve for the constants. We can find $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ by expanding the right-hand side and matching coefficients of powers of $s.$ **Step 4:** Take the inverse Laplace transform. We split the quadratic term to match the standard forms: $$ \dfrac{Bs+C}{s^2+\omega^2} = B\left(\dfrac{s}{s^2+\omega^2}\right) + \dfrac{C}{\omega}\left(\dfrac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2}\right). $$ Then we apply the inverse transforms: $$ \mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\dfrac{s}{s^2+\omega^2}\right\}=\cos(\omega t), \qquad \mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\dfrac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2}\right\}=\sin(\omega t). $$ Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "0db35afe-1ae8-50e9-a89d-2c65a3bc7956" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14743 :tutorial/title "Partial Fractions With Irreducible Quadratic Factors"} :step/id #uuid "7fe41923-9e55-52ed-b19d-70a8608c1ef8" :step/math-academy-id 612643 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148462}} {:db/id 17592186148666 :tutorial/content "When $Y(s)$ is a rational function, we often use partial fractions to rewrite it in a form where we can apply $\mathcal L^{-1}.$ Sometimes the denominator contains an *irreducible quadratic factor*, such as $s^2+\omega^2.$ In that case, the partial fraction term must have a linear numerator. **Step 1:** Write the correct decomposition form. :step/math-academy-id 30977 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125534}} {:db/id 17592186125534 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125838 :tutorial/content "Given a function of three variables $f(x,y,z),$ we can find formulas for $f_r, f_\theta,$ and $f_z,$ where $(r,\theta,z)$ are cylindrical polar coordinates. The results that we need are as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \\ \frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂f}{∂z}.\end{aligned} $$ Notice that the first and second equations are identical to the equations derived for plane polar coordinates, as we would expect. The difference here is that we now have a third equation that deals with the $z$-dependence. But since the $z$-coordinate is the same in both Cartesian and cylindrical polar coordinates, we can simply differentiate with respect to $z$ as usual. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "733b56f3-7c9a-59a6-bc6b-ef87bf07d149" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4975 :tutorial/title "The Multivariable Chain Rule With Cylindrical Polar Coordinates"} {:db/id 17592186125562 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125847 :tutorial/content "Up to now, we've been using the following formulas: $$ \begin{aligned}{f}_{r} & ={f}_{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{f}_{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \\ {f}_{\theta } & =-r{f}_{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r{f}_{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned} $$ We can treat the above as a system of equations in the "unknowns" $f_x$ and $f_y.$ Solving this system gives explicit expressions for $f_x$ and $f_y$ in terms of functions of $r$ and $\theta.$ For example, suppose we want an explicit formula for $f_x.$ We can eliminate $f_y$ by multiplying the first equation by $r\cos\theta$ and the second equation by $\sin\theta$ to give $$ \begin{aligned}r{f}_{r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta & =r{f}_{x}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +r{f}_{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ {f}_{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta & =-r{f}_{x}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +r{f}_{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned} $$ Subtracting the second equation from the first gives $$ r f_r \cos\theta - f_\theta \sin\theta = r f_x(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta), $$ which simplifies to $$ f_x = f_r \cos\theta - \dfrac1r f_\theta \sin\theta. $$ We can use a similar procedure to write $f_y$ in terms of functions of $r$ and $\theta.$ Our results as summarized below: $$ \eqalign{ \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial r} \cos \theta -\dfrac{1}{r} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial \theta}\sin \theta\[1ex] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial r} \sin \theta + \dfrac{1}{r} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial \theta}\cos \theta } $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e3237863-f115-5396-a03f-fd481d101761" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5358 :tutorial/title "Differentiating of a Function Given in Polar Coordinates With Respect to Cartesian Coordinates"} :step/id #uuid "443067c1-4f4c-574c-818f-cec45ee26f17" :step/math-academy-id 33488 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125533}} {:db/id 17592186125563 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125848 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we have a function $f(x,y,z),$ and we wish to find formulas for $f_\rho,$ $f_\theta,$ and $f_\phi$, where 17592186125534 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125838 :tutorial/content "Given a function of three variables $f(x,y,z),$ we can find formulas for $f_r, f_\theta,$ and $f_z,$ where $(r,\theta,z)$ are The results that we need are as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \\ \frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂f}{∂z}.\end{aligned} $$ Notice that the first and second equations are identical to the equations derived for plane polar coordinates, as we would expect. The difference here is that we now have a third equation that deals with the $z$-dependence. But since the $z$-coordinate is the same in both Cartesian and cylindrical polar coordinates, we can simply differentiate with respect to $z$ as usual. {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "c9126714-6e57-5593-b5b4-4801efbfb113" :question/math-academy-id "q-95111" :question/problem "Given that $q(x,y)=xy,$ find $\frac{∂q}{∂\theta },$ where where $C$ is a curve in the $xy$-plane defined using plane polar coordinates as $$ r = r(\theta),\qquad \theta_1 \leq \theta \leq \theta_2. $$ To calculate this line integral, we need to recall the following facts: - A polar curve is just a special type of parametric curve in the parameter $\theta,$ where $$ x = r(\theta)\cos\theta, \quad y = r(\theta)\sin\theta, \qquad \theta_1 \leq \theta \leq \theta_2. $$ - The arc length element $\textrm d s$ in plane polar coordinates is given by $$ \textrm ds = \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\,. $$ Substituting the above formulas into our line integral, we get the following result: $$ \int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\,. $$ Let's go through an example in which we apply this result." :tutorial/id #uuid "f970309b-6c25-53f1-a3b5-b094ebe87109" :question/math-academy-id "q-76690" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by $$ {\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,. $$ The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives $$ \begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \\ & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \\ & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned} $$ So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ Now, since $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\ & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{4}⁡\theta } \\ & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\ & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\ & =|\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta | \\ & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned} $$ Notice that $|\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta |=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ because $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta >0.$ Next, we have $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned} $$ and therefore $$ \begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\ & =\sqrt{1} \\ & =1.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \\ & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta \\ & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta \\ & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\ & =-0-(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by $$ {\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,. $$ The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives $$ \begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ & =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \\ & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \\ & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned} $$ So, along our curve, we have $x=2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ Now, if $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ & =4{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned} $$ Next, we have $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned} $$ and therefore $$ \begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta & =\sqrt{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\ & =\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\ & =\sqrt{4} \\ & =2.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we can write the integral as $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta \\ & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid "3a1fe02b-b141-526c-b50f-2169f538c454" :step/next {:db/id 17592186513008}} {:db/id 17592186512999 gives $$ \begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned} $$ So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$ Now, since $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y$, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\ & =\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned} $$ Next, we have $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned} $$ and therefore $$ \begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\ & =1.\end{aligned} $$ We can now write the integral as $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned} $$ Let's use integration by parts. We denote $$ \begin{aligned}u=\theta & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}\theta =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned} $$ Now, substituting into the formula for the integration by parts, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta & =\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /3}-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta \\ & =(\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{6}-0)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{6}+(\frac{1}{2}-1) \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi -3}{6}.\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid "84c36a68-d168-50c2-9fa4-68085a6b5cc6"} {:db/id 17592186513008 :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by $$ {\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,. $$ The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives $$ \begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ & =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \\ & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \\ & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned} $$ So, along our curve, we have $x=2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ Now, if $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ & =4{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned} $$ Next, we have $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned} $$ and therefore $$ \begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta & =\sqrt{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\ & =\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\ & =\sqrt{4} \\ & =2.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we can write the integral as $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta \\ & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi
