"77b8e530-6866-509a-8397-d35f1b4f5874" :topic/math-academy-id 2097} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134636 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135034 :tutorial/content "The standard inner product of $\Bbb R^n,$ i.e. the dot product, does not meet the criteria of an inner product on $\Bbb C^n.$ For example, if $\langle \,\cdot\,, \,\cdot\, \rangle$ is a valid inner product on $\Bbb C^n,$ then for any vector $\mathbf a \in \Bbb C^n,$ we must have $$ \langle\mathbf a, \, \mathbf a\rangle \ge 0. $$ But for many vectors in $\Bbb C^n,$ such as $\begin{bmatrix}\text{i} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ in $\Bbb C^2,$ the dot product fails to satisfy this criterion: $$ \begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}\text{i} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}\text{i} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} & ={\text{i}}^{2}+{0}^{2} \\ & =-1 \\ & <0\,\times \end{aligned} $$ Thankfully, there is an elegant way to generalize the dot product to satisfy the desired criterion on $\Bbb C^n.$ We can just take the complex conjugate of each element in the right vector before carrying out the dot product. More formally, for two vectors $\mathbf x, \mathbf y\in \mathbb C^n$ given by ![](images/26/26b805ac1354eab1901a0874f66882bc1ec07dc3351c95ad2cf9b16aaf59d2fb.svg) we define the **standard Hermitian inner product** as $$ \begin{aligned}⟨x,y⟩ & ={x}_{1}\cdot \overset{―}{{y}_{1}}+{x}_{2}\cdot \overset{―}{{y}_{2}}+⋯+{x}_{n}\cdot \overset{―}{{y}_{n}} \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\cdot \overset{―}{{y}_{i}},\end{aligned} $$ where $\overline{y_i}$ is the complex conjugate of $y_i.$ Using the standard Hermitian inner product instead of the dot product, our desired criterion is satisfied: $$ \begin{aligned}⟨\begin{bmatrix}\text{i} \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}\text{i} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}⟩ & =\text{i}\cdot \overset{―}{\,\text{i}\,}+0\cdot \overset{―}{\,0\,} \\ & =\text{i}\cdot (-\text{i})+0\cdot 0 \\ & =1+0 \\ & =1 \\ & \ge 0\,✓\end{aligned} $$ It can be verified that the Hermitian inner product satisfies *all* the criteria of an inner product on $\Bbb C^n.$ Furthermore, since the complex conjugate leaves real numbers unchanged, the Hermitian inner product simplifies to the dot product on $\Bbb R^n.$ In other words, the dot product is just a special case of the Hermitian inner product!" :tutorial/id #uuid "ca70c748-2628-5d2d-b0dc-ab7a0675355a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3605 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid :tutorial/content "The standard inner product of $\Bbb R^n,$ i.e. the dot product, does not meet the criteria of an inner product on $\Bbb C^n.$ For example, if $\langle \,\cdot\,, \,\cdot\, \rangle$ is a valid inner product on $\Bbb C^n,$ then for any vector $\mathbf a \in \Bbb C^n,$ we must have $$ \langle\mathbf a, \, \mathbf a\rangle \ge 0. $$ But for many vectors in $\Bbb C^n,$ such as $\begin{bmatrix}\text{i} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ in $\Bbb C^2,$ the dot product fails to satisfy this criterion: $$ \begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}\text{i} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}\text{i} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} & ={\text{i}}^{2}+{0}^{2} \\ & =-1 \\ & <0\,\times \end{aligned} $$ Thankfully, there is an elegant way to generalize the dot product to satisfy the desired criterion on $\Bbb C^n.$ We can just take the complex conjugate of each element in the right vector before carrying out the dot product. More formally, for two vectors $\mathbf x, \mathbf y\in \mathbb C^n$ given by ![](images/26/26b805ac1354eab1901a0874f66882bc1ec07dc3351c95ad2cf9b16aaf59d2fb.svg) we define the **standard Hermitian inner product** as $$ \begin{aligned}⟨x,y⟩ & ={x}_{1}\cdot \overset{―}{{y}_{1}}+{x}_{2}\cdot \overset{―}{{y}_{2}}+⋯+{x}_{n}\cdot \overset{―}{{y}_{n}} \\ & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\cdot \overset{―}{{y}_{i}},\end{aligned} $$ where $\overline{y_i}$ is the complex conjugate of $y_i.$ Using the standard Hermitian inner product instead of the dot product, our desired criterion is satisfied: $$ \begin{aligned}⟨\begin{bmatrix}\text{i} \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}\text{i} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}⟩ & =\text{i}\cdot \overset{―}{\,\text{i}\,}+0\cdot \overset{―}{\,0\,} \\ & =\text{i}\cdot (-\text{i})+0\cdot 0 \\ & =1+0 \\ & =1 \\ & \ge 0\,✓\end{aligned} $$ It can be verified that the Hermitian inner product satisfies *all* the criteria of an inner product on $\Bbb C^n.$ Furthermore, since the complex conjugate leaves real numbers unchanged, the Hermitian inner product simplifies to the dot product on $\Bbb R^n.$ In other words, the dot product is just a special case of the Hermitian inner product!" :tutorial/id #uuid "ca70c748-2628-5d2d-b0dc-ab7a0675355a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3605 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "2fac0a4e-d3e8-507c-b2ff-dcb288cf0e43" :question/math-academy-id "q-97258" :question/problem "Consider the standard Hermitian inner product $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ over $C.$ Which of the following statements are true? Select all that apply. - **I.** $⟨a,a⟩\in R$ for any $a\in {C}^{n}$ - **II.** $⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C$ - **III.** $⟨a,b⟩=⟨b,a⟩$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties: - It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have $\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$ - It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have $\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$ - It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have $\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$ - It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have $\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$ With that in mind, let's examine our statements. - Statement I is true. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number. - Statement II is false. To factor out a constant multiple from the second argument, we must change it to its complex conjugate. - Statement III is false. The inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry. Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} :step/id #uuid "042f271a-62ae-5a4a-884d-ff79b9db9024" :step/next {:db/id 17592186445244}} {:db/id 17592186445242 :step/content {:db/id 17592186360767 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0e841129-5370-59a4-a247-981a63a55e7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186357872} {:answer/id #uuid "0f6fe134-1090-5f97-9ea8-128ddfc3b774" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\text{i}" :db/id 17592186357876} {:answer/id #uuid "c020effb-ac1b-5c1a-b136-a3f990641cda" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\text{i}" :db/id 17592186359435} {:answer/id #uuid "cb7d8484-175b-5e8d-bc3b-f162579d8e47" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\text{i}" :db/id 17592186359541} {:answer/id #uuid "e819a706-cc55-53d4-ad1b-913fba1a9b02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5+3\text{i}" :db/id 17592186359809}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186359541} :answer-field/id #uuid "a14982e8-8062-5f22-9abd-32b12535e617" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360273}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "34140471-4f5c-5a2d-9e46-e76840a3d73f" :question/math-academy-id "q-97193" :question/problem "Given that $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ is the standard Hermitian inner product over $C,$ find $⟨a,\,(4-\text{i})b+c⟩$ if $\,$ $⟨b,a⟩=-1-\text{i}\,$ and $\,⟨a,c⟩=5.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties. - It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have $\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$ - It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have $\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$ First, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ is antilinear in the second For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have $\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$ With that in mind, let's examine our statements. - Statement I is true. Indeed, the inner product in ${C}^{n}$ is linear in the first argument. So, a constant multiple from the first argument can be factored out. - Statement II is true. By the antilinearity of a complex inner product in the second argument and linearity in the first argument, we have $$ ⟨a,\overset{―}{\alpha }b⟩=\overset{―}{(\overset{―}{\alpha })}⟨a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩=⟨\alpha a,b⟩. $$ - Statement III is false. Notice that $⟨a,a⟩\in R$ for any $a\in {C}^{n}.$ Therefore, if $a\ne 0,$ then $$ ⟨ia,a⟩=i⟨a,a⟩\notin R. $$ Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""} :step/id #uuid over $C.$ Which of the following statements are true? Select all that apply. - **I.** $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨a,b⟩}$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$ - **II.** $i⟨a,b⟩=⟨a,-ib⟩$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$ - **III.** There is vector $a\in {C}^{n}$ such that $⟨a,a⟩<0$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties: - It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have $\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$ - It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have $\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$ - It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have $\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$ - It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have $\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$ With that in mind, let's examine our statements. - Statement I is false. A complex number is equal to its conjugate if and only if it is a real number. The inner product over $C$ is a complex number in general. - Statement II is true. Indeed, by the antilinearity of a complex inner product in the second argument, we have $$ ⟨a,-ib⟩=\overset{―}{(-i)}⟨a,b⟩=i⟨a,b⟩. $$ - Statement III is false. The inner product over $C$ is positive-definite. So, for any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have $\,$ $⟨a,a⟩\ge 0.$ Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""} :step/id #uuid "c0e9081f-8d78-5a6a-b192-5ac752a618f5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186445243}} {:db/id 17592186445242 :step/content {:db/id 17592186360767 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0e841129-5370-59a4-a247-981a63a55e7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186357872} {:answer/id #uuid "0f6fe134-1090-5f97-9ea8-128ddfc3b774" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\text{i}" :db/id 17592186357876} {:answer/id #uuid "c020effb-ac1b-5c1a-b136-a3f990641cda" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\text{i}" :db/id 17592186359435} {:answer/id #uuid "cb7d8484-175b-5e8d-bc3b-f162579d8e47" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\text{i}" :db/id 17592186359541} {:answer/id #uuid "e819a706-cc55-53d4-ad1b-913fba1a9b02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5+3\text{i}" :db/id 17592186359809}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186359541} :answer-field/id #uuid "a14982e8-8062-5f22-9abd-32b12535e617" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360273}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "34140471-4f5c-5a2d-9e46-e76840a3d73f" :question/math-academy-id "q-97193" :question/problem "Given that $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ is the standard Hermitian inner product over $C,$ find $⟨a,\,(4-\text{i})b+c⟩$ if $\,$ $⟨b,a⟩=-1-\text{i}\,$ and $\,⟨a,c⟩=5.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties. - It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have $\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$ - It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have $\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$ - It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have $\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$ - It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have $\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$ First, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ is antilinear in the second argument: $$ \begin{aligned}⟨a,\,(4-\text{i})b+c⟩ & =⟨a,(4-\text{i})b⟩+⟨a,c⟩ \\ & =(\overset{―}{4-\text{i}})⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩ \\ & =(4+\text{i})⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry: $$ \begin{aligned}(4+\text{i})⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c\text{ }⟩ & =(4+\text{i})\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}+⟨a,c⟩\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we substitute the values for $⟨b,a⟩$ and $⟨a,c⟩:$ $$ \begin{aligned}(4+\text{i})\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}+⟨a,c⟩ & =(4+\text{i})\cdot (\overset{―}{-1-\text{i}})+5 \\ & =(4+\text{i})\cdot (-1+\text{i})+5 \\ & =-5+3\text{i}+5 \\ & =3\text{i}\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid "22a3d38c-45ed-5261-9a9f-bdb8efdf26a5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186445241}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0e841129-5370-59a4-a247-981a63a55e7e" Indeed, the inner product in ${C}^{n}$ is linear in the first argument. So, a constant multiple from the first argument can be factored out. - Statement II is true. In this lesson, we will learn about other types of line integral. Suppose that $C$ is a path in the $xy$-plane with initial point $A$ and terminal point $B.$ The line integral of the function $f(x,y)$ **with respect to $\boldsymbol x$** along the path $C$ is denoted $$ \int_C f(x,y)\,\textrm d x. $$ To understand what this integral represents, we imagine traversing $C$ from $A$ to $B.$ At each point $P$ that lies on $C,$ we project the point on $f$ that lies directly above $P$ onto the plane $y=0.$ Doing this for every point on $C$ traces out a curve. The line integral of $f$ with respect to $x$ gives the (signed) area bounded by this curve and the $x$-axis. This integral represents the total area accumulated when [math]f[/math] is projected on the plane [math]y=0[/math] as [math]C[/math] is traversed from the initial point [math]A[/math] to the terminal point [math]B.[/math] ![](images/62/62c07a36cbf79459021ee7be125536a8f9c1bc3c193a99eabfcd3fc851b8eb0c.png) To calculate a line integral with respect to $x,$ we must first parameterize $C$ using a parameter $t\in [a,b].$ Then, we apply the change of variables formula $$ \int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}x = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t. $$ Let's take a look at a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "2f1254b7-43b2-5b19-b5e9-cf33ff6cffe8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5812 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid #uuid "7d157e41-c50b-570b-8b5b-b8a5a0d03163" :topic/math-academy-id 1944} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125649 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125889 :tutorial/content "The **critical points** of a function $f(\mathbf x)$ are the points $\mathbf x = \mathbf a$ in the domain of $f$ such that $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) =\mathbf 0^T$ or $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a)$ does not exist. A critical point such that $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0^T$ is called a **stationary point**. For example, consider the function $f(x,y) = x^2 - 2x + y^2+6y.$ The domain of $f$ is $\mathbb{R}^2,$ and the first partial derivatives of $f$ are $$ \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} = 2x-2, \qquad \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} = 2y+6. $$ So, the first derivative of $f$ is ![](images/9e/9ea3f2d1dd0994be64602aeaffcf5d8424f52daa03844e21e65469f779d9b009.svg) To find the critical points, we need to find the points $(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ such that ![](images/23/23faa4c01362cad11c2ab6ad19045ca44a09460da1c719c8212480f27f21c5b1.svg) or $\boldsymbol f'(x,y)$ does not exist: - Setting $\boldsymbol f'(x,y) = \mathbf{0}^T,$ we obtain the following system: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}2x-2 &=0 \\ 2y+6 &=0\end{aligned}\right. $$ This system has the solution $x=1$ and $y=-3.$ Consequently, $(1,-3)$ is a critical point of $f.$ - $\boldsymbol f'(x,y)$ exists everywhere, so there are no more critical points to be found. Therefore, the only critical point of $f$ is $(1,-3).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "66c2c3d5-6a0a-561b-81c6-ba81419caa61" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7876 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "59e0e71c-41de-59e8-af18-15eaf180ea00" :step/math-academy-id 45414 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125650}} {:db/id 17592186125650 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124653 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124216 :question/id #uuid "593eeb42-56b8-5177-8a9f-38d08a5186c1" :question/math-academy-id "e-12584"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "045854fc-9cad-5005-a306-9550848e25df" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048385} {:db/id 17592186049676} {:db/id 17592186049962}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125004} {:db/id 17592186125006} {:db/id 17592186235545} {:db/id 17592186237887} {:db/id 17592186238078} {:db/id 17592186348429} {:db/id 17592186348435} {:db/id 17592186434984} {:db/id 17592186511482} {:db/id 17592186511496} {:db/id 17592186511526} {:db/id 17592186511549}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Critical Points of a Function"} :step/id #uuid "c1edc476-8e7a-5e8a-83d5-126f47cd2bfb" :step/math-academy-id 45415 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125651}} {:db/id 17592186125651 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125890 :tutorial/content "Recall that, for functions of two variables $f(x,y)$, there are typically three possible types of critical points that can occur: - Local minimum points. For example, the elliptic paraboloid $z = f(x,y) = x^2+y^2$ has a minimum point at $(0,0),$ as shown below. ![](images/14/14e8d23a4bc649257c2f7351e0d2c1d62e39a8cd8eed1467e65853ee121b836e.png) - Local maximum points. For example, the elliptic paraboloid $z = f(x,y) = -x^2-y^2$ has a maximum point at $(0,0),$ as shown below. ![](images/00/008803f43cb2161624f8ef295c70a125b8be64d93184928bd2176a6debaa9f85.png) - Saddle points. For example, the hyperbolic paraboloid $z = f(x,y) = y^2-x^2$ has a saddle point at $(0,0),$ as shown below. ![](images/12/1214b413073ad87a302fb1297cef47208a922e368d680a9f69ec8fb18d9ca8a0.png) Local maximum and local minimum points are analogous to what you would have seen in single-variable calculus. A saddle point occurs when the slopes are zero in all directions, yet it is not a local maximum or minimum. The hyperbolic paraboloid shown above reaches a local maximum at $(0,0)$ along the $xz$-plane, yet this is a local minimum along the $yz$-plane." :tutorial/id #uuid "fe3c5f00-f720-5573-a01f-c37f0a3e447f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7877 :tutorial/title "Classifying Stationary Points"} :step/id #uuid "c5093fcf-6163-5240-9022-125813bd45bf" :step/math-academy-id 45418 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125652}} {:db/id 17592186125652 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125891 :tutorial/content "The **second partial derivatives test** helps to determine whether a stationary point of a function of two variables gives rise to a local maximum, a local minimum, or a saddle point. Suppose that $\mathbf x = \mathbf{a}$ is a critical point of $f(\mathbf x),$ and let $H(\mathbf{a})$ denote the determinant of $\boldsymbol f''(x,y)$ evaluated at $\mathbf{a}$ (recall that $H(\mathbf a)$ is called the *Hessian determinant* of $f$ at $\mathbf a$). The second partial derivative test states the following: - If $H(\mathbf{a}) > 0,$ then: - if $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(\mathbf{a}) < 0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $\mathbf{a},$ and - if $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(\mathbf{a}) > 0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $\mathbf{a}.$ - If $H(\mathbf{a}) < 0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $\mathbf{a}.$ - If $H(\mathbf{a}) = 0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive, and we need to classify the point using some other method. As an example, consider the function $f (x, y) = 3 + 2x^2 - x y + y^2.$ Let's find the critical points of this function and then classify them using the second partial derivatives test. We start by computing the partial derivatives: $$ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 4x -y, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 2y -x $$ The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $\boldsymbol f'(x,y) = \mathbf{0}^T,$ we obtain the following system: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}4x-y &=0 \\ 2y-x &=0,\end{aligned}\right. $$ The solution to this system is $x=0, y=0.$ Hence, $(0,0)$ is the only stationary point. To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test. the determinant $H(0,0),$ we get $$ H(0,0) = \det(\boldsymbol f''(0,0)) = 4 \cdot 2 - (-1)^2 = 7 > 0. $$ Finally, since $H(0,0) > 0$ and $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(0,0) = (\boldsymbol f''(0,0))_{11}= 4 >0,$ the function $f$ has a local minimum at $(0,0).$ In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(0,0).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8248e727-7421-5535-ba58-b5ed98f7ac38" For example, consider the function $f(x,y) = x^2 - 2x + y^2+6y.$ The domain of $f$ is $\mathbb{R}^2,$ and the first partial derivatives of $f$ are $$ \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} = 2x-2, \qquad \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} = 2y+6. $$ So, the first derivative of $f$ is ![](images/9e/9ea3f2d1dd0994be64602aeaffcf5d8424f52daa03844e21e65469f779d9b009.svg) To find the critical points, we need to find the points $(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ such that ![](images/23/23faa4c01362cad11c2ab6ad19045ca44a09460da1c719c8212480f27f21c5b1.svg) or $\boldsymbol f'(x,y)$ does not exist: - Setting $\boldsymbol f'(x,y) = \mathbf{0}^T,$ we obtain the following system: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}2x-2 &=0 \\ 2y+6 &=0\end{aligned}\right. $$ This system has the solution $x=1$ and $y=-3.$ Consequently, $(1,-3)$ is a critical point of $f.$ - $\boldsymbol f'(x,y)$ exists everywhere, so there are no more critical points to be found. As an example, consider the function $f (x, y) = 3 + 2x^2 - x y + y^2.$ Let's find the critical points of this function and then classify them using the second partial derivatives test. We start by computing the partial derivatives: $$ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 4x -y, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 2y -x $$ The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. First, we compute the second partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x-y)=4 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y-x)=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y-x)=-1\end{aligned} $$ So, the second derivative is $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them: - Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ Computing the determinant $H(0,0),$ we get $$ H(0,0) = \det(\boldsymbol f''(0,0)) = 4 \cdot 2 - (-1)^2 = 7 > 0. $$ Finally, since $H(0,0) > 0$ and $\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(0,0) = (\boldsymbol f''(0,0))_{11}= 4 >0,$ the function $f$ has a local minimum at $(0,0).$ In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(0,0).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8248e727-7421-5535-ba58-b5ed98f7ac38" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7878 :tutorial/title "The Second Partial Derivatives Test"} :step/id #uuid "f1821258-7802-571e-a84f-0738986e608c" :step/math-academy-id 45419 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125653}} {:db/id 17592186125891 :tutorial/content "The **second partial derivatives test** helps to determine whether a stationary point of a function of two variables gives rise to a local maximum, a local minimum, or a saddle point. :question/math-academy-id "q-104994" :question/problem "The function $f(x,y)$ has the first derivative $$ {f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4x+2y-6 & 2x+2y\end{aligned}], $$ and has a stationary point at $(3,-3).$ If $H$ denotes the Hessian determinant of $f,$ which of the following statements are true? I. $H(3,-3)>0$ II. $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)<0$ III. The point $(3,-3)$ is a local minimum of $f$" :question/worked-solution "The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following: - If $H(a)>0,$ then: - if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$ - if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$ - If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$ - If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive. First, we notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4x+2y-6 & 2x+2y\end{aligned}],$ we must have $$ \frac{∂f}{∂x}=4x+2y-6,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2x+2y. $$ Now, we compute the second partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x+2y-6)=4 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+2y)=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+2y)=2\end{aligned} $$ So, the second derivative is $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ Evaluating the second derivative at $(3,-3),$ we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(3,-3)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn. - Statement I is true. Indeed, computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(3,-3),$ we get $$ H(3,-3)=det({f}^{″}(3,-3))=4\cdot 2-{2}^{2}=4>0. $$ - Statement II is false. We have $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)=({f}^{″}(3,-3))_{11}=4>0.$ - Statement III is true. Indeed, since $H(3,-3)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)>0,$ the point $(3,-3)$ is a local minimum by the second partial derivative test. Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} :step/id #uuid "11e5811c-fb05-517a-b6a3-b32833e3131b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186520616}} {:db/id 17592186520567 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125083 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1caf69dd-971a-5d35-89cb-d9626dcb78d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(-3,2)$" :db/id 17592186520031} {:answer/id #uuid "23d7c23e-2e7c-57ed-a669-10ce3af13e38" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(1,-2)$" :db/id 17592186520042} {:answer/id #uuid "2c29ee3e-35ef-5627-a600-d2e0619b9541" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(1,-2)$" :db/id 17592186520058} {:answer/id #uuid "4396e4d8-a763-52af-afef-ded9f6e55a26" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local maximum at $(1,-2)$" :db/id 17592186520088} {:answer/id #uuid "fe0c6bef-702a-5967-84e7-559ce04a5279" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local maximum at $(-3,2)$" :db/id 17592186520365}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186520042} :answer-field/id #uuid "40aea253-69a0-5d33-b3f4-8166b4cfbd4b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186123098}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "c1fd6c16-60ce-56fa-b03a-b1f876d9acf4" :question/math-academy-id "q-37590" :question/problem "Find and categorize all local the extrema of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1,$ and determine which of the following statements is true." :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist. The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following: - If $H(a)>0,$ then: - if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$ - if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$ - If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$ - If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive. First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1)\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}2(x+y+1) & 2(x+3y+5)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned} $$ The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+1 &=0 \\ x+3y+5 &=0.\end{aligned}\right. $$ Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get $$ 2y+4=0\,⟹\,y=-2. $$ Then, substituting this into the first equation, we obtain $$ x+(-2)+1=0\,⟹\,x=1. $$ Hence, $(1,-2)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$ To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test. First, we compute the second partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+y+1))=2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+3y+5))=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+y+1))=2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+3y+5))=6\end{aligned} $$ So, the second derivative is $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,-2),$ we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-2)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ Computing the determinant $H(1,-2),$ we get $$ H(1,-2)=det({f}^{″}(1,-2))=2\cdot 6-{2}^{2}=8>0. $$ Finally, notice that $$ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,-2)=({f}^{″}(1,-2))_{11}=2>0. $$ Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(1,-2).$"} :step/id #uuid "6c650994-2746-52bb-b204-a4b55b445bee" :step/next {:db/id 17592186520612}} {:db/id 17592186520605 :step/content {:db/id 17592186434982 :question/math-academy-id "q-81179" :question/problem "Find and categorize all the local extrema of the function $f(x,y)$ given that $$ {f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2(xy-3) & {x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}. $$" :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist. The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following: - If $H(a)>0,$ then: - if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$ - if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$ - If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$ - If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive. First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2(xy-3) & {x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix},$ we must have $$ \frac{∂f}{∂x}=2(xy-3)\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}. $$ The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}xy-3 &=0 \\ {x}^{2}-9{y}^{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right. $$ Solving the first equation for $y,$ we get $$ xy-3=0\,⟹\,y=\frac{3}{x}. $$ Then, substituting this into the second equation, we get $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-9{(\frac{3}{x})}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{81}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ \frac{{x}^{4}-81}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-81 & =0 \\ x & =-3,3.\end{aligned} $$ Back-substituting these values into $y=\frac{3}{x},$ we obtain $$ x=-3\,⟹\,y=\frac{3}{-3}=-1,\,\,x=3\,\,\,\,\,\,⟹\,y=\frac{3}{3}=1. $$ Hence, $(-3,-1)$ and $(3,1)$ are stationary points of $f(x,y).$ To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test. First, we compute the second partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-6)=2y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-9{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-6)=2x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-9{y}^{2})=-18y\end{aligned} $$ So, the second derivative is $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2y & 2x \\ 2x & -18y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them: - Evaluating the second derivative at $(3,1),$ we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(3,1)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 6 & -18\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Computing the determinant $H(3,1),$ we get $$ H(3,1)=det({f}^{″}(3,1))=2\cdot (-18)-{6}^{2}=-72<0, $$ Therefore, $f(3,1)$ is a saddle point. - Evaluating the second derivative at $(-3,-1),$ we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-3,-1)=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -6 \\ -6 & 18\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Computing the determinant $H(-3,-1),$ we get $$ H(-3,-1)=det({f}^{″}(-3,-1))=(-2)\cdot 18-(-6)^{2}=-72<0, $$ Therefore, $f(-3,-1)$ is a saddle point. In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has saddle points at $(3,1)$ and $(-3,-1).$"} :step/id #uuid "d8b6c8ec-acd4-54ce-8211-2be9c4fc4606" :step/next {:db/id 17592186520526}} {:db/id 17592186520612 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125084 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "114d029d-432f-5d2d-a8e0-da4352b9cbe0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(0,0)$ and a local maximum at $(2,2)$" :db/id 17592186520012} {:answer/id #uuid "5e1b31e7-050e-5530-973b-420e7f556047" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(0,0)$ and a local minimum at $(2,2)$" :db/id 17592186520137} {:answer/id #uuid "8a1bf858-df10-5d12-842f-190930cca500" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has saddle points at $(0,0)$ and $(2,2)$" :db/id 17592186520195} {:answer/id #uuid "a61d9d31-5126-5495-bb34-7b540584d0e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(0,0)$ and a saddle point at $(-2,-2)$" :db/id 17592186520217} {:answer/id #uuid "da384a82-fb82-524f-a94b-1ea107ebde1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(0,0)$ and a local maximum at $(-2,-2)$" :db/id 17592186520300}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186520137} :answer-field/id #uuid "d3b332ce-1536-5642-87d8-20b5ef880b58" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186123104}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e71f4d1b-7ab2-518d-aa98-4d69ed0f6542" :question/math-academy-id "q-37592" :question/problem "Find and categorize all the local extrema of the function $f(x,y)$ given that $$ {f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y & 3{y}^{2}-6x\end{aligned}]. $$" :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist. The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following: - If $H(a)>0,$ then: - if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$ - if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$ - If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$ - If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive. First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y & 3{y}^{2}-6x\end{aligned}],$ we must have $$ \frac{∂f}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}-6y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{y}^{2}-6x. $$ The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y &=0 \\ 3{y}^{2}-6x &=0.\end{aligned}\right. $$ Solving the first equation for $y,$ we get $$ 3{x}^{2}-6y=0\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}. $$ Then, substituting this into the second equation, we get $$ \begin{aligned}3{(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})}^{2}-6x & =0 \\ \frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}-2x & =0 \\ {x}^{4}-8x & =0 \\ x({x}^{3}-8) & =0 \\ x & =0,2.\end{aligned} $$ Back-substituting these values into $y=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2},$ we obtain $$ x=0\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}=0,\,\,x=2\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2}(2)^{2}=2. $$ Hence, $(0,0)$ and $(2,2)$ are stationary points of $f(x,y).$ To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist. The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following: - If $H(a)>0,$ then: - if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$ - if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$ - If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$ - If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive. First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1)\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}2(x+y+1) & 2(x+3y+5)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned} $$ The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+1 &=0 \\ x+3y+5 &=0.\end{aligned}\right. $$ Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get $$ 2y+4=0\,⟹\,y=-2. $$ Then, substituting this into the first equation, we obtain $$ x+(-2)+1=0\,⟹\,x=1. $$ Hence, $(1,-2)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$ To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test. First, we compute the second partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+y+1))=2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+3y+5))=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+y+1))=2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+3y+5))=6\end{aligned} $$ So, the second derivative is $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,-2),$ we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-2)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ Computing the determinant $H(1,-2),$ we get $$ H(1,-2)=det({f}^{″}(1,-2))=2\cdot 6-{2}^{2}=8>0. $$ Finally, notice that $$ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,-2)=({f}^{″}(1,-2))_{11}=2>0. $$ Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(1,-2).$"} :step/id #uuid "6c650994-2746-52bb-b204-a4b55b445bee" :step/next {:db/id 17592186520612}} {:db/id 17592186520526 :step/content {:db/id 17592186520472 :question/math-academy-id "q-37592" :question/problem "Find and categorize all the local extrema of the function $f(x,y)$ given that $$ {f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y & 3{y}^{2}-6x\end{aligned}]. $$" :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist. The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following: - If $H(a)>0,$ then: - if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$ - if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$ - If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$ - If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive. First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y & 3{y}^{2}-6x\end{aligned}],$ we must have $$ \frac{∂f}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}-6y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{y}^{2}-6x. $$ The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y &=0 \\ 3{y}^{2}-6x &=0.\end{aligned}\right. $$ Solving the first equation for $y,$ we get $$ 3{x}^{2}-6y=0\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}. $$ Then, substituting this into the second equation, we get $$ \begin{aligned}3{(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})}^{2}-6x & =0 \\ \frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}-2x & =0 \\ {x}^{4}-8x & =0 \\ x({x}^{3}-8) & =0 \\ x & =0,2.\end{aligned} $$ Back-substituting these values into $y=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2},$ we obtain $$ x=0\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}=0,\,\,x=2\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2}(2)^{2}=2. $$ Hence, $(0,0)$ and $(2,2)$ are stationary points of $f(x,y).$ To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test. First, we compute the second partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-6y)=6x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{y}^{2}-6x)=-6 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}-6y)=-6\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{y}^{2}-6x)=6y\end{aligned} $$ So, the second derivative is $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6x & -6 \\ -6 & 6y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them: - Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ -6 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ Computing the determinant $H(0,0),$ we get $$ H(0,0)=det({f}^{″}(0,0))=0\cdot 0-(-6)^{2}=-36<0. $$ Therefore, $f(0,0)$ is a saddle point. - Evaluating the second derivative at $(2,2),$ we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(2,2)=[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 \\ -6 & 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ Computing the determinant $H(2,2),$ we get $$ H(2,2)=det({f}^{″}(2,2))=12\cdot 12-(-6)^{2}=108>0. $$ Finally, since $H(2,2)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(2,2)=({f}^{″}(2,2))_{11}=12>0,$ the function $f$ has a local minimum at $(2,2).$ In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(0,0)$ and a local minimum at $(2,2).$"} :step/id #uuid "e28c95c3-e780-5712-a484-551662e9b69b" :step/next categorize all the local extrema of the function $f(x,y)$ given that $$ {f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2(xy-3) & {x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}. $$" :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist. The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following: - If $H(a)>0,$ then: - if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$ - if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$ - If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$ - If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive. First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2(xy-3) & {x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix},$ we must have $$ \frac{∂f}{∂x}=2(xy-3)\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}. $$ The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}xy-3 &=0 \\ {x}^{2}-9{y}^{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right. $$ Solving the first equation for $y,$ we get $$ xy-3=0\,⟹\,y=\frac{3}{x}. $$ Then, substituting this into the second equation, we get $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-9{(\frac{3}{x})}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{81}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ \frac{{x}^{4}-81}{{x}^{2}} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-81 & =0 \\ x & =-3,3.\end{aligned} $$ Back-substituting these values into $y=\frac{3}{x},$ we obtain $$ x=-3\,⟹\,y=\frac{3}{-3}=-1,\,\,x=3\,\,\,\,\,\,⟹\,y=\frac{3}{3}=1. $$ Hence, $(-3,-1)$ and $(3,1)$ are stationary points of $f(x,y).$ To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test. First, we compute the second partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-6)=2y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-9{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-6)=2x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-9{y}^{2})=-18y\end{aligned} $$ So, the second derivative is $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2y & 2x \\ 2x & -18y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them: - Evaluating the second derivative at $(3,1),$ we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(3,1)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 6 & -18\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Computing the determinant $H(3,1),$ we get $$ H(3,1)=det({f}^{″}(3,1))=2\cdot (-18)-{6}^{2}=-72<0, $$ Therefore, $f(3,1)$ is a saddle point. - Evaluating the second derivative at $(-3,-1),$ we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-3,-1)=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -6 \\ -6 & 18\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Computing the determinant $H(-3,-1),$ we get $$ H(-3,-1)=det({f}^{″}(-3,-1))=(-2)\cdot 18-(-6)^{2}=-72<0, $$ Therefore, $f(-3,-1)$ is a saddle point. In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has saddle points at $(3,1)$ and $(-3,-1).$"} :step/id #uuid "d8b6c8ec-acd4-54ce-8211-2be9c4fc4606" :step/next {:db/id 17592186520526}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id 17592186167934 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168044 :tutorial/content "In the earlier topics, we saw that *symmetry* can force many Fourier coefficients to be zero automatically. In particular, if a $2\pi$-periodic function is *even*, then its Fourier series has *cosine terms only*. A **Fourier cosine series** uses this idea when a function is initially given only on the half-interval $[0,\pi),$ but we want a full Fourier series on $[-\pi,\pi)$ (and then a $2\pi$-periodic extension to all real $x$). 17592186180341 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180787 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathbf F$ be a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ and $C$ be a *closed* curve in the $xy$-plane. Imagine that $\mathbf F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water, and $C$ is a curve that allows water to flow through it (like a fishing net). The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol C$** is a scalar number that tells us how much water is escaping the region bounded by $C.$ We have three possible scenarios: - If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*. ![](images/6f/6ff4d006d3fbf4a434f35a13c8591fc166ff6c74adf2b7969752b7541e486df2.png) - If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*. ![](images/38/3812148e855a84e3233316acc8bbf59bd7cd802a874c9e4807c6efd7ca6754cf.png) - If the net flow through $C$ is zero, the flux equals zero. The following vector field has zero flux across $C$ because the amount of water flowing in through $C$ equals the amount of water flowing out through $C.$ ![](images/56/56aef4f217e9981755826745a97e8389d86b49518ffd7d3ebc75e5ee2dc28f8b.png) The following two vector fields also have a zero flux across $C$ because the water flow is tangential to $C$ at every point along $C.$ ![](images/63/637677324152af3d428e405c89025f35dbe5d71e2e8f0a0797ef3aca30bae7e1.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "ecd8591f-8e5b-50b2-91a1-4f15bd97b2c2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9521 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1e80fc64-e097-5e8d-a35c-056416216619" :step/math-academy-id 184955 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180342}} {:db/id 17592186180342 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180788 :tutorial/content "If $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by the line integral $$ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s, $$ where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ The symbol $\oint\limits$ means integration over the closed curve. It's helpful to spend some time understanding where this definition comes from, so let's derive it using the closed curve $C$ below. ![](images/6d/6dfe8a071798c93f19507808596b7d32af90367b2666643d092a7c50afe5e929.png) First, we pick a point $P$ on $C.$ At this point, we draw the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the outward-pointing normal vector $\mathbf n$ to $C.$ ![](images/49/498e1afbaac8bc8297213eae09cc8bf8742b29f45dda1dfafff868c67ebb9de9.png) We wish to calculate the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P.$ Now, $\mathbf F$ is made up of two components: - a component parallel to $\mathbf n,$ which contributes to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ and - a component perpendicular to $\mathbf n,$ which does *not* contribute to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$ We're only interested in the contribution made to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$ This is given by the scalar projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n.$ ![](images/ac/ac3aae49f372908f2f9aeb53e3fc98bff117846fca05a8c696009e443390811c.png) Therefore, the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P$ is given by $$ \begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{n}F & =\frac{F\cdot n}{||n||}=F\cdot n.\end{aligned} $$ The expression above represents the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at a single point only. Therefore, to calculate the total net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ we sum (integrate) this expression over the entire curve. This gives $$ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s. $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a328d4d8-bfe8-50eb-8bbd-281b3bb07afe" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9522 :tutorial/title "Constructing an Integral Formula for the Flux"} :step/id #uuid "9dac0bb5-3a03-56c0-a614-dc9f045cb3e3" :step/math-academy-id 184956 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180343}} {:db/id 17592186180343 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180789 :tutorial/content "Consider the circle $S$ and vector field $\mathbf F$ below. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. ![](images/e6/e679efaa2612d45bbfe8b918de7148853b64eaf530af34a525ef1735e0946b09.png) By drawing an outward-pointing unit normal vector, it's clear that there is a net flow *out* through $C.$ ![](images/fb/fbcd6fd0fadcc955212a145de9edb4654ddb92ddebb8ba31eb775cff676efeeb.png) Therefore, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is positive, and we have $$ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s > 0. $$ When measuring flux through a closed curve, the curve's orientation does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same in either case. ![](images/a3/a3d398d382e6bc94ddde77e650d50a6b5ec050083f89f64104f6f2fd172a9239.png) So, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $-C$ is also positive, and we have $$ \oint\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s > 0. $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "36b855d8-9994-5c22-bbc4-e28065875f84" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9523 :tutorial/title 17592186180345}} {:db/id 17592186180345 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180790 :tutorial/content "To calculate the flux of a vector field over a smooth, closed curve, we can use the formula $$ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s. $$ If $C=C_1\cup C_2 \cup \cdots \cup C_n$ is piecewise smooth, we have to calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over each smooth face. That is, $$ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \cdots + \int\limits_{C_n} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s, $$ where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ on $C_i.$ As an example, let's consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf i + (y-x)^3\,\mathbf j$ and the rectangle $C$ shown below. ![](images/5c/5cbd62feddcce7a676a76117de09154da21abdd8b039c0e45a7a0e7d5fb00e9c.png) To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C,$ we sum the fluxes of $\mathbf F$ over each side: $$ \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s $$ To demonstrate how to compute these integrals, let's construct the flux integral across the side $C_4,$ given by $$ \int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s. $$ The side $C_4$ and its outward-pointing unit normal are shown below. ![](images/06/06fd5a2ecbd709e8e835f2a57ef3ada772526366d51e5e16474d9b8635500e8e.png) Since this side is perpendicular to the $y$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have $$ \mathbf n = -\mathbf j. $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i+(y-x)^{3}\,j)\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\ & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i)\cdot (-j)+((y-x)^{3}\,j))\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\ & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}0-(y-x)^{3}\,\text{d}s \\ & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(x-y)^{3}\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned} $$ Following a similar procedure for the other sides, we can construct the full expression for the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "472c362c-27a5-5041-90c3-4533c63b736d" 17592186180791 :tutorial/content "Calculating the flux of a vector field across a rectangle or square requires computing four flux integrals. However, we can often simplify our calculations if the vector field displays symmetry. To demonstrate, consider the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ and a square $C$ with side length $6$ centered at $O,$ as shown below. Let's calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$ ![](images/8e/8e1767b9bea45e742df4953f0ec50b2d43c9622994035342307dc2be6abba8de.png) If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by $$ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s, $$ where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have $$ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s, $$ where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below. ![](images/65/65a8c37c64580f7d1f41f32722f20dfee2b8fd98333920a0feae781ea8d9541e.png) Since the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ is parallel to $C_2$ and $C_4,$ there is zero net flow through these two sides. Therefore, $$ \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s = 0. $$ This is easy to verify, since, $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}-5\,i\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\ & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}0\,\text{d}s \\ & =0\end{aligned} $$ and similarly for the integral along $C_4.$ So, our expression for the flux reduces to $$ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s. $$ Since the vector field is uniform, the net inflow through $C_1$ will cancel with the net outflow through $C_3.$ That is $$ \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s = -\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s +\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s =0. $$ Therefore, we conclude that $$ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0. $$" :tutorial/id #uuid The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol C$** is a scalar number that tells us how much water is escaping the region bounded by $C.$ We have three possible scenarios: - If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*. ![](images/6f/6ff4d006d3fbf4a434f35a13c8591fc166ff6c74adf2b7969752b7541e486df2.png) - If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*. ![](images/38/3812148e855a84e3233316acc8bbf59bd7cd802a874c9e4807c6efd7ca6754cf.png) - If the net flow through $C$ is zero, the flux equals zero. The following vector field has zero flux across $C$ because the amount of water flowing in through $C$ equals the amount of water flowing out through $C.$ ![](images/56/56aef4f217e9981755826745a97e8389d86b49518ffd7d3ebc75e5ee2dc28f8b.png) The following two vector fields also have a zero flux across $C$ because the water flow is tangential to $C$ at every point along $C.$ ![](images/63/637677324152af3d428e405c89025f35dbe5d71e2e8f0a0797ef3aca30bae7e1.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "ecd8591f-8e5b-50b2-91a1-4f15bd97b2c2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9521 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1e80fc64-e097-5e8d-a35c-056416216619" :step/math-academy-id 184955 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180342}} {:db/id 17592186180787 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathbf F$ be a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ and $C$ be a *closed* curve in the $xy$-plane. It's helpful to spend some time understanding where this definition comes from, so let's derive it using the closed curve $C$ below. ![](images/6d/6dfe8a071798c93f19507808596b7d32af90367b2666643d092a7c50afe5e929.png) First, we pick a point $P$ on $C.$ At this point, we draw the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the outward-pointing normal vector $\mathbf n$ to $C.$ ![](images/49/498e1afbaac8bc8297213eae09cc8bf8742b29f45dda1dfafff868c67ebb9de9.png) We wish to calculate the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P.$ Now, $\mathbf F$ is made up of two components: - a component parallel to $\mathbf n,$ which contributes to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ and - a component perpendicular to $\mathbf n,$ which does *not* contribute to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$ We're only interested in the contribution made to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$ This is given by the scalar projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n.$ ![](images/ac/ac3aae49f372908f2f9aeb53e3fc98bff117846fca05a8c696009e443390811c.png) Therefore, the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P$ is given by $$ \begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{n}F & =\frac{F\cdot n}{||n||}=F\cdot n.\end{aligned} $$ The expression above represents the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at a single point only. Therefore, to calculate the total net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ we sum (integrate) this expression over the entire curve. #uuid "4f8760a0-8c8e-5ec6-9492-0ecc32789da6" :step/math-academy-id 184958 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180345}} {:db/id 17592186180345 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180790 :tutorial/content "To calculate the flux of a vector field over a smooth, closed curve, we can use the formula $$ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s. $$ If $C=C_1\cup C_2 \cup \cdots \cup C_n$ is piecewise smooth, we have to calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over each smooth face. That is, $$ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \cdots + \int\limits_{C_n} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s, $$ where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ on $C_i.$ As an example, let's consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf i + (y-x)^3\,\mathbf j$ and the rectangle $C$ shown below. ![](images/5c/5cbd62feddcce7a676a76117de09154da21abdd8b039c0e45a7a0e7d5fb00e9c.png) To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C,$ we sum the fluxes of $\mathbf F$ over each side: $$ \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s $$ To demonstrate how to compute these integrals, let's construct the flux integral across the side $C_4,$ given by $$ \int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s. $$ The side $C_4$ and its outward-pointing unit normal are shown below. ![](images/06/06fd5a2ecbd709e8e835f2a57ef3ada772526366d51e5e16474d9b8635500e8e.png) Since this side is perpendicular to the $y$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have $$ \mathbf n = -\mathbf j. $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i+(y-x)^{3}\,j)\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\ & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i)\cdot (-j)+((y-x)^{3}\,j))\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\ & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}0-(y-x)^{3}\,\text{d}s \\ & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(x-y)^{3}\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned} $$ Following a similar procedure for the other sides, we can construct the full expression for the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "472c362c-27a5-5041-90c3-4533c63b736d" {:db/id 17592186180347}} {:db/id 17592186180347 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180791 :tutorial/content "Calculating the flux of a vector field across a rectangle or square requires computing four flux integrals. However, we can often simplify our calculations if the vector field displays symmetry. To demonstrate, consider the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ and a square $C$ with side length $6$ centered at $O,$ as shown below. Let's calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$ ![](images/8e/8e1767b9bea45e742df4953f0ec50b2d43c9622994035342307dc2be6abba8de.png) If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by $$ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s, $$ where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have $$ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s, $$ where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below. ![](images/65/65a8c37c64580f7d1f41f32722f20dfee2b8fd98333920a0feae781ea8d9541e.png) Since the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ is parallel to $C_2$ and $C_4,$ there is zero net flow through these two sides. Therefore, $$ \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s = 0. $$ This is easy to verify, since, $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}-5\,i\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\ & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}0\,\text{d}s \\ & =0\end{aligned} $$ and similarly for the integral along $C_4.$ So, our expression for the flux reduces to $$ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s. $$ Since the vector field is uniform, the net inflow through $C_1$ will cancel with the net outflow through $C_3.$ That is $$ \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s = -\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s +\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s =0. $$ Therefore, we conclude that $$ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0. $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "53e768e4-a3bb-5b89-83b9-a97e9ff4a921" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9525 :tutorial/title "Using Symmetry to Simplify Flux Calculations"} :step/id #uuid "5c82115b-5b07-5765-b4a2-64382478cffb" :step/math-academy-id 184965 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180348}} {:db/id 17592186180791 :tutorial/content "Calculating the flux of a vector field across a rectangle or square requires computing four flux integrals. We call the larger eigenvalue (the one that is more positive, or less negative) the **dominant eigenvalue**. Again, we are considering a decoupled linear system ![](images/e1/e1efdd0b8c037c01450042384ce3bac663d0b549fa9557d0db09b692754cab0f.svg) Recall that a homogeneous linear system has a single equilibrium point at the origin $(0,0).$ To classify this equilibrium, we look at the signs of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2.$ First of all, the coordinate axes are straight-line solutions: - On the $x$-axis, we have $y(t)= 0$ and $x(t)=c_1e^{\lambda_1 t}$. - If $\lambda_1<0,$ the $x$-axis is a *stable* line. - If $\lambda_1>0,$ the $x$-axis is an *unstable* line. - On the $y$-axis, we have $x(t)=0$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{\lambda_2 t}.$ - If $\lambda_2<0,$ the $y$-axis is a *stable* line. - If $\lambda_2>0,$ the $y$-axis is an *unstable* line. As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following: - *Unstable node (source)* if $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2>0.$ - *Stable node (sink)* if $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2<0.$ In fact, it's asymptotically stable, as the trajectories converge to the origin. - *Saddle point* if $\lambda_1\lambda_2<0$ (one positive, one negative). Let's see some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "6fd81402-072b-5676-9cac-f53af20f3174" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14462 :tutorial/title "Classification of Equilibria"} :step/id #uuid "b8abcadd-58fc-5f3e-a1a9-f6f32aaa7405" :step/math-academy-id 588125 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167851}} {:db/id 17592186167851 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166915 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166540 :question/id #uuid "4926ad20-fc6b-5a7d-80ee-aa39421c174d" :question/math-academy-id "e-21607"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "24bd917d-c4b3-5bf5-9426-a87a579b03c1" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048990}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167200} {:db/id 17592186167236} {:db/id 17592186308409} {:db/id 17592186308410} {:db/id 17592186308411} {:db/id 17592186391158} {:db/id 17592186391169} {:db/id 17592186420019} {:db/id 17592186420021} {:db/id 17592186420025} {:db/id 17592186444147}] :knowledge-point/title "Classifying Decoupled Systems of Linear Differential Equations"} :step/id #uuid "6cadc020-1f0c-5e3d-88b7-c3977e63cc74" :step/math-academy-id 588126} {:db/id 17592186167852 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168020 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a decoupled system $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}\right. $$ where $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2<0$ (the opposite case, where $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2>0,$ is similar). Let's now determine the behavior along the axes. - The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form ![](images/4d/4dc3aaf0f7dfd85070df84c13abe2cf02d85a704167569b3d3a76f2b58178c5b.svg) Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin. This is called an **unstable axis**. - The straight-line solutions on the $y$-axis have the form ![](images/76/76f6b9bbcdff2c87295fb0cd14dbdbbaa5e6c75eeb49c1cc158a4e8bd3da059d.svg) Since $\lambda_2<0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_2 t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $y$-axis move *toward* the origin. Let's now determine the behavior along the axes. - The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form ![](images/4d/4dc3aaf0f7dfd85070df84c13abe2cf02d85a704167569b3d3a76f2b58178c5b.svg) Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin. This is called an **unstable axis**. - The straight-line solutions on the $y$-axis have the form ![](images/76/76f6b9bbcdff2c87295fb0cd14dbdbbaa5e6c75eeb49c1cc158a4e8bd3da059d.svg) Since $\lambda_2<0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_2 t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $y$-axis move *toward* the origin. This is called a **stable axis**. Because one axis is stable and the other is unstable, the origin (equilibrium point) is called a **saddle point**. In the phase portrait, we draw - arrows on the $x$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin), while - arrows on the $y$-axis pointing *inward* (toward the origin). Again, we are considering a decoupled linear system ![](images/e1/e1efdd0b8c037c01450042384ce3bac663d0b549fa9557d0db09b692754cab0f.svg) Recall that a homogeneous linear system has a single equilibrium point at the origin $(0,0).$ To classify this equilibrium, we look at the signs of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2.$ First of all, the coordinate axes are straight-line solutions: - On the $x$-axis, we have $y(t)= 0$ and $x(t)=c_1e^{\lambda_1 t}$. - If $\lambda_1<0,$ the $x$-axis is a *stable* line. - If $\lambda_1>0,$ the $x$-axis is an *unstable* line. - On the $y$-axis, we have $x(t)=0$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{\lambda_2 t}.$ - If $\lambda_2<0,$ the $y$-axis is a *stable* line. - If $\lambda_2>0,$ the $y$-axis is an *unstable* line. As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following: - *Unstable node (source)* if $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2>0.$ - *Stable node (sink)* if $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2<0.$ In fact, it's asymptotically stable, as the trajectories converge to the origin. - *Saddle point* if $\lambda_1\lambda_2<0$ (one positive, one negative). Let's now determine the behavior along the axes. - The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form ![](images/4d/4dc3aaf0f7dfd85070df84c13abe2cf02d85a704167569b3d3a76f2b58178c5b.svg) Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin. This is called an **unstable axis**. - The straight-line solutions on the $y$-axis have the form ![](images/76/76f6b9bbcdff2c87295fb0cd14dbdbbaa5e6c75eeb49c1cc158a4e8bd3da059d.svg) Since $\lambda_2<0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_2 t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $y$-axis move *toward* the origin. This is called a **stable axis**. Because one axis is stable and the other is unstable, the origin (equilibrium point) is called a **saddle point**. In the phase portrait, we draw - arrows on the $x$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin), while - arrows on the $y$-axis pointing *inward* (toward the origin). A typical trajectory bends from the stable direction and then peels away along the unstable direction. ![](images/f2/f2538a59050e604d85fd9726e688cfbd2a5c9bdff4d15dd5ed465ed04f7290b4.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "8fe29b2e-2a4a-5a2d-aaea-49ed3c5a7c1c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14565 :tutorial/title "One Positive and One Negative Eigenvalue"} {:db/id 17592186168057 :tutorial/content "Let's analyze the case where the origin is a source, with ![](images/b8/b89d2dea375e40cafca8a025742ea1ba94b01ff3dd5926dc21b62444847e237f.svg) For a decoupled system with solutions ![](images/6b/6b0666459fb6515324b663cc73f0e9327d845f40fd7772aa8850a4f14b55239d.svg) and ![](images/e7/e78f66d899f375fcf9894ab58968f92123556325139411dd278712df59c7e0ce.svg) trajectories move away from the origin as ![](images/e5/e54727d514ed264e6dd30c7f4044746e6d2b4b462dc3776daecf7eb68634c358.svg) - "![](images/aa/aaeba63f6237121fe226eb30e5378d3e93129bb2782b9c8acb8d73ac719676b3.png) Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above. Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?" :question/worked-solution "Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have $$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{bmatrix}x(t) $$ where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$ Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form $$ {c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}. $$ Now, notice that: - The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form ${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$ - The tangents along the $y$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form ${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$ Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-y(t)\end{aligned}\right. $$"} :step/id #uuid Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following: - Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form ${c}_{1}{e}^{5t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ lie on the $x$-axis and move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line. - Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form ${c}_{2}{e}^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ lie on the $y$-axis and also move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line. Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{an unstable node (source)}.$ **Note:** The phase portrait of the system looks as follows: These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form $$ {c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}. $$ Now, notice that: - The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form ${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$ - The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form ${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ must also approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}>0.$ Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}>0$ is the following: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=4y(t)\end{aligned}\right. $$"} :step/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186199396}} {:db/id 17592186199393 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199515 :tutorial/content "If $A$ is the matrix corresponding to the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ then: - The maximum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}$ of $A,$ and the maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}.$ - The minimum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{min}}$ of $A,$ and the minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{min}}.$ We'll prove this result at the end of the lesson. Suppose we're given that the maximum value of the quadratic form $$ Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-10\: \! x_1x_2+x_2^2 $$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1$ is $6.$ Let's use this to find a unit vector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}$ where this maximum value is attained. So first, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form: ![](images/a6/a6165f41eb43e8f6e8fd4399f1c428f73481de9d4b5ec41293f3ec0e4f062fc6.svg) Next, we find the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}=6{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}A-6I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -5 \\ -5 & 1\end{bmatrix}-6\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-5 & -5 \\ -5 & -5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$ Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](images/30/30699c4f0abcb099a6f7a76cbd76674757c3f7de313e034d0870d1fce27fdd8c.svg) Finally, dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get ![](images/ef/ef14ea5facf5010b99721cf915f44162dfa52e089508fb78c2d02d9aad66f1a4.svg) Let's check that this is indeed the vector we were looking for: $$ \begin{aligned}Q({u}_{\text{max}}) & ={(\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}-10(\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}})(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})+{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{10}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\ & =6\,✓\end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c50ae6a7-1f29-5274-bd82-d2d8acfef6b7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7954 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id
