:step/math-academy-id 45757 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199404}} {:db/id 17592186199396 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199516 :tutorial/content "Suppose we're given that the maximum value of the quadratic form $$ Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-2x_1x_2+x_2^2, $$ over the ellipse $4x_1^2+x_2^2=4$ equals $5.$ How can we find a vector $\mathbf{x}$ at which this maximum is attained? We can find this vector by applying a suitable change of variable. This change of variable should transform our problem into one where we need to maximize a related quadratic form $Q'$ on the unit circle. Let's see how this is done. First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form: ![](images/7b/7b1fd813963e16887c57d6c10be1bfe288e3209fd3a02ca6e6236b7261feb7b1.svg) Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows: $$ {x_1^2}+ \dfrac{x_2^2}{2^2}=1 $$ which represents an ellipse with semiaxes $a=1$ (along the $x_1$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the $x_2$-axis). If we introduce new variables $$ y_1={x_1}, \qquad y_2 = \dfrac{x_2}{2}, $$ the equation of the ellipse will transform into $y_1^2+y_2^2 = 1,$ or $\|\mathbf{y}\|=1.$ So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix ![](images/80/80f8e821a60b63dde0f314460adfd31faca5d82315243fb2a3ebdec75bc61538.svg) we obtain that $\mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y}.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get $$ Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = (P\mathbf{y})^T A \, (P\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{y}^T \! (P^TAP) \mathbf{y}=Q'(\mathbf{y}). $$ As a result, since $P^T=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in the new coordinates is $$ \begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\ & =PAP \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, the goal is to maximize $Q'(\mathbf{y})$ when $\| \mathbf{y} \|=1,$ which we do using our usual methods. Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $5,$ we have $$ \max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{y} \|=1 \} = \lambda_{\max} = 5. $$ Next, we find the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}=5{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}B-5I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$ Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-5I)\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](images/4b/4b51afece6e21c2fe073a5346557f42f9f03ae3400407d18ed6af3af8f32e310.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-2x_1x_2+x_2^2, $$ over the ellipse $4x_1^2+x_2^2=4$ equals $5.$ How can we find a vector $\mathbf{x}$ at which this maximum is attained? We can find this vector by applying a suitable change of variable. This change of variable should transform our problem into one where we need to maximize a related quadratic form $Q'$ on the unit circle. Let's see how this is done. First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form: ![](images/7b/7b1fd813963e16887c57d6c10be1bfe288e3209fd3a02ca6e6236b7261feb7b1.svg) Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows: $$ {x_1^2}+ \dfrac{x_2^2}{2^2}=1 $$ which represents an ellipse with semiaxes $a=1$ (along the $x_1$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the $x_2$-axis). If we introduce new variables $$ y_1={x_1}, \qquad y_2 = \dfrac{x_2}{2}, $$ the equation of the ellipse will transform into $y_1^2+y_2^2 = 1,$ or $\|\mathbf{y}\|=1.$ So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix ![](images/80/80f8e821a60b63dde0f314460adfd31faca5d82315243fb2a3ebdec75bc61538.svg) we obtain that $\mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y}.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get $$ Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = (P\mathbf{y})^T A \, (P\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{y}^T \! (P^TAP) \mathbf{y}=Q'(\mathbf{y}). $$ As a result, since $P^T=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in the new coordinates is $$ \begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\ & =PAP \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, the goal is to maximize $Q'(\mathbf{y})$ when $\| \mathbf{y} \|=1,$ which we do using our usual methods. Without loss of generality, we can assume that the eigenvalues are $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n,$ where $\lambda_{\textrm{max}} = \lambda_1.$ - The columns $\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_n$ of $P$ form an orthonormal set of unit eigenvectors of $A.$ So, $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}} = \mathbf{u}_1.$ Take $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y.$ Since, $P$ is orthonormal, we have $$ \|\mathbf x\| = \|P \mathbf y \| = \|\mathbf y\| $$ and $$ Q(\mathbf x) = \mathbf x^T\!A\mathbf x = (P\mathbf y)^T\!A(P\mathbf y) = \mathbf{y}^T (P^T\!AP) \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}^T D \mathbf{y} $$ for all $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$ Therefore, we can conclude the following: - $\|\mathbf x\| =1 \Longleftrightarrow \|\mathbf y\| =1$ for all $\mathbf y$ such that $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y$ - Restricted to the unit sphere of $\Bbb R^n,$ the images of the quadratic forms $Q(\mathbf x)$ and $Q'(\mathbf y)= \mathbf y^T D\mathbf y$ coincide: $$ \{\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x: \: \: \|\mathbf x\|=1\}= \{\mathbf y^TD\mathbf y: \: \: \|\mathbf y\|=1\} \subset \mathbb R $$ Now, for any unit vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={Q}^{′}(y) \\ & ={\lambda }_{1}{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{2}{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{n}{y}_{n}^{2} \\ & \le {\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{n}^{2} \\ & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{y}_{n}^{2}) \\ & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,‖y{‖}^{2} \\ & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have that that $$ M = \max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{y} \| = 1 \} \le \lambda_{\textrm{max}}. $$ On the other hand, if we take ![](images/53/53a051ea36059c9222e717c65adc6531bc313c9807d44a39b262433acfdcbc5c.svg) then $Q(P\mathbf{e}_1) = Q'(\mathbf{e}_1) = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ So, we conclude that $M = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ Finally, since $\mathbf{u}_1 = P\mathbf{e}_1$ we have that $Q(\mathbf u_1) = \mathbf e_1^T D \mathbf e_1 = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ Therefore, the maximum value is attained at "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form: $$ A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} $$ Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows: $$ \frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1 $$ This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables $\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$ the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$ So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix $$ P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}, $$ we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get $$ Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y). $$ As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is $$ \begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\ & =PAP \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have $$ max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25. $$ Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$ $$ \begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$ Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get $$ {u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}. $$ Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate system using the change-of-coordinates matrix: $$ \begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid "3781c4aa-7e7b-5b51-9af4-d354711b0091"} {:db/id 17592186410201 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form: $$ A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix} $$ Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows: $$ \frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1 $$ This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables $\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$ So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix $$ P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}, $$ we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get $$ Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y). $$ As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is $$ \begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\ & =PAP \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have $$ max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20. $$ Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$ $$ \begin{aligned}B-20I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}-20\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$ Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get $$ {u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}. $$ Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate system using the change-of-coordinates matrix: $$ \begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid "80ab5b9e-fd44-5cd4-b555-7638c14ed974" :step/next {:db/id 17592186410200}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-1.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: - The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$ $$ max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}} $$ The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$ - The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$ $$ min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}} $$ The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$ First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form: $$ A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} $$ Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-1:$ $$ \begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}-(-1)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 $v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get $$ {u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}. the matrix of our quadratic form: $$ A=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 8 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix} $$ Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows: $$ \frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1 $$ This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables $\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$ So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix $$ P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}, $$ we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get $$ Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y). $$ As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is $$ \begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\ & =PAP \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 8 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 16 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}-12 & 16 \\ 16 & 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following: $$ \begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-12-\lambda & 16 \\ 16 & 12-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-12-\lambda )(12-\lambda )-256 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-400 & =0 \\ (\lambda -20)(\lambda +20) & =0 \\ \lambda & =20,\,-20\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we have $$ max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20. $$"} :question/math-academy-id "q-170514" :question/problem "The minimum value of $Q(x)=8{x}_{1}^{2}-30{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-50{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+25{x}_{2}^{2}=100,$ is $-250.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form: $$ A=\begin{bmatrix}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{bmatrix} $$ Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows: $$ \frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1 $$ This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=5$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables $\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{5}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$ the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$ So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix $$ P=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}, $$ we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get $$ Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y). $$ As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is $$ \begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\ & =PAP \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}40 & -75 \\ -30 & -100\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-250,$ we have $$ min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-250. $$ Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-250:$ $$ \begin{aligned}B-(-250I) & =\begin{bmatrix}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{bmatrix}+250\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}450 & -150 \\ -150 & 50\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$ Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-250I))y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get $$ {u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}. $$ Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate system using the change-of-coordinates matrix: $$ \begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid "8691c397-86b9-56c4-bc27-77cec1d7f354" :step/next {:db/id 17592186422486}} {:db/id 17592186422490 :step/content :question/math-academy-id "q-170514" :question/problem "The minimum value of $Q(x)=8{x}_{1}^{2}-30{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-50{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+25{x}_{2}^{2}=100,$ is $-250.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form: $$ A=\begin{bmatrix}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{bmatrix} $$ Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows: $$ \frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1 $$ This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=5$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables $\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{5}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$ the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$ So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix $$ P=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}, $$ we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get $$ Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y). $$ As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is $$ \begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\ & =PAP \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}40 & -75 \\ -30 & -100\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-250,$ we have $$ min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-250. $$ Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-250:$ $$ \begin{aligned}B-(-250I) & =\begin{bmatrix}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{bmatrix}+250\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}450 & -150 \\ -150 & 50\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$ Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-250I))y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get $$ {u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}. $$ Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate system using the change-of-coordinates matrix: $$ \begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid "8691c397-86b9-56c4-bc27-77cec1d7f354" :step/next {:db/id 17592186422486}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form: $$ A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix} $$ Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows: $$ \frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1 $$ This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables $\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$ So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix $$ P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}, $$ we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get $$ Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y). $$ As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is $$ \begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\ & =PAP \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have $$ max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20. $$ Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$ $$ \begin{aligned}B-20I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}-20\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$ Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get $$ {u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}. $$ Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate system using the change-of-coordinates matrix: $$ \begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid "5f8ca3b8-f2b1-5dda-8678-447d69f170dd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442119}} {:db/id 17592186442119 :step/content {:db/id 17592186378969 constraint equation as follows: $$ \frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1 $$ This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables $\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$ So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix $$ P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}, $$ we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get $$ Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y). $$ As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is $$ \begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\ & =PAP \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 8 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 16 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}-12 & 16 \\ 16 & 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following: $$ \begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-12-\lambda & 16 \\ 16 & 12-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-12-\lambda )(12-\lambda )-256 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-400 & =0 \\ (\lambda -20)(\lambda +20) & =0 \\ \lambda & =20,\,-20\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we have $$ max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20. $$"} $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: - The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$ $$ max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}} $$ The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$ - The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$ $$ min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}} $$ The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$ First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form: $$ A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} $$ Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=2:$ $$ \begin{aligned}A-2I & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}-2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$ Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get $$ {u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}. $$"} :step/id #uuid "ac5650ea-7fcf-5017-b806-6806b8006acb" :step/next {:db/id 17592186502171}}] :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{3}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-2.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: - The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$ $$ max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}} $$ The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$ - The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$ $$ min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}} $$ The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$ First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form: $$ A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} $$ Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-2:$ $$ \begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}-(-2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$ Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get $$ {u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}. $$"} :step/id #uuid "f7f8da2b-1589-5952-8f0d-950254eb7239" :step/next {:db/id 17592186514549}} {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-170561" :question/problem "The minimum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}-36{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $-72.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form: $$ A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix} $$ Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows: $$ \frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1 $$ This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables $\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$ the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$ So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix $$ P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}, $$ we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get $$ Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y). $$ As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is $$ \begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\ & =PAP \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-72,$ we have $$ min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-72. $$ Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-72:$ $$ \begin{aligned}B-(-72)I & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}+72\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}108 & -108 \\ -108 & 108\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$ Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-72)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get $$ {u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}. $$ Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate system using the change-of-coordinates matrix: $$ \begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid "7b55ab94-44ca-5e5f-8316-aab35be9951d"} {:db/id 17592186514542 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices write the constraint equation as follows: $$ \frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1 $$ This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables $\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$ So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix $$ P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}, $$ we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get $$ Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y). $$ As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is $$ \begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\ & =PAP \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -6 \\ -6 & -9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -18 \\ -6 & -9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}18 & -18 \\ -18 & -9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-18,$ we have $$ min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-18. $$ Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-18:$ $$ \begin{aligned}B-(-18)I & =\begin{bmatrix}18 & -18 \\ -18 & -9\end{bmatrix}+18\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}36 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$ Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-18)I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get $$ {u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}. $$ Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate system using the change-of-coordinates matrix: $$ \begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid "491341df-0c55-56c0-a053-5047b84d6caf"} {:db/id 17592186519649 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198685 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices equal to $0.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: - The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$ $$ max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}} $$ The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$ - The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$ $$ min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}} $$ The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$ First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form: $$ A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{bmatrix} $$ Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=0:$ $$ \begin{aligned}A-0I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{bmatrix}-0\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$ Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get $$ {u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}. $$"} :step/id #uuid "a61dcaf7-f154-5c88-a2cc-4dd236b50f6e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186199307 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199474 :tutorial/content "Consider the following repeated integral: $$ \displaystyle \int_0^1 \int_0^{1-x} \int_0^{1-x-y} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x $$ For this repeated integral, the integration domain is the type I region $$ R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 1-x, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1-x-y \right\} $$ as shown below. ![](images/56/56ef205e4a92cf96d2ddb81635b5776ededf880d4507e68db1d66ae045533705.png) Suppose we wish to change the order of integration so that we integrate first with respect to $y,$ then over a region $D$ in the $xz$-plane. In other words, we wish to express our repeated integral in the form $$ \int_0^1 \int_0^{1-x} \int_0^{1-x-y} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x = \iint\limits_D \left[ \int_{u_1(x,z)}^{u_2(x,z)} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}A. $$ To change the order of integration from $\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x$ to $\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}A,$ we write $R$ as a type III region. To visualize $R$ as a type III region, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below. ![](images/3c/3c444ce37b1799e950b52789d7837b699938bec602e274fed7c91640a31812a2.png) The arrow enters the region through the back boundary and leaves through the front boundary: - The front boundary of the region is $$ z = 1-x-y, $$ and writing this in the form $y = u_2(x,z),$ we have $$ y = 1-x-z. $$ - The back boundary of the region is $y = 0.$ Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is $$ R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (x,z) \in D, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 1-x-z \right\}, $$ as shown in the diagram below. ![](images/31/31c74e0c21a02898e584d141e942037cedf392680b9bc3bd84ae8831fb55224c.png) Therefore, by swapping the order of integration so that it is integrated first with respect to $y$ and then over $D,$ we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}{\int }_{0}^{1-x-y}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{1-x-z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA.\end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b266db14-83cd-503a-9a9a-0a046db8b914" "Recall that if the solution ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ of the least-squares problem $A\mathbf x=\mathbf{b}$ is unique, then $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ lies in $\textrm{Col}(A).$ Furthermore, $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is the vector in $\textrm{Col}(A)$ that's closest to $\mathbf b.$ In terms of vector spaces, the vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{b}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of $A.$ Therefore, the error vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Col}(A).$ ![](images/3a/3a1c79036954f0e04212892b7e3d79c75f8cd7b81d7785441f090f89a4eb6faf.png) A similar property holds for weighted least-squares solutions: *If the solution ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ of the least-squares problem $W\!A\mathbf x=W\mathbf{b}$ is unique, then $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Col}(A)$ with respect to the weighted dot product defined as $$ \langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle_W = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2 x_i y_i, $$ where the $w_i$'s are the weights from the main diagonal of the weight matrix $W.$* We previously considered the weighted least-squares problem $W\!Ax=W\mathbf{b},$ where ![](images/d4/d44c48deb0864fb8fd6aa92ce8af408b600de8abf2039a3f3cd7397fabc7d9fe.svg) It's easy to show (using the usual techniques) that the unique weighted least-squares solution is given by ![](images/db/db8f62fcb085d8c1fcfc22bb53cb8f22bd9a65b211e5fd5d4017e30bf9bdb4c7.svg) Computing our error vector $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} = A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b},$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}ε & =A\hat{x}-b \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 0 \\ 18\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 4 \\ 14\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 0 \\ 18\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, let $\mathbf a_1$ and $\mathbf a_2$ denote the columns of $A\mathbin{:}$ ![](images/3f/3fbafcf3f9d80d2d54089647b2f0239662dcbe56c9ba68539e2303ce752d28ee.svg) Notice that the error vector $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ is *not* orthogonal to the columns of $A\mathbin{:}$ - Computing $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \cdot \mathbf a_1,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}ε\cdot {a}_{1} & =⟨\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}⟩ \\ & =(1)(1)+(4)(1)+(-4)(2) \\ & =-3 \\ & \ne 0.\end{aligned} $$ - Computing $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \cdot \mathbf a_2,$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}ε\cdot {a}_{2} & =⟨\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}⟩ \\ & =(1)(-1)+(4)(0)+(-4)(-1) \\ & =3 \\ & \ne 0.\end{aligned} $$ However, if we check the orthogonality with respect to the *weighted* dot product $$ \langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle_W = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2 x_i y_i = 4x_1y_1 + x_2y_2 + x_3y_3, \quad $$ we obtain the following: $$ \begin{aligned}{⟨ε,{a}_{1}⟩}_{W} & ={⟨\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}⟩}_{W} \\ & =4(1)(1)+(4)(1)+(-4)(2) \\ & =0\,✓ \\ {⟨ε,{a}_{2}⟩}_{W} & ={⟨\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}⟩}_{W} \\ & =4(1)(-1)+(4)(0)+(-4)(-1) \\ & =0\,✓\end{aligned} $$ This means that $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Col}(A)$ with respect to the weighted dot product. We can write this as $$ A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \perp_W \textrm{Col}(A). $$ In terms of vector spaces, the vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is the orthogonal projection with respect to $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle_W$ of the vector $\mathbf{b}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of $A.$ Furthermore, the weighted least-squares problem with weight matrix $W$ is equivalent to finding a vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that $$ \Vert A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert_W $$ is as small as possible." :tutorial/id #uuid "91e0f414-7785-5748-bba9-04278c6519ad" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6084 :tutorial/title "A Geometric Interpretation of the Weighted Least-Squares Solution"} :step/id #uuid "373b333f-64bb-5518-823a-a53a7c7b2614" :step/math-academy-id 37006}] :activity/title "Weighted Least-Squares" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162229} {:db/id 17592186163036 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163308 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the least-squares problem $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ where ![](images/4d/4d538e6a37eccc1f49f34d3aa1b31a0539d50b351e6029595af1b1f7e0f2967a.svg) Recall that the corresponding least-squares solution is a vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that $$ \Vert A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert $$ is as small as possible. In real-world problems, the coefficients stored in $A$ might come from sources that are not equally reliable. For example, the coefficients might be collected from population surveys with different sample sizes. As a result, we might want to assign a greater "weight" to the more reliable data. For example, suppose we require the weight of the coefficients in the first row to be twice the weights of the other rows. Then, we can re-state our problem by saying that, for the matrix of weights $W,$ given by ![](images/72/7268fdd7c8701a9cf780342d6eab11015d7764694d17c28a2fae2336db267223.svg) we wish to find vectors ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that $$ \Vert W (A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}) \Vert $$ is as small as possible. Therefore, instead of solving $A\mathbf x = \mathbf{b},$ we now need to solve the least-squares problem $$ W\!A\mathbf x = W\mathbf{b}. $$ To get the normal equation corresponding to this least-squares problem, we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\!A)^T{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned} $$ Now, since ![](images/0c/0c7459270d9d27c40bdf5b0e6dc7eb0c7e17951541b77936804a9057f488c13f.svg) the normal equation can be written as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 0 \\ 18\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -4 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}36 \\ 0 \\ 18\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}9 & -6 \\ -6 & 5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}72 \\ -54\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$ Solving the final equation, we obtain the least-squares solution ![](images/72/7259d4c16fa297be7b02cab3ed48a848d1fa73de61c2f14351885072c93c6362.svg)" :tutorial/id Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have $$ {x}_{1}=\frac{4}{3}-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}. $$ Hence, the general solution is $$ \begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3}-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{3} \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R. $$ Therefore, we have $$ the matrix $A^T \! A.$ Also, since $A^T \! A$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A$ must be always non-negative real numbers. Let's compute the singular values of the matrix $A,$ given by ![](images/a9/a9edbe1fee59758c9557d95ea8f62468f9f3cb98449c437a274bdbf5c30f7dc6.svg) Now, since - $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix, and - $A^T$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix, then $A^T \! A$ must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix: $$ \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A} $$ Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$ Next, we compute the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}8-\lambda & 2 \\ 2 & 5-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda & =9,\,4\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned} $$ Note the following: - When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order. - If $A$ is a $m\times n$ matrix, then $A^T A$ is a $n\times n$ positive semi-definite matrix. :topic/math-academy-id 3013} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186163068 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163326 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ drawn from a population with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2,$ then the sample mean, denoted $\overline{X},$ is given by $$ \overline{X} = \dfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i. $$ The sample mean is a random variable whose probability distribution (also called the **sampling distribution**) has an expected value of $\mu\mathbin{:}$ $$ \textrm{E}[\overline{X}] = \mu $$ In other words, the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is an unbiased estimate of the population mean $\mu.$ Let's now find the variance of the sampling distribution of $\overline{X}.$ Using the properties of variance for sums of independent random variables, we obtain the following: $$ \begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}] & =\text{Var}[\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}] \\ & ={(\frac{1}{n})}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}] \\ & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot \text{Var}[{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}] \\ & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot (\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]+\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]+⋯+\text{Var}[{X}_{n}]) \\ & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot ({\sigma }^{2}+{\sigma }^{2}+⋯+{\sigma }^{2}) \\ & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot n{\sigma }^{2} \\ & =\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}\end{aligned} $$ To summarize, we have the following important result: $$ \textrm{Var}[\overline{X}] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n} $$ It should be noted that we don't yet know the sampling distribution of $\overline{X}.$ What we *do* know is that whatever the sampling distribution of $\overline{X}$ is, it has mean $\mu$ and variance $\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "58763c8a-23b3-55bb-9b5c-4781a3c271b4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6276 17592186162169} {:db/id 17592186163068 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163326 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ drawn from a population with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2,$ then the sample mean, denoted $\overline{X},$ is given by $$ \overline{X} = \dfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i. $$ The sample mean is a random variable whose probability distribution (also called the **sampling distribution**) has an expected value of $\mu\mathbin{:}$ $$ \textrm{E}[\overline{X}] = \mu $$ In other words, the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is an unbiased estimate of the population mean $\mu.$ Let's now find the variance of the sampling distribution of $\overline{X}.$ Using the properties of variance for sums of independent random variables, we obtain the following: $$ \begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}] & =\text{Var}[\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}] \\ & ={(\frac{1}{n})}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}] \\ & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot \text{Var}[{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}] \\ & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot (\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]+\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]+⋯+\text{Var}[{X}_{n}]) \\ & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot ({\sigma }^{2}+{\sigma }^{2}+⋯+{\sigma }^{2}) \\ & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot n{\sigma }^{2} \\ & =\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}\end{aligned} $$ To summarize, we have the following important result: $$ \textrm{Var}[\overline{X}] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n} $$ It should be noted that we don't yet know the sampling distribution of $\overline{X}.$ What we *do* know is that whatever the sampling distribution of $\overline{X}$ is, it has mean $\mu$ and variance $\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "58763c8a-23b3-55bb-9b5c-4781a3c271b4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6276 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} \text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}. $$ We're told that the bushes in the population have heights $4\,\text{ft}$ and $5\,\text{ft},$ and these are distributed in the ratio $3:2.$ Therefore, to compute the population's mean and variance, we can consider a population consisting of $3+2=5$ bushes only with the following heights: $$ 4\,\text{ft},\,4\,\text{ft},\,4\,\text{ft},\,5\,\text{ft},\,5\,\text{ft}. $$ Therefore, the population mean is $$ \begin{aligned}\mu & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\ & =\frac{1}{5}(3\cdot 4+2\cdot 5) \\ & =\frac{1}{5}(12+10) \\ & =\frac{22}{5} \\ & =4.4\,\text{ft},\end{aligned} $$ and the population variance is $$ \begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2}-{\mu }^{2} \\ & =\frac{1}{5}(3\cdot {4}^{2}+2\cdot {5}^{2})-{4.4}^{2} \\ & =\frac{1}{5}(98)-19.36 \\ & =19.6-19.36 \\ & =0.24\,{\text{ft}}^{2}.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, the population standard deviation is $\sigma =\sqrt{0.24},$ and we have that $$ \text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\frac{0.24}{n}}. $$ We require that the standard error is less than $0.01\,\text{ft}.$ Therefore $$ \begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{0.24}{n}} & <0.01 \\ \sqrt{n} & >\frac{\sqrt{0.24}}{0.01} \\ \sqrt{n} & >\sqrt{\frac{0.24}{{0.01}^{2}}} \\ \sqrt{n} & >\sqrt{2\,400} \\ n & >2\,400.\end{aligned} $$ \text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu ,\,\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}, $$ and the standard error is given by $$ \text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}. $$ We're told that the coins in the population have denominations $$1$ and $$0.50,$ and these are distributed in the ratio $1:4.$ Therefore, to compute the population's mean and variance, we can consider a population consisting of $1+4=5$ coins only with the following denominations: $$ $1,\,$0.5,\,$0.5,\,$0.5,\,$0.5. $$ Therefore, the population mean is $$ \begin{aligned}\mu & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\ & =\frac{1}{5}(1+4\cdot 0.5) \\ & =\frac{1}{5}(1+2) \\ & =\frac{3}{5} \\ & =$0.6,\end{aligned} $$ and the population variance is $$ \begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2}-{\mu }^{2} \\ & =\frac{1}{5}({1}^{2}+4\cdot {0.5}^{2})-{0.6}^{2} \\ & =\frac{1}{5}(2)-0.36 \\ & =0.4-0.36 \\ & =0.04.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, the population standard deviation is $\sigma =\sqrt{0.04}=0.2,$ and we have that $$ \text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{0.2}{\sqrt{n}}. $$ We require that the standard error is less than $$0.02.$ Therefore $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{0.2}{\sqrt{n}} & <0.02 \\ \sqrt{n} & >\frac{0.2}{0.02} \\ \sqrt{n} & >10 \\ n & >{10}^{2} \\ n & >100.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the smallest sample size is $n=101.$"} :step/id :question/problem "A sample ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3}$ of three nails is drawn from a population. The population has nails of two different lengths, $5\,\text{cm}$ and $\text{10}\,\text{cm},$ distributed in the ratio $4:1.$ Calculate the standard error of $\overset{―}{X}.$ Round your answer to two decimal places." :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population variance ${\sigma }^{2},$ then $$ \text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu ,\,\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}, $$ and the standard error is given by $$ \text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}. $$ We're told that the nails in the population have lengths $5\,\text{cm}$ and $\text{10}\,\text{cm},$ and these are distributed in the ratio $4:1.$ Therefore, to compute the population mean and variance, we can consider a population consisting of $4+1=5$ nails only with the following lengths: $$ 5\,\text{cm},\,5\,\text{cm},\,5\,\text{cm},\,5\,\text{cm}\,10\,\text{cm}. $$ Therefore, the population mean is $$ \begin{aligned}\mu & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\ & =\frac{1}{5}(4\cdot 5+10) \\ & =\frac{1}{5}(20+10) \\ & =\frac{30}{5} \\ & =6\,\text{cm},\end{aligned} $$ and the population variance is $$ \begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2}-{\mu }^{2} \\ & =\frac{1}{5}(4\cdot {5}^{2}+{10}^{2})-{6}^{2} \\ & =\frac{1}{5}(200)-36 \\ & =40-36 \\ & =4\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.\end{aligned} $$ Since the sample size $n=3,$ we have $$ \text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}=\frac{4}{3}\,{\text{cm}}^{2}. $$ Finally, $$ \text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}}≈1.15\,\text{cm} $$ rounded to two decimal places."} "dc1ec685-f38d-51a2-9240-4f3a1f1346e1" :step/math-academy-id 592748} {:db/id 17592186167903 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168038 :tutorial/content "When the auxiliary equation has purely imaginary roots, the solutions are trigonometric, and the boundary conditions usually force $\lambda$ to take on a discrete set of values. So, we again look for values of $\lambda$ that allow a nontrivial solution. We will now find the **eigenvalues** and **eigenfunctions** for the boundary value problem: $$ y'' + 9\lambda^2 y = 0, \qquad y'(0) = 0, \quad y(4) = 0, \quad 0 \leq x \leq 4, \quad \lambda \geq 0. $$ We consider two cases based on the value of $\lambda,$ since they correspond to different forms of the general solution. **Case 1: $\lambda = 0$** Setting $\lambda = 0$ gives the equation $y'' = 0.$ Integrating this equation twice gives the general solution: $$ y = Ax + B. $$ To apply the boundary conditions, we first find the derivative, $y' = A.$ - Applying $y'(0) = 0$ gives $A = 0.$ The solution becomes $y = B.$ - Applying $y(4) = 0$ then gives $B = 0.$ This yields the trivial solution $y \equiv 0.$ Since an eigenfunction must be nontrivial, $\lambda = 0$ is *not* an eigenvalue. **Case 2: $\lambda > 0$** The auxiliary equation is $m^2 + 9\lambda^2 = 0,$ which has roots $m = \pm 3i\lambda.$ The general solution is therefore $$ y = A\cos (3\lambda x) + B\sin (3\lambda x). $$ Now we apply the boundary conditions. First, we find the derivative: $$ y' = -3A\lambda\sin(3\lambda x) + 3B\lambda\cos(3\lambda x). $$ - Applying the condition $y'(0) = 0$ yields: $$ -3A\lambda\sin(0) + 3B\lambda\cos(0) = 0 \quad\implies\quad 3B\lambda = 0. $$ Since we are in the case where $\lambda > 0,$ this requires $B = 0.$ The solution simplifies to: $$ y = A\cos (3\lambda x). $$ - Next, applying the condition $y(4) = 0$ yields: $$ A\cos (12\lambda) = 0. $$ For a nontrivial solution, we must have $A \neq 0,$ which means we require $$ \cos (12\lambda) = 0. $$ This condition is met when $12\lambda$ is an odd multiple of $\pi/2:$ $$ 12\lambda = \dfrac{(2n+1)\pi}{2}, \quad \text{for } n = 0, 1, 2, \dots $$ Solving for $\lambda$ gives the set of **eigenvalues**: $$ \lambda_n = \dfrac{(2n+1)\pi}{24}. $$ The corresponding **eigenfunctions** are $$ y_n(x) = A_n \cos(3\lambda_n x) , \quad A_n \in \mathbb{R}. $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2e52b01a-4f53-5d27-9984-dd731308d87d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14650 :tutorial/title "Trigonometric Eigenfunctions"} :step/id #uuid "3e7ba88a-596c-53db-b70b-6b89ee975318" :step/math-academy-id 592751 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167902}} {:db/id 17592186167958 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168055 :tutorial/content "Next, we consider the case $\lambda \neq 0.$ To find the fundamental solutions of $$ y'' - 18\lambda y' + 81\lambda^2y = 0, $$ for $\lambda \neq 0,$ we set $y = e^{m x}.$ The auxiliary equation is $$ \begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-18\lambda m+81{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-9\lambda )(m-9\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ This gives a repeated root $m = 9\lambda.$ The general solution is $$ y = Ae^{9\lambda x} + Bxe^{9\lambda x}. $$ Now we apply the boundary conditions. - Applying the first boundary condition, $y(0) = 0,$ yields $$ y(0) = Ae^{0} + B(0)e^{0} = 0 \quad \implies \quad A = 0. $$ So, the solution simplifies to $y = Bxe^{9\lambda x}.$ Its derivative is $$ y' = Be^{9\lambda x} + 9B\lambda xe^{9\lambda x}. $$ - Applying the second boundary condition, $4y(3) + 5y'(3) = 0,$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}4(3B{e}^{27\lambda })+5(B{e}^{27\lambda }+27B\lambda {e}^{27\lambda }) & =0 \\ 12B{e}^{27\lambda }+5B{e}^{27\lambda }+135B\lambda {e}^{27\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{27\lambda }(17+135\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ For a nontrivial solution (an eigenfunction), we require $B\neq 0.$ Since $e^{27\lambda}$ is never zero, we must have $$ 17+135\lambda = 0 \quad \implies \quad \lambda = -\dfrac{17}{135}. $$ This is our **eigenvalue**. The corresponding **eigenfunction** is $$ y(x) = Bxe^{9(-17/135) x} = Bxe^{-17x/15}. $$ Note that any nonzero constant multiple of this function is also an eigenfunction." :tutorial/id #uuid "f4d9fb35-7991-5b49-bfd6-c82ad2ef1c69" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14892 :tutorial/title "Non-Trivial Solution of the Eigenvalue Problem"} :step/id #uuid "81f0071e-ac02-5b8f-ba91-88209136e903" :step/math-academy-id 608067 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167901}} {:db/id 17592186167959 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168056 :tutorial/content "We begin by considering the case $\lambda = 0.$ Setting $\lambda = 0$ in the original equation, $y'' - 18\lambda y' + 81\lambda^2y = 0,$ gives a much simpler equation: $$ y'' = 0. $$ Integrating this equation twice with respect to $x$ gives the general solution $$ y = Ax + B. $$ Now we apply the boundary conditions. - The first condition, $y(0) = 0,$ implies: $$ y(0) = A(0) + B = 0 \quad \implies \quad B=0. $$ So the solution must be of the form $y = Ax.$ - For the second condition, we first find the derivative, $y' = A.$ Applying the condition $4y(3) + 5y'(3) = 0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}4(A\cdot 3)+5(A) & =0 \\ 12A+5A & =0 \\ 17A & =0\,\,⟹\,\,A=0.\end{aligned} $$ Since both $A=0$ and $B=0,$ we are left with the trivial solution $y \equiv 0.$ By definition, an eigenfunction must be a *nontrivial* solution. Therefore, $\lambda = 0$ is *not* an eigenvalue. The corresponding **eigenfunction** is $$ y(x) = Bxe^{9(-17/135) x} = Bxe^{-17x/15}. $$ Note that any nonzero constant multiple of this function is also an eigenfunction." :tutorial/id #uuid "f4d9fb35-7991-5b49-bfd6-c82ad2ef1c69" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14892 :tutorial/title "Non-Trivial Solution of the Eigenvalue Problem"} :step/id #uuid "81f0071e-ac02-5b8f-ba91-88209136e903" :step/math-academy-id 608067 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167901}} {:db/id 17592186168055 :tutorial/content "Next, we consider the case $\lambda \neq 0.$ To find the fundamental solutions of $$ y'' - 18\lambda y' + 81\lambda^2y = 0, $$ for $\lambda \neq 0,$ we set $y = e^{m x}.$ The auxiliary equation is $$ \begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-18\lambda m+81{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-9\lambda )(m-9\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ This gives a repeated root $m = 9\lambda.$ The general solution is $$ y = Ae^{9\lambda x} + Bxe^{9\lambda x}. $$ Now we apply the boundary conditions. - Applying the first boundary condition, $y(0) = 0,$ yields $$ y(0) = Ae^{0} + B(0)e^{0} = 0 \quad \implies \quad A = 0. $$ So, the solution simplifies to $y = Bxe^{9\lambda x}.$ Its derivative is $$ y' = Be^{9\lambda x} + 9B\lambda xe^{9\lambda x}. $$ - Applying the second boundary condition, $4y(3) + 5y'(3) = 0,$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}4(3B{e}^{27\lambda })+5(B{e}^{27\lambda }+27B\lambda {e}^{27\lambda }) & =0 \\ 12B{e}^{27\lambda }+5B{e}^{27\lambda }+135B\lambda {e}^{27\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{27\lambda }(17+135\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ For a nontrivial solution (an eigenfunction), we require $B\neq 0.$ Since $e^{27\lambda}$ is never zero, we must have $$ 17+135\lambda = 0 \quad \implies \quad \lambda = -\dfrac{17}{135}. $$ This is our **eigenvalue**. 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c6e87982-ab6f-5e96-94e7-996ae7f3b605" :question/math-academy-id "q-338845" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem $$ {y}^{″}-10\lambda {y}^{′}+25{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,1\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \in R. $$ Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants. $\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}. $\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. **Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation $$ {y}^{″}=0. $$ Integrating this equation gives $$ y=Ax+B. $$ Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue. **Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$ To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is $$ \begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-10\lambda m+25{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-5\lambda )(m-5\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have the double root $m=5\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are $$ {y}_{1}(x)={e}^{5\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{5\lambda x} $$ and the general solution is $$ y=A{e}^{5\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{5\lambda x}. $$ Differentiating gives $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =5A\lambda {e}^{5\lambda x}+B{e}^{5\lambda x}+5B\lambda x{e}^{5\lambda x}.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}5A\lambda {e}^{5\lambda }+B{e}^{5\lambda }+5B\lambda {e}^{5\lambda } & =0 \\ 5A\lambda +B+5B\lambda & =0 \\ (5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}A{e}^{10\lambda }+2B{e}^{10\lambda }+2(5A\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }+B{e}^{10\lambda }+10B\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+2(5A\lambda +B+10B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+10A\lambda +2B+20B\lambda & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+(4+20\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+4(1+5\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$ $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B &=0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+4(1+5\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right. $$ This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives $$ |\begin{aligned}5\lambda & 1+5\lambda \\ 1+10\lambda & 4(1+5\lambda )\end{aligned}|=0. $$ So, we get $$ \begin{aligned}5\lambda \cdot 4(1+5\lambda )-(1+5\lambda )(1+10\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )[20\lambda -(1+10\lambda )] & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )[20\lambda -1-10\lambda ] & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )(10\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{10}.$ Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue: - Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}.$ Then, we have the solution $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{5{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{5{\lambda }_{1}x} \\ & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned} $$ and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into $$ (5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B=0 $$ we get $$ -A+(1-1)B=0 $$ which gives $A=0,$ and where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is $$ {y}_{1}(x)=Bx{e}^{-x}. $$ - For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{10},$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{5{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{5{\lambda }_{2}x} \\ & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned} $$ and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into $$ (5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B=0 $$ we get $$ \frac{1}{2}A+\frac{3}{2}B=0\,⇒\,A=-3B $$ where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-3B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\ & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-3) \\ & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-3)\end{aligned} $$ where we have set $C=B.$ So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $Bx{e}^{-x}\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-3).$"} :step/id #uuid "10ec5288-96c7-54f4-a406-4dc3fa372454" $$ {y}^{″}=0. $$ Integrating this equation gives $$ y=Ax+B. $$ Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields $A=0.$ Thus, we have a nontrivial solution, so $\lambda =0$ is a parameter \begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+16{\lambda }^{2} & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have $m=\pm 4\text{i}\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are $$ {y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda x)+4B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x). $$ Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields $$ -4A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+4B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=0 $$ which gives $B=0.$ So, we have $$ y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x). $$ Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields $$ -4A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda \pi )=0. $$ For nontrivial solutions, we require $$ 4\lambda \pi =n\pi $$ for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues: $$ {\lambda }_{n}=\frac{n}{4}. $$ The Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants. $\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}. $\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. **Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation $$ {y}^{″}=0. $$ Integrating this equation gives $$ y=Ax+B. $$ Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ and $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue. **Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$ To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is $$ \begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-12\lambda m+36{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-6\lambda )(m-6\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have the double root $m=6\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are $$ {y}_{1}(x)={e}^{6\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{6\lambda x} $$ and the general solution is $$ y=A{e}^{6\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{6\lambda x}. $$ Differentiating gives $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda x}+B{e}^{6\lambda x}+6B\lambda x{e}^{6\lambda x}.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}6A\lambda +B & =0 \\ (6\lambda )A+B & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the boundary condition $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}A{e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+2(6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+6B\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+B+2(6A\lambda +B+6B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+B+12A\lambda +2B+12B\lambda & =0 \\ (1+12\lambda )A+(3+12\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$ $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}(6\lambda )A+B &=0 \\ (1+12\lambda )A+(3+12\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right. $$ This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives $$ |\begin{aligned}6\lambda & 1 \\ 1+12\lambda & 3+12\lambda \end{aligned}|=0. $$ So, we get $$ \begin{aligned}6\lambda (3+12\lambda )-(1)(1+12\lambda ) & =0 \\ 18\lambda +72{\lambda }^{2}-1-12\lambda & =0 \\ 72{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (12\lambda -1)(6\lambda +1) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{12}.$ Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue: - Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6}.$ Then, we have the solution $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x} \\ & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned} $$ and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into $$ (6\lambda )A+B=0 $$ we get $$ -A+B=0\,⇒\,A=B $$ where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is $$ {y}_{1}(x)=B{e}^{-x}(x+1). $$ - For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{12},$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x} \\ & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned} $$ and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into $$ (6\lambda )A+B=0 $$ we get $$ \frac{1}{2}A+B=0\,⇒\,A=-2B $$ where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-2B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\ & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-2) \\ & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-2)\end{aligned} $$ where we have set $C=B.$ So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $B{e}^{-x}(x+1)\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-2).$"} :step/id #uuid {y}^{′}+36{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1,\,\lambda \in R. $$ Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants. $\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}. $\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. **Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation $$ {y}^{″}=0. $$ Integrating this equation gives $$ y=Ax+B. $$ Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ and $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue. **Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$ To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is $$ \begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-12\lambda m+36{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-6\lambda )(m-6\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have the double root $m=6\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are $$ {y}_{1}(x)={e}^{6\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{6\lambda x} $$ and the general solution is $$ y=A{e}^{6\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{6\lambda x}. $$ Differentiating gives $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda x}+B{e}^{6\lambda x}+6B\lambda x{e}^{6\lambda x}.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}6A\lambda +B & =0 \\ (6\lambda )A+B & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the boundary condition $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}A{e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+2(6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+6B\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+B+2(6A\lambda +B+6B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+B+12A\lambda +2B+12B\lambda & =0 \\ (1+12\lambda )A+(3+12\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$ $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}(6\lambda )A+B &=0 \\ (1+12\lambda )A+(3+12\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right. $$ This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives $$ |\begin{aligned}6\lambda & 1 \\ 1+12\lambda & 3+12\lambda \end{aligned}|=0. $$ So, we get $$ \begin{aligned}6\lambda (3+12\lambda )-(1)(1+12\lambda ) & =0 \\ 18\lambda +72{\lambda }^{2}-1-12\lambda & =0 \\ 72{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (12\lambda -1)(6\lambda +1) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{12}.$ Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue: - Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6}.$ Then, we have the solution $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x} \\ & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned} $$ and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into $$ (6\lambda )A+B=0 $$ we get $$ -A+B=0\,⇒\,A=B $$ where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is $$ {y}_{1}(x)=B{e}^{-x}(x+1). $$ - For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{12},$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x} \\ & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned} $$ and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into $$ (6\lambda )A+B=0 $$ we get $$ \frac{1}{2}A+B=0\,⇒\,A=-2B $$ where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-2B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\ & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-2) \\ & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-2)\end{aligned} $$ where we have set $C=B.$ So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $B{e}^{-x}(x+1)\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-2).$"} :step/id #uuid :question/math-academy-id "q-338909" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem $$ {y}^{″}+16{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(\pi )=0,\,0\le x\le \pi ,\,\lambda \ge 0. $$ Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem. $\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$ $\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$" :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. **Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation $$ {y}^{″}=0. $$ Integrating this equation gives $$ y=Ax+B. $$ Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields $A=0.$ Thus, we have a nontrivial solution, so $\lambda =0$ is a parameter value corresponding to the eigenvalue. **Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$ To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is $$ \begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+16{\lambda }^{2} & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have $m=\pm 4\text{i}\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are $$ {y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda x) $$ and the general solution is $$ y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda x). $$ Differentiating gives $$ {y}^{′}=-4A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda x)+4B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x). $$ Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields $$ -4A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+4B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=0 $$ which gives $B=0.$ So, we have $$ y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x). $$ Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields $$ -4A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda \pi )=0. $$ For nontrivial solutions, we require $$ 4\lambda \pi =n\pi $$ for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues: $$ {\lambda }_{n}=\frac{n}{4}. $$ The corresponding eigenfunctions are $$ {y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4{\lambda }_{n}x),\,{B}_{n}\in R. $$"} :step/id #uuid {N}_{0}.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues: $$ {\lambda }_{n}=\frac{(1+2n)^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{144}. $$ The corresponding eigenfunctions are $$ equation gives $$ y=Ax+B. $$ Applying the conditions $y(0)=0$ and $y(1)+{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue. **Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$ To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is $$ \begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-8\lambda m+16{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-4\lambda )(m-4\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have the double root $m=4\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are $$ {y}_{1}(x)={e}^{4\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{4\lambda x} $$ and the general solution is $$ y=A{e}^{4\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{4\lambda x}. $$ Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields $$ A+B\cdot 0=0 $$ which gives $A=0.$ So, we have $$ y=Bx{e}^{4\lambda x}. $$ Differentiating gives $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=B{e}^{4\lambda x}+4B\lambda x{e}^{4\lambda x}.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the boundary condition $y(1)+{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}B{e}^{4\lambda }+B{e}^{4\lambda }+4B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ 2B{e}^{4\lambda }+4B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{4\lambda }+2B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{4\lambda }(1+2\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ For nontrivial solutions, we require $B\ne 0.$ Thus, since ${e}^{4\lambda }>0,$ we must have $$ \lambda =-\frac{1}{2}. $$ Therefore, the corresponding eigenfunction is $$ \begin{aligned}y(x) & =Bx{e}^{4\lambda x} \\ & =Bx{e}^{-2x}.\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid "f1e042a8-1faa-5865-8d30-e1ea1fe82b24" :step/next {:db/id 17592186441532}} {:db/id Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants. $\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}. $\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. **Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation $$ {y}^{″}=0. $$ Integrating this equation gives $$ y=Ax+B. $$ Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue. **Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$ To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is $$ \begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-8\lambda m+16{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-4\lambda )(m-4\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have the double root $m=4\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are $$ {y}_{1}(x)={e}^{4\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{4\lambda x} $$ and the general solution is $$ y=A{e}^{4\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{4\lambda x}. $$ Differentiating gives $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =4A\lambda {e}^{4\lambda x}+B{e}^{4\lambda x}+4B\lambda x{e}^{4\lambda x}.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}4A\lambda {e}^{4\lambda }+B{e}^{4\lambda }+4B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ 4A\lambda +B+4B\lambda & =0 \\ (4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}A{e}^{8\lambda }+2B{e}^{8\lambda }+2(4A\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }+B{e}^{8\lambda }+8B\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+2(4A\lambda +B+8B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+8A\lambda +2B+16B\lambda & =0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+(4+16\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+4(1+4\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$ $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}(4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B &=0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+4(1+4\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right. $$ This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives $$ |\begin{aligned}4\lambda & 1+4\lambda \\ 1+8\lambda & 4(1+4\lambda )\end{aligned}|=0. $$ So, we get $$ \begin{aligned}4\lambda \cdot 4(1+4\lambda )-(1+4\lambda )(1+8\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )[16\lambda -(1+8\lambda )] & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )[16\lambda -1-8\lambda ] & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )(8\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{8}.$ Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue: - Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4}.$ Then, we have the solution $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{4{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{4{\lambda }_{1}x} \\ & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned} $$ and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into $$ (4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B=0 $$ we get $$ -A+(1-1)B=0 $$ which gives $A=0,$ and where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is $$ {y}_{1}(x)=Bx{e}^{-x}. $$ - For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{8},$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{4{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{4{\lambda }_{2}x} \\ & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned} $$ and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into $$ (4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B=0 $$ we get $$ \frac{1}{2}A+\frac{3}{2}B=0\,⇒\,A=-3B $$ where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-3B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\ & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-3) \\ & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-3)\end{aligned} $$ where we have set $C=B.$ So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $Bx{e}^{-x}\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-3).$"} :step/id #uuid "f8b73451-fda1-5086-8156-fc15d81c7a88"
