and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. **Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation $$ {y}^{″}=0. $$ Integrating this equation gives $$ y=Ax+B. $$ Applying the conditions $y(0)=0$ and $y(1)+{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue. **Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$ To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is $$ \begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-8\lambda m+16{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-4\lambda )(m-4\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have the double root $m=4\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are $$ {y}_{1}(x)={e}^{4\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{4\lambda x} $$ and the general solution is $$ y=A{e}^{4\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{4\lambda x}. $$ Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields $$ A+B\cdot 0=0 $$ which gives $A=0.$ So, we have $$ y=Bx{e}^{4\lambda x}. $$ Differentiating gives $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=B{e}^{4\lambda x}+4B\lambda x{e}^{4\lambda x}.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the boundary condition $y(1)+{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}B{e}^{4\lambda }+B{e}^{4\lambda }+4B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ 2B{e}^{4\lambda }+4B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{4\lambda }+2B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{4\lambda }(1+2\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ For nontrivial solutions, we require $B\ne 0.$ Thus, since ${e}^{4\lambda }>0,$ we must have $$ \lambda =-\frac{1}{2}. $$ Therefore, the corresponding eigenfunction is $$ \begin{aligned}y(x) & =Bx{e}^{4\lambda x} \\ & =Bx{e}^{-2x}.\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid "f1e042a8-1faa-5865-8d30-e1ea1fe82b24" :step/next {:db/id 17592186441532}} Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants. $\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}. $\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. **Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation $$ {y}^{″}=0. $$ Integrating this equation gives $$ y=Ax+B. $$ Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue. **Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$ To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is $$ \begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-8\lambda m+16{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-4\lambda )(m-4\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have the double root $m=4\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are $$ {y}_{1}(x)={e}^{4\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{4\lambda x} $$ and the general solution is $$ y=A{e}^{4\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{4\lambda x}. $$ Differentiating gives $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =4A\lambda {e}^{4\lambda x}+B{e}^{4\lambda x}+4B\lambda x{e}^{4\lambda x}.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}4A\lambda {e}^{4\lambda }+B{e}^{4\lambda }+4B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ 4A\lambda +B+4B\lambda & =0 \\ (4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}A{e}^{8\lambda }+2B{e}^{8\lambda }+2(4A\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }+B{e}^{8\lambda }+8B\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+2(4A\lambda +B+8B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+8A\lambda +2B+16B\lambda & =0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+(4+16\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+4(1+4\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$ $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}(4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B &=0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+4(1+4\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right. $$ This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives $$ |\begin{aligned}4\lambda & 1+4\lambda \\ 1+8\lambda & 4(1+4\lambda )\end{aligned}|=0. $$ So, we get $$ \begin{aligned}4\lambda \cdot 4(1+4\lambda )-(1+4\lambda )(1+8\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )[16\lambda -(1+8\lambda )] & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )[16\lambda -1-8\lambda ] & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )(8\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{8}.$ Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue: - Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4}.$ Then, we have the solution $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{4{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{4{\lambda }_{1}x} \\ & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned} $$ and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into $$ (4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B=0 $$ we get $$ -A+(1-1)B=0 $$ which gives $A=0,$ and where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is $$ {y}_{1}(x)=Bx{e}^{-x}. $$ - For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{8},$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{4{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{4{\lambda }_{2}x} \\ & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned} $$ and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into $$ (4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B=0 $$ we get $$ \frac{1}{2}A+\frac{3}{2}B=0\,⇒\,A=-3B $$ where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-3B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\ & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-3) \\ & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-3)\end{aligned} $$ where we have set $C=B.$ So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $Bx{e}^{-x}\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-3).$"} :step/id #uuid "f8b73451-fda1-5086-8156-fc15d81c7a88" does not correspond to an eigenvalue. **Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$ To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is $$ \begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+25{\lambda }^{2} & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have $m=\pm 5\text{i}\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are $$ {y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\lambda x),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\lambda x) $$ and $$ which gives $A=0.$ So, we have $$ y=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\lambda x). $$ Differentiating gives $$ {y}^{′}=5B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(5\lambda x). $$ Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields $$ 5B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(10\lambda )=0. $$ For nontrivial solutions, we require $$ 10\lambda =\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi =\frac{(2n+1)\pi }{2} $$ for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues: $$ {\lambda }_{n}=\frac{(2n+1)\pi }{20}. $$ The corresponding eigenfunctions are $$ {y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5{\lambda }_{n}x),\,{B}_{n}\in R. $$"} :step/id #uuid "2a58e732-9b94-5f3d-88a9-7a4d9823485f" :step/next {:db/id 17592186522856}} {:db/id 17592186522842 :step/content {:db/id 17592186522787 and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. **Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation $$ {y}^{″}=0. $$ Integrating this equation gives $$ y=Ax+B. $$ Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+6{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue. **Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$ To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is $$ \begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-12\lambda m+36{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-6\lambda )(m-6\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have the double root $m=6\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are $$ {y}_{1}(x)={e}^{6\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{6\lambda x} $$ and the general solution is $$ y=A{e}^{6\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{6\lambda x}. $$ Differentiating gives $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda x}+B{e}^{6\lambda x}+6B\lambda x{e}^{6\lambda x}.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+6B\lambda {e}^{6\lambda } & =0 \\ 6A\lambda +B+6B\lambda & =0 \\ (6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+6{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}A{e}^{12\lambda }+2B{e}^{12\lambda }+6(6A\lambda {e}^{12\lambda }+B{e}^{12\lambda }+12B\lambda {e}^{12\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+6(6A\lambda +B+12B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+36A\lambda +6B+72B\lambda & =0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+(8+72\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+8(1+9\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$ $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}(6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B &=0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+(8+72\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right. $$ This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives $$ |\begin{aligned}6\lambda & 1+6\lambda \\ 1+36\lambda & 8+72\lambda \end{aligned}|=0. $$ So, we get $$ \begin{aligned}6\lambda (8+72\lambda )-(1+6\lambda )(1+36\lambda ) & =0 \\ 48\lambda +432{\lambda }^{2}-(1+42\lambda +216{\lambda }^{2}) & =0 \\ 216{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (12\lambda +1)(18\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{18}.$ Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue: - Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12}.$ Then, we have the solution $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x} \\ & =A{e}^{-x/2}+Bx{e}^{-x/2}\end{aligned} $$ and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into $$ (6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B=0 $$ we get $$ -\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{1}{2}B=0 $$ which gives $A=B,$ where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =B{e}^{-x/2}+Bx{e}^{-x/2} \\ & =B{e}^{-x/2}(x+1).\end{aligned} $$ - For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{18},$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x} \\ & =A{e}^{x/3}+Bx{e}^{x/3}\end{aligned} $$ and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into $$ (6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B=0 $$ we get $$ \frac{1}{3}A+\frac{4}{3}B=0\,⇒\,A=-4B $$ where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-4B{e}^{x/3}+Bx{e}^{x/3} \\ & =B{e}^{x/3}(x-4) \\ & =C{e}^{x/3}(x-4)\end{aligned} $$ where we have set $C=B.$ So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $B{e}^{-x/2}(x+1)\text{ and }C{e}^{x/3}(x-4).$"} :step/id #uuid $y(0)={y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not a parameter of the eigenvalue. **Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$ To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is $$ \begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+4\lambda & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have $m=\pm 2\text{i}\sqrt{\lambda }.$ So, the fundamental solutions are $$ {y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda }),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda }) $$ and the general solution is $$ y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda })+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda }). $$ Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields $$ A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)=0 $$ which gives $A=0.$ So, we have $$ y=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda }). $$ Differentiating, we get $$ {y}^{′}=2B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda }). $$ Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields $$ 2B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{\lambda })=0. $$ For nontrivial solutions, we require $$ 2\sqrt{\lambda }=\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi =\frac{(1+2n)\pi }{2} $$ for $n\in {N}_{0}.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues: $$ {\lambda }_{n}=\frac{(1+2n)^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{16}. $$ The corresponding eigenfunctions are $$ {y}^{′}+64{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1,\,\lambda \in R. $$ Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants. $\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}. $\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. **Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation $$ {y}^{″}=0. $$ Integrating this equation gives $$ y=Ax+B. $$ Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ and $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue. **Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$ To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is $$ \begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-16\lambda m+64{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-8\lambda )(m-8\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have the double root $m=8\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are $$ {y}_{1}(x)={e}^{8\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{8\lambda x} $$ and the general solution is $$ y=A{e}^{8\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{8\lambda x}. $$ Differentiating gives $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =8A\lambda {e}^{8\lambda x}+B{e}^{8\lambda x}+8B\lambda x{e}^{8\lambda x}.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}8A\lambda +B & =0 \\ (8\lambda )A+B & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the boundary condition $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}A{e}^{8\lambda }+B{e}^{8\lambda }+2(8A\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }+B{e}^{8\lambda }+8B\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+B+2(8A\lambda +B+8B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+B+16A\lambda +2B+16B\lambda & =0 \\ (1+16\lambda )A+(3+16\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$ $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}(8\lambda )A+B &=0 \\ (1+16\lambda )A+(3+16\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right. $$ This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives $$ |\begin{aligned}8\lambda & 1 \\ 1+16\lambda & 3+16\lambda \end{aligned}|=0. $$ So, we get $$ \begin{aligned}8\lambda (3+16\lambda )-(1)(1+16\lambda ) & =0 \\ 24\lambda +128{\lambda }^{2}-1-16\lambda & =0 \\ 128{\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (16\lambda -1)(8\lambda +1) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{8}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{16}.$ Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue: - Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{8}.$ Then, we have the solution $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{8{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{8{\lambda }_{1}x} \\ & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned} $$ and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into $$ (8\lambda )A+B=0 $$ we get $$ -A+B=0\,⇒\,A=B $$ where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is $$ {y}_{1}(x)=B{e}^{-x}(x+1). $$ - For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{16},$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{8{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{8{\lambda }_{2}x} \\ & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned} $$ and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into $$ (8\lambda )A+B=0 $$ we get $$ \frac{1}{2}A+B=0\,⇒\,A=-2B $$ where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-2B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\ & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-2) \\ & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-2)\end{aligned} $$ where we have set $C=B.$ So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $B{e}^{-x}(x+1)\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-2).$"} :step/id #uuid the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda >0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. **Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation $$ {y}^{″}=0. $$ Integrating this equation gives $$ y=Ax+B. $$ Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields $A=0.$ Thus, we have a nontrivial solution, so $\lambda =0$ is a parameter corresponding to the eigenvalue. **Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$ To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is $$ \begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+25\lambda & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have $m=\pm 5\text{i}\sqrt{\lambda }.$ So, the fundamental solutions are $$ {y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda }),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda }) $$ and the general solution is $$ y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda })+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda }). $$ Differentiating, we get $$ {y}^{′}=-5A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda })+5B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda }). $$ Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields $$ -5A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+5B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=0 $$ which gives $B=0.$ So, we have $$ y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda }). $$ Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields $$ -5A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\pi \sqrt{\lambda })=0. $$ For nontrivial solutions, we require $$ 5\pi \sqrt{\lambda }=n\pi $$ for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues: $$ {\lambda }_{n}=\frac{{n}^{2}}{25}. $$ The corresponding eigenfunctions are $$ {y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x\sqrt{{\lambda }_{n}}),\,{B}_{n}\in R. $$"} :step/id #uuid Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants. $\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}. $\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. **Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation $$ {y}^{″}=0. $$ Integrating this equation gives $$ y=Ax+B. $$ Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+6{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue. **Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$ To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is $$ \begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-12\lambda m+36{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-6\lambda )(m-6\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have the double root $m=6\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are $$ {y}_{1}(x)={e}^{6\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{6\lambda x} $$ and the general solution is $$ y=A{e}^{6\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{6\lambda x}. $$ Differentiating gives $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda x}+B{e}^{6\lambda x}+6B\lambda x{e}^{6\lambda x}.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+6B\lambda {e}^{6\lambda } & =0 \\ 6A\lambda +B+6B\lambda & =0 \\ (6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+6{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}A{e}^{12\lambda }+2B{e}^{12\lambda }+6(6A\lambda {e}^{12\lambda }+B{e}^{12\lambda }+12B\lambda {e}^{12\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+6(6A\lambda +B+12B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+36A\lambda +6B+72B\lambda & =0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+(8+72\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+8(1+9\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$ $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}(6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B &=0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+(8+72\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right. $$ This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives $$ |\begin{aligned}6\lambda & 1+6\lambda \\ 1+36\lambda & 8+72\lambda \end{aligned}|=0. $$ So, we get $$ \begin{aligned}6\lambda (8+72\lambda )-(1+6\lambda )(1+36\lambda ) & =0 \\ 48\lambda +432{\lambda }^{2}-(1+42\lambda +216{\lambda }^{2}) & =0 \\ 216{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (12\lambda +1)(18\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{18}.$ Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue: - Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12}.$ Then, we have the solution $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x} \\ & =A{e}^{-x/2}+Bx{e}^{-x/2}\end{aligned} $$ and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into $$ (6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B=0 $$ we get $$ -\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{1}{2}B=0 $$ which gives $A=B,$ where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =B{e}^{-x/2}+Bx{e}^{-x/2} \\ & =B{e}^{-x/2}(x+1).\end{aligned} $$ - For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{18},$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x} \\ & =A{e}^{x/3}+Bx{e}^{x/3}\end{aligned} $$ and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into $$ (6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B=0 $$ we get $$ \frac{1}{3}A+\frac{4}{3}B=0\,⇒\,A=-4B $$ where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-4B{e}^{x/3}+Bx{e}^{x/3} \\ & =B{e}^{x/3}(x-4) \\ & =C{e}^{x/3}(x-4)\end{aligned} $$ where we have set $C=B.$ So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $B{e}^{-x/2}(x+1)\text{ and }C{e}^{x/3}(x-4).$"} :step/id #uuid Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants. $\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}. $\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. **Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation $$ {y}^{″}=0. $$ Integrating this equation gives $$ y=Ax+B. $$ Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ and $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue. **Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$ To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is $$ \begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-16\lambda m+64{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-8\lambda )(m-8\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have the double root $m=8\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are $$ {y}_{1}(x)={e}^{8\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{8\lambda x} $$ and the general solution is $$ y=A{e}^{8\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{8\lambda x}. $$ Differentiating gives $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =8A\lambda {e}^{8\lambda x}+B{e}^{8\lambda x}+8B\lambda x{e}^{8\lambda x}.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}8A\lambda +B & =0 \\ (8\lambda )A+B & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Applying the boundary condition $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields $$ \begin{aligned}A{e}^{8\lambda }+B{e}^{8\lambda }+2(8A\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }+B{e}^{8\lambda }+8B\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+B+2(8A\lambda +B+8B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+B+16A\lambda +2B+16B\lambda & =0 \\ (1+16\lambda )A+(3+16\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned} $$ So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$ $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}(8\lambda )A+B &=0 \\ (1+16\lambda )A+(3+16\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right. $$ This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives $$ |\begin{aligned}8\lambda & 1 \\ 1+16\lambda & 3+16\lambda \end{aligned}|=0. $$ So, we get $$ \begin{aligned}8\lambda (3+16\lambda )-(1)(1+16\lambda ) & =0 \\ 24\lambda +128{\lambda }^{2}-1-16\lambda & =0 \\ 128{\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (16\lambda -1)(8\lambda +1) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{8}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{16}.$ Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue: - Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{8}.$ Then, we have the solution $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{8{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{8{\lambda }_{1}x} \\ & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned} $$ and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into $$ (8\lambda )A+B=0 $$ we get $$ -A+B=0\,⇒\,A=B $$ where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is $$ {y}_{1}(x)=B{e}^{-x}(x+1). $$ - For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{16},$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{8{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{8{\lambda }_{2}x} \\ & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned} $$ and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into $$ (8\lambda )A+B=0 $$ we get $$ \frac{1}{2}A+B=0\,⇒\,A=-2B $$ where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-2B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\ & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-2) \\ & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-2)\end{aligned} $$ where we have set $C=B.$ So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $B{e}^{-x}(x+1)\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-2).$"} :step/id #uuid 17592186189368 :tutorial/content "It's often helpful to use the double-angle formula for sine when computing the slope of the tangent to a polar curve, as this often makes the differentiation easier. Let's consider the polar curve $r = 1-2\cos\theta,$ whose graph is shown below ![](images/53/53c660d25a8bec2346cacd95d70fb3f4ee27afe039bd23cbe7affa3cf04eb09a.png) Recall that the slope of the tangent (in terms of $\theta$) is given by $$ \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}. $$ First, to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use $$ x = r \cos \theta, \qquad y = r \sin \theta. $$ Using the fact that $r = 1-2\cos\theta,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}x & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}\theta )\operatorname{cos}\theta \\ & =\operatorname{cos}\theta -2{cos}^{2}\theta , \\ y & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}\theta )\operatorname{sin}\theta \\ & =\operatorname{sin}\theta -2\operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta \\ & =\operatorname{sin}\theta -\operatorname{sin}2\theta .\end{aligned} $$ Notice that we used the double-angle formula $\color{black}\sin2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ to simplify our expression for $y.$ To compute our derivative, we need to calculate $x'(\theta)$ and $y'(\theta).$ - First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(\theta ) & =(\operatorname{cos}\theta -2{cos}^{2}\theta )^{'} \\ & =(\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{'}-(2{cos}^{2}\theta )^{'} \\ & =(-\operatorname{sin}\theta )-(2\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}\theta \cdot (-\operatorname{sin}\theta )) \\ & =-\operatorname{sin}\theta +2\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta \\ & =-\operatorname{sin}\theta +2\cdot \operatorname{sin}2\theta \\ & =2\operatorname{sin}2\theta -\operatorname{sin}\theta \end{aligned} $$ - Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{'}(\theta ) & ={(\operatorname{sin}\theta -\operatorname{sin}2\theta )}^{'} \\ & ={(\operatorname{sin}\theta )}^{'}-{(\operatorname{sin}2\theta )}^{'} \\ & =\operatorname{cos}\theta -2\operatorname{cos}2\theta \end{aligned} $$ Finally, the slope of the tangent is given by $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{'}(\theta )}{{x}^{'}(\theta )} \\ & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta -2\text{ }\,\operatorname{cos}2\theta }{2\text{ }\,\operatorname{sin}2\theta -\operatorname{sin}\theta }.\end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "adced1fe-4c40-50d1-a9b4-12fcf213b6e7" (in terms of $\theta$) is given by $$ \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}. $$ First, to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use $$ x = r \cos \theta, \qquad y = r \sin \theta. $$ Using the fact that $r = 1-2\cos\theta,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}x & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}\theta )\operatorname{cos}\theta \\ & =\operatorname{cos}\theta -2{cos}^{2}\theta , \\ y & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}\theta )\operatorname{sin}\theta \\ & =\operatorname{sin}\theta -2\operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta \\ & =\operatorname{sin}\theta -\operatorname{sin}2\theta .\end{aligned} $$ Notice that we used the double-angle formula $\color{black}\sin2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ to simplify our expression for $y.$ To compute our derivative, we need to calculate $x'(\theta)$ and $y'(\theta).$ - First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(\theta ) & =(\operatorname{cos}\theta -2{cos}^{2}\theta )^{'} \\ & =(\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{'}-(2{cos}^{2}\theta )^{'} \\ & =(-\operatorname{sin}\theta )-(2\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}\theta \cdot (-\operatorname{sin}\theta )) \\ & =-\operatorname{sin}\theta +2\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta \\ & =-\operatorname{sin}\theta +2\cdot \operatorname{sin}2\theta \\ & =2\operatorname{sin}2\theta -\operatorname{sin}\theta \end{aligned} $$ - Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}{y}^{'}(\theta ) & ={(\operatorname{sin}\theta -\operatorname{sin}2\theta )}^{'} \\ & ={(\operatorname{sin}\theta )}^{'}-{(\operatorname{sin}2\theta )}^{'} \\ & =\operatorname{cos}\theta -2\operatorname{cos}2\theta \end{aligned} $$ Finally, the slope of the tangent is given by $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{'}(\theta )}{{x}^{'}(\theta )} \\ & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta -2\text{ }\,\operatorname{cos}2\theta }{2\text{ }\,\operatorname{sin}2\theta -\operatorname{sin}\theta }.\end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "adced1fe-4c40-50d1-a9b4-12fcf213b6e7" 17592186189169 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189401 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables, where the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is given by $\mu_{X \mid y}$. In other words, $$ \textrm{E}\begin{bmatrix}X\, & \,Y=y\end{bmatrix} = \mu_{X \mid y} $$ The **conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$** is defined as $$ \textrm{Var}\begin{bmatrix}X\, & \,Y=y\end{bmatrix} = \textrm{E}\big\begin{bmatrix}(X - \mu_{X \mid y} \big)^2 \, & \, Y=y\end{bmatrix} $$ This is similar to the definition of $\textrm{Var}[X]$ in that it represents the average (squared) distance of the random variable $X$ from the mean. The difference here is that the expected values are now dependent on the outcome of $Y$. Similarly to the case of $\textrm{Var}[X]$, this often isn't the easiest formula to use in practice. However, it can be shown that the definition of conditional variance is equivalent to $$ \begin{aligned} Var\begin{bmatrix}X & Y = y\end{bmatrix} &= E\begin{bmatrix}X^{2} & Y = y\end{bmatrix} - μ_{X\begin{vmatrix}y}^{2} \\ = [∑_(x)x^{2}f_{X\mid Y}(x \mid y)] - μ_{X\end{vmatrix}y}^{2} \end{aligned} $$ where $f_{X\mid Y}(x \, \mid \, y)$ is the conditional PMF of $X$ given $Y$. Note that these formulas are analogous to those for $\textrm{Var}[X]$. Finally, we have an analogous definition for the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X=x$: $$ \begin{aligned} Var\begin{bmatrix}Y & X = x\end{bmatrix} &= E\begin{bmatrix}(Y - μ_{Y \mid x})^{2} & X = x\end{bmatrix} \\ &= E\begin{bmatrix}Y^{2} & X = x\end{bmatrix} - μ_{Y\begin{vmatrix}x}^{2} \\ = [∑_(y)y^{2}f_{Y\mid X}(y \mid x)] - μ_{Y\end{vmatrix}x}^{2} \end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ce4fb1c3-94ee-51c3-b10d-ce6ea0c7ff38" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6431 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "12bb1f79-4af3-56c1-b495-e654c2cf5d1c" :step/math-academy-id 38850 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189167}} {:db/id 17592186189183 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188339 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186188046 :question/id #uuid "3764cb54-7fd2-584a-9dc7-eda88368b032" :question/math-academy-id "e-10352"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "abfaf356-6b74-5dfd-8070-e3a60dc372c5" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188680} {:db/id 17592186188687} {:db/id 17592186511456} {:db/id 17592186511574}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Conditional Variance Using Row Totals"} :step/id #uuid "7f447a96-6d58-5356-934d-4d4a94738359" :step/math-academy-id 38984 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189168}}] :activity/title "Conditional Variance for Discrete Random Variables" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186188511} {:db/id 17592186189169 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189401 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables, where the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is given by $\mu_{X \mid y}$. =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2} \\ & =[{\sum }_{y}{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2}.\end{aligned} $$ In order to find ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ let's first find the marginal distribution for $X,$ corresponding to the row totals: | $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=8$ | ${f}_{X}(x)$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $X=0$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{2}{9}$ | $\frac{1}{27}$ | $\frac{16}{27}$ | | $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{27}$ | $\frac{7}{27}$ | $\frac{1}{9}$ | $\frac{11}{27}$ | The conditional probability mass function of $Y$ given that $X=x$ is $$ {f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)}. $$ Therefore, dividing each joint probability by the corresponding row total, we obtain the conditional probability mass function of $Y$ given that $X=x:$ 17592186167794 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168150 :tutorial/content "Given a continuous function $f(x)$ on a closed interval $[a, b],$ the mean value theorem for integrals guarantees that there exists a number $c \in [a,b]$ such that $$ \int_a^b f(x)\, \textrm d x = f(c) \cdot (b-a), $$ which can be visualized as shown below. ![](images/0a/0afb9b15787eb89f73f322290bdbe2288027c54924d274c438773ce151a17291.png) We have a similar theorem for functions with two variables. The so-called **mean value theorem for double integrals** states: *If the function $f(x,y)$ is continuous on a closed and bounded region $D,$ then there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that* $$ \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D). $$ This has a nice geometrical interpretation when $f$ is non-negative on $D.$ In this case, the theorem tells us that there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ The diagram below shows the case when $D$ is rectangular, and the corresponding cylinder is a rectangular solid. ![](images/8e/8ed477207ee61fbdaf963ed8a127e3f1d4cf76707d2eeb4b450fd49f78e15b7e.png) In general, the point $(a,b)$ mentioned in the theorem is not unique. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "b65eeb5f-8a44-55b9-819c-1c6c0d979d1e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7778 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "037c5a22-eee3-557c-b683-370d2389ad82" :step/math-academy-id 45031 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167795}} {:db/id 17592186167795 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168151 :tutorial/content "Consider the continuous function $$ f(x,y) = x+3y^2+2 $$ and the region $D$ given by $$ D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \: 0 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}. $$ According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that $$ \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D). $$ Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(x+3{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}A \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(x+3{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[xy+{y}^{3}+2y]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2x+12)\,\text{d}x \\ & ={[{x}^{2}+12x]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\ & =28.\end{aligned} $$ Next, we have $$ \textrm{Area}(D) = 2 \cdot 2 = 4. $$ So, our mean-value equation simplifies to $$ \begin{aligned}28 & =f(a,b)\cdot 4 \\ 7 & =f(a,b) \\ 7 & =a+3{b}^{2}+2 \\ a & =5-3{b}^{2}.\end{aligned} $$ This equation describes part of a parabola in the $xy$-plane, as shown below. ![](images/46/46873c4ecb290380488e589082fc0759324d3540494f5b83e2d64db5d9cdf62a.png) To find a particular point that satisfies the mean value theorem, we can set, for example, $b=1 \in [0,2]$ and obtain $a=2.$ So, the point $(2,1)$ satisfies the mean value theorem for double integrals. Consequently, the two solids below must have the same volume. ![](images/82/82d3a762ab323339570e6010038e75ce95f3fdbde958a2ffa876972cbf91e8fb.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "b890c915-3364-5ac3-b88b-298ed92d9def" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7784 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "32b5b570-9467-5bff-bc3b-29964ed86c09" :step/math-academy-id 45050 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167790}}] :activity/title "The Average Value of a Multivariable Function" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186166974} {:db/id 17592186167794 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168150 :tutorial/content "Given a continuous function $f(x)$ on a closed interval $[a, b],$ the mean value theorem for integrals guarantees that there exists a number $c \in [a,b]$ such that $$ \int_a^b f(x)\, \textrm d x = f(c) \cdot (b-a), $$ which can be visualized as shown below. ![](images/0a/0afb9b15787eb89f73f322290bdbe2288027c54924d274c438773ce151a17291.png) We have a similar theorem for functions with two variables. three-dimensional space. Before we begin, we need to discuss the meaning behind the triple integral of a function over a non-rectangular domain. To help us, consider the region $R$ shown below. ![](images/ba/ba2c52d81578e4754732a99f459b037bb7ceb35b60e3a711ed239855d837a93f.png) Let's discuss how to define the following triple integral: $$ \iiint\limits_R 4xyz\,\textrm d V $$ We start by enclosing the region $R$ by a rectangular solid $R'$ whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axes, as shown below. ![](images/e5/e5548c26288c4b8ba6ac9e450ad0a78be55ae6a6ab6e4ef7a52a086bc997ed11.png) Now, we extend the integrand to the rectangular region $R'$ by defining a new function $f(x,y,z)$ that's equal to $0$ outside $R$ and equals $4xyz$ inside $R\mathbin{:}$ $$ {\begin{aligned}4xyz, & (x,y,z)\in {R}^{'}\cap R \\ 0, & (x,y,z)\in {R}^{'}∖R\end{aligned} $$ Although $f(x,y,z)$ might not be continuous at the boundary of $R,$ the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over the rectangular domain $R'$ will exist. Therefore, we can immediately express our triple integral as a repeated integral as follows: \[ \iint\limits_{D} \int\limits_{u_1(x,y)}^{u_2(x,y)} f(x,y,z) \: \textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}A, \] > where [math]D[/math] is a region in the [math]xy[/math]-plane. Then, we can decompose it further by writing down the double integral as a repeated integral: However, in many cases, the evaluation will be easier if we can decompose the triple integral into simple integrals. In our example above, we can write our triple integral as a repeated integral right away (skipping the step with the double integral): $$ \displaystyle \iiint \limits_{R} f(x,y,z)\: \textrm{d}V = \int_{\color{red}a}^{\color{red}b} \int_{\color{blue}v_1(x)}^{\color{blue}v_2(x)} \int_{\color{purple}u_1(x,y)}^{\color{purple}u_2(x,y)} f(x,y,z)\: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x. $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bed273a6-d7dd-5650-9b07-0e8553964639" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7741 :tutorial/title "Skipping the Intermediate Step"} {:activity/expected-seconds 480.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186167820} :activity/id #uuid "1dc924a5-3bab-5d8c-ba48-dfffbc669f9b" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050221 :topic/id #uuid "3748163a-70f7-518f-9382-77b8230a6624" :topic/math-academy-id 3237} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186167820 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167977 :tutorial/content "Given two solutions to a linear system of differential equations, any *constant-coefficient* linear combination of those solutions is also a solution to the system. This property of linear systems is called the **linearity principle** (or the **superposition principle**). Let's state this again, more precisely. If $\mathbf{u}(t)$ and $\mathbf{v}(t)$ are solutions to the homogeneous matrix differential equation $$ \mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t), $$ then the expression $$ c \, \mathbf{u}(t) + d \, \mathbf{v}(t) $$ is also a solution to that equation for all $c,d\in\mathbb{R}.$ We can prove this by substituting $\mathbf x(t) = c\mathbf{u}(t) +d\mathbf{v}(t)$ into the matrix differential equation and verifying that it results in a true statement: $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t) \\ (c\,u(t)+d\,v(t))^{′} & =A(c\,u(t)+d\,v(t)) \\ c\,{u}^{′}(t)+d\,{v}^{′}(t) & =cA\,u(t)+dA\,v(t) \\ c\,{u}^{′}(t)+d\,{v}^{′}(t) & =c\,{u}^{′}(t)+d\,{v}^{′}(t)\,✓\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $c\,\mathbf{u}(t) +d\,\mathbf{v}(t)$ is a solution! However, using it directly requires working with complex exponentials, which can be cumbersome. A more direct method is to find just *one* of the complex solutions, say $\mathbf x_1(t) = \mathbf{v}_1 e^{{\color{black}\lambda_1} t},$ and separate it into its *real and imaginary parts*. $$ \begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t} \\ & ={{{w}_{1}(t)}_{⏟}}_{\text{Real Part}}\,+\,\text{i}\,\,\,{{{w}_{2}(t)}_{⏟}}_{\text{Imaginary Part}}\end{aligned} $$ The general *real-valued* solution is then a linear combination of these two parts: $$ \mathbf x(t) = c_1 \mathbf w_1(t) + c_2 \mathbf w_2(t) $$ **Note:** This method may seem surprising. Why can we construct the general solution using only *one* of the complex solutions, $\mathbf x_1(t)?$ The reason is that the second solution, $\mathbf x_2(t),$ doesn't provide any new information. For a real matrix $A,$ the complex eigenvalues and eigenvectors come in *conjugate pairs*, which means $\mathbf x_2(t)$ is simply the complex conjugate of $\mathbf x_1(t).$ Since $\mathbf x_2(t) = \mathbf w_1 (t) - \textrm{i} \, \mathbf w_2(t),$ it is also a linear combination of the real and imaginary parts of $\mathbf x_1(t).$ To build our general solution, we just need two *linearly independent* real solutions. The key facts are the following: - For a system with complex eigenvalues, the real part $\mathbf w_1(t)$ and the imaginary part $\mathbf w_2(t)$ are *always* linearly independent. - Since they are two linearly independent solutions, they can form the basis for the general solution. So, we can use them directly and bypass the need to work with $\mathbf x_2(t)$ at all. Let's see a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "a93ff6d6-1eb0-5e42-8b69-ae73fc891839" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4283 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186157477} {:db/id 17592186158396 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158469 :tutorial/content "For a $2 \times 2$ matrix differential equation $$ \mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t), $$ we know that if $A$ has distinct eigenvalues, the general solution is $$ \mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{black}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{black}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{black}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{black}\lambda_2} t}. $$ This formula works even when the eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$ are complex. However, using it directly requires working with complex exponentials, which can be cumbersome. A more direct method is to find just *one* of the complex solutions, say $\mathbf x_1(t) = \mathbf{v}_1 e^{{\color{black}\lambda_1} t},$ and separate it into its *real and imaginary parts*. $$ \begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t} \\ & ={{{w}_{1}(t)}_{⏟}}_{\text{Real Part}}\,+\,\text{i}\,\,\,{{{w}_{2}(t)}_{⏟}}_{\text{Imaginary Part}}\end{aligned} $$ The general *real-valued* solution is then a linear combination of these two parts: $$ \mathbf x(t) = c_1 \mathbf w_1(t) + c_2 \mathbf w_2(t) $$ **Note:** This method may seem surprising. Why can we construct the general solution using only *one* of the complex solutions, $\mathbf x_1(t)?$ The reason is that the second solution, $\mathbf x_2(t),$ doesn't provide any new information. For a real matrix $A,$ the complex eigenvalues and eigenvectors come in *conjugate pairs*, which means $\mathbf x_2(t)$ is simply the complex conjugate of $\mathbf x_1(t).$ Since $\mathbf x_2(t) = \mathbf w_1 (t) - \textrm{i} \, \mathbf w_2(t),$ it is also a linear combination of the real and imaginary parts of $\mathbf x_1(t).$ To build our general solution, we just need two *linearly independent* real solutions. The key facts are the following: - For a system with complex eigenvalues, the real part $\mathbf w_1(t)$ and the imaginary part $\mathbf w_2(t)$ are *always* linearly independent. - Since they are two linearly independent solutions, they can form the basis for the general solution. So, we can use them directly and bypass the need to work with $\mathbf x_2(t)$ at all. "Recall that if $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ are the *spherical* polar coordinates of a point $P$ in the three-dimensional space, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found using the following formulas: $$ x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad z = \rho\cos\phi $$ ![](images/92/925aae5386657b35b3214db2a5348fc88872faec5ef63bc6237deed6e041f3de.png) With that in mind, let's find a parametrization of the sphere whose cartesian equation is $$ x^2+y^2+z^2=1. $$ This equation represents a unit sphere (i.e., a sphere of radius $1$) centered at the origin. Given a point $P$ on the sphere, the variable $\rho$ represents the *radial* distance between the origin and $P.$ Since every point on the sphere is a distance of $1$ from $O,$ we must have $\rho =1$ at every point on the sphere. Therefore, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following: $$ \begin{aligned}f(\theta ,ϕ) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\ & =⟨\rho \operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ,\,\rho \operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ,\,\rho \operatorname{cos}ϕ⟩ \\ & =⟨1\cdot \operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ,\,1\cdot \operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ,\,1\cdot \operatorname{cos}ϕ⟩ \\ & =⟨\operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ,\,\operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{sin}ϕ,\,\operatorname{cos}ϕ⟩\end{aligned} $$ where $\theta \in [0,2\pi)$ and $\phi \in [-\pi,\pi].$ As a result, the vector-valued function $$ \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi) = \big\langle \cos\theta\sin\phi, \: \sin\theta\sin\phi, \: \cos\phi \big\rangle, \qquad \theta \in [0,2\pi), \quad \phi \in [-\pi,\pi], $$ represents a parametrization of our sphere. **Watch out!** There are many possible parameterizations of the given sphere. Here, we found one of them." :tutorial/id #uuid "aee82c05-631b-590f-9841-c5436482a696" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5306 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid :question/math-academy-id "q-102354" :question/problem "Given the orthogonal basis $B$ of ${R}^{3}$ and the vector $x$ below, find the value of $\frac{5}{3}{x}_{1}$, where ${x}_{1}$ is the first component of $[x]_{B}.$ $$ B=\{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\}\,x=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4 \\ 8\end{bmatrix} $$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $B$ as ${q}_{1},\,{q}_{2},\,{q}_{3}.$ Since $B$ is an orthogonal basis, we have that $[x]_{B}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}$, where ${x}_{i}=\frac{x\cdot {q}_{i}}{{q}_{i}\cdot {q}_{i}}.$ Computing ${x}_{1},$ we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{x\cdot {q}_{1}}{{q}_{1}\cdot {q}_{1}} \\ & =\frac{2\cdot 1+4\cdot 2+8\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\ & =\frac{2+8+8}{1+4+1} \\ & =\frac{18}{6} \\ & =3.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \frac{5}{3}{x}_{1}=\frac{5}{3}\cdot 3=5. $$"} :step/id 17592186153285 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153326 :tutorial/content "The **unit step function**, $u(t)$, is used to model quantities that change suddenly at a specific time, such as the application of a force, the switching of a circuit, or the start of a signal. transform, $$ \begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,{e}^{at}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-a)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned} $$ Now recall that $$ F(s)=\int_0^{\infty} e^{-st}\,f(t)\,\textrm{d}t, \qquad s>s_0. $$ Comparing the two integrals, we see that $$ \int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s-a)t}\,f(t)\,\textrm{d}t =F(s-a). $$ For this to make sense, we need $s-a>s_0,$ which is equivalent to $$ s>s_0+a. $$ This result is known as the **First Shifting Theorem**: $$ \mathcal{L}\{e^{at}f(t)\} = F(s-a). $$ In the next slide, we will apply this result to a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "44078a68-8d27-5f6e-adec-348668ecef51" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14326 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "23a4eff8-b2bf-51f0-87ea-b1466d7af3ca" :step/math-academy-id 600094 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222358}} {:db/id 17592186222358 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222509 :tutorial/content "The **First shifting Theorem** states that if $$ \mathcal L\{f(t)\}=F(s) $$ for $s>s_0$, then $$ \mathcal L\{e^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a), \qquad s>s_0+a. $$ So, when you multiply a function by $e^{at}$, you do two things: - *Replace* $s$ with $s-a$ in the known transform $F(s)$. - *Shift the domain* from $s>s_0$ to $s>s_0+a$. To see this in action, consider the following example. We are given that $$ \mathcal{L}\{\sin(\omega t)\}=\frac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2}, \qquad s>0. $$ Suppose we want to compute $$ \mathcal{L}\{e^{2t}\sin(3t)\}. $$ First, we identify the base transform: $$ \mathcal{L}\{\sin(3t)\}=\frac{3}{s^2+3^2} $$ Next, we apply the first shifting theorem with $a=2$, which means we replace $s$ by $s-2$: $$ \begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\} & =\frac{3}{(s-2)^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\ & =\frac{3}{(s-2)^{2}+9}.\end{aligned} $$ Since the original transform is valid for $s>0$, the shifted transform is valid for $$ s>2. $$ This example illustrates the general pattern: multiplying by $e^{at}$ leads to a simple substitution $s:= s-a$, along with a corresponding shift in the domain." :tutorial/id #uuid "511f0e8e-f19d-5e1e-955e-97dbd8386ea2" "Using the first shifting theorem, we can obtain new Laplace transforms from old ones without performing any additional integration. If $$ \mathcal L\{f(t)\}=F(s) $$ for $s>s_0$, then $$ \mathcal L\{e^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a), \qquad s>s_0+a. $$ The table below shows some general results we can obtain using the first shifting theorem. | $f(t)$ | $F(s)=\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\}$ | Compare With | | --- | --- | --- | | $e^{at} t^n$ | $\dfrac{n!}{(s-a)^{n+1}}$ | $\mathcal L \{t^n\} = \dfrac{n!}{s^{n+1}}$ | | $e^{at}\sin \omega t$ | $\dfrac{\omega}{(s-a)^2+\omega^2}$ | $\mathcal L\{\sin\omega t\} = \dfrac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2}$ | | $e^{at}\cos \omega t$ | $\dfrac{s-a}{(s-a)^2+\omega^2}$ | $\mathcal L\{\cos\omega t\} = \dfrac{s}{s^2+\omega^2}$ | So, each new entry in our table is obtained by taking a known transform and replacing $s$ with $s-a$, and then shifting the domain accordingly." :tutorial/id #uuid "dbf3c06b-f0f4-528b-aff6-5b6adcae65b8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14692 :tutorial/title "A Laplace Transforms Comparison Table"} :step/id #uuid "aa6dc187-37cc-58ad-bd19-cba1f304979e" :step/math-academy-id 600111}] :activity/title "The First Shifting Theorem of Laplace Transforms" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186221462} {:db/id 17592186222357 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222476 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we learned how to compute Laplace transforms. We now examine how the Laplace transform changes when a function is multiplied by an exponential. Suppose $$ \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}=F(s) $$ exists for $s>s_0.$ We want to compute the Laplace transform of $e^{at}f(t).$ Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, $$ \begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,{e}^{at}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-a)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned} $$ Now recall that $$ F(s)=\int_0^{\infty} e^{-st}\,f(t)\,\textrm{d}t, \qquad s>s_0. $$ Comparing the two integrals, we see that $$ \int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s-a)t}\,f(t)\,\textrm{d}t =F(s-a). $$ For this to make sense, we need $s-a>s_0,$ which is equivalent to $$ s>s_0+a. $$ This result is known as the **First Shifting Theorem**: $$ \mathcal{L}\{e^{at}f(t)\} = F(s-a). $$ In the next slide, we will apply this result to a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "44078a68-8d27-5f6e-adec-348668ecef51" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14326 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "23a4eff8-b2bf-51f0-87ea-b1466d7af3ca" :step/math-academy-id 600094 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222358}} {:db/id 17592186222476 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we learned how to compute Laplace transforms. We now examine how the Laplace transform changes when a function is multiplied by an exponential. Suppose $$ \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}=F(s) $$ exists for $s>s_0.$ We want to compute the Laplace transform of $e^{at}f(t).$ Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, $$ \begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,{e}^{at}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-a)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned} $$ Now recall that $$ F(s)=\int_0^{\infty} e^{-st}\,f(t)\,\textrm{d}t, \qquad s>s_0. $$ Comparing the two integrals, we see that $$ \int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s-a)t}\,f(t)\,\textrm{d}t =F(s-a). $$ For this to make sense, we need $s-a>s_0,$ which is equivalent to $$ s>s_0+a. $$ This result is known as the **First Shifting Theorem**: $$ \mathcal{L}\{e^{at}f(t)\} = F(s-a). $$ In the next slide, we will apply this result to a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "44078a68-8d27-5f6e-adec-348668ecef51" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14326 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186222358 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222509 :tutorial/content "The **First shifting Theorem** states that if $$ \mathcal L\{f(t)\}=F(s) $$ for $s>s_0$, then $$ \mathcal L\{e^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a), \qquad s>s_0+a. $$ So, when you multiply a function by $e^{at}$, you do two things: - *Replace* $s$ with $s-a$ in the known transform $F(s)$. - *Shift the domain* from $s>s_0$ to $s>s_0+a$. To see this in action, consider the following example. We are given that $$ \mathcal{L}\{\sin(\omega t)\}=\frac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2}, \qquad s>0. $$ Suppose we want to compute $$ \mathcal{L}\{e^{2t}\sin(3t)\}. $$ First, we identify the base transform: $$ \mathcal{L}\{\sin(3t)\}=\frac{3}{s^2+3^2} $$ Next, we apply the first shifting theorem with $a=2$, which means we replace $s$ by $s-2$: $$ \begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\} & =\frac{3}{(s-2)^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\ & =\frac{3}{(s-2)^{2}+9}.\end{aligned} $$ Since the original transform is valid for $s>0$, the shifted transform is valid for $$ s>2. $$ This example illustrates the general pattern: multiplying by $e^{at}$ leads to a simple substitution $s:= s-a$, along with a corresponding shift in the domain." :tutorial/id #uuid "511f0e8e-f19d-5e1e-955e-97dbd8386ea2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14590 :tutorial/title "Using the First Shifting Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "3390cec0-8a87-5c98-86f2-ba843c736c0d" :step/math-academy-id 600095 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222359}} {:db/id 17592186222509 :tutorial/content "The **First shifting Theorem** states that if $$ \mathcal L\{f(t)\}=F(s) $$ for $s>s_0$, then $$ \mathcal L\{e^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a), \qquad s>s_0+a. $$ So, when you multiply a function by $e^{at}$, you do two things: - *Replace* $s$ with $s-a$ in the known transform $F(s)$. - *Shift the domain* from $s>s_0$ to $s>s_0+a$. Laplace transform of $f(t)=2{e}^{-3t}+7{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}$ for $s>5.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms: $$ \begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{2{e}^{-3t}+7{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\} \\ & =L\{2{e}^{-3t}\}+L\{7{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\} \\ & =2L\{{e}^{-3t}\}+7L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\}\end{aligned} $$ We are given that, for $s>0,$ $$ \begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we have the following: $$ \begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{2}\} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\end{aligned} $$ The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\} & =\frac{2}{(s-5)^{3}}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is $$ \begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =2L\{{e}^{-3t}\}+7L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\} \\ & =2\cdot \frac{1}{s+3}+7\cdot \frac{2}{(s-5)^{3}} \\ & =\frac{2}{s+3}+\frac{14}{(s-5)^{3}}.\end{aligned} $$ This transform is valid for $s>5.$"} :step/id :question/worked-solution "The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the Laplace transform of $f(t)=2{e}^{-3t}+7{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}$ for $s>5.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms: $$ \begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{2{e}^{-3t}+7{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\} \\ & =L\{2{e}^{-3t}\}+L\{7{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\} \\ & =2L\{{e}^{-3t}\}+7L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\}\end{aligned} $$ We are given that, for $s>0,$ $$ \begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we have the following: $$ \begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{2}\} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\end{aligned} $$ The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\} & =\frac{2}{(s-5)^{3}}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is $$ \begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =2L\{{e}^{-3t}\}+7L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\} \\ & =2\cdot \frac{1}{s+3}+7\cdot \frac{2}{(s-5)^{3}} \\ & =\frac{2}{s+3}+\frac{14}{(s-5)^{3}}.\end{aligned} $$ This transform is valid for $s>5.$"} :step/id are given that, for $s>0,$ $$ \begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we have the following: $$ \begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}} \\ L\{{t}^{3}\} & =\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}\end{aligned} $$ The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore, $$ L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\}=\frac{6}{(s-2)^{4}}. $$ Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is $$ \begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =6L\{t\}+4L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}\} \\ & =6\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+4\cdot \frac{6}{(s-2)^{4}} \\ & =\frac{6}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{24}{(s-2)^{4}}.\end{aligned} $$ This transform is valid for $s>2.$"} :step/id #uuid "1ca3e022-cc39-56cd-87c5-f311545581d9"} {:db/id 17592186498616 :step/content {:db/id :tutorial/content "A linear transformation $\mathbf{Q}:\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is an **orthogonal linear transformation** if for any $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ we have that $$ \mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y}. $$ In this case, we say that $\mathbf{Q}$ *preserves the dot product*. The linear transformation $\mathbf{Q}$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following: - The matrix $Q$ of transformation $\mathbf{Q}$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is orthogonal. - $\| \mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{x}) \| = \| \mathbf{x} \|$. In other words, $\mathbf{Q}$ preserves vector norms. - If $\mathbf{x} \perp \mathbf{y}$ then $\mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{x}) \perp \mathbf{Q}(\mathbf{y})$ for any $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$ In general, $\mathbf{Q}$ preserves the angle between any two vectors. - $\mathbf{Q}$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set." :tutorial/id #uuid :question/math-academy-id "q-40491" :question/problem "Let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following are orthogonal sets? - **U.** $U={Q(\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix})}$ - **W.** $W={Q(\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -1\end{bmatrix})}$ - **V.** $V={Q(\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix})}$ Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$ Let's denote the elements of $U,W,$ and $V$ respectively as $\,$ ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})},\,$ ${Q({w}_{1}),Q({w}_{2})},\,$ and $\,{Q({v}_{1}),Q({v}_{2}),Q({v}_{3})}.$ The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthogonal if the following conditions on each set hold: - $Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})=0.$ - $Q({w}_{1})\cdot Q({w}_{2})=0.$ - $Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{2})=0,\,Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{3})=0,\,Q({v}_{2})\cdot Q({v}_{3})=0.$ With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn. - For the set $U,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2}) & ={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}=18-18=0.\,✓\end{aligned} $$ So, the set $U$ is orthogonal. - For the set $W,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}Q({w}_{1})\cdot Q({w}_{2}) & ={w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=1-1=0.\,✓\end{aligned} $$ So, the set $W$ is orthogonal. - For the Set $V,$ notice that $$ \begin{aligned}Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{2}) & ={v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=2+12-5=9\ne 0.\,\times \end{aligned} $$ So, $V$ is not an orthogonal set. Therefore, the correct answer is "$U$ and $W$ only"."} :step/id #uuid "5c0620be-2d88-50a9-b295-5b90712b0a8b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186406659}} {:db/id 17592186406659 :step/content {:db/id 17592186406654 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24e42699-a0f0-5e81-a194-c91514b7e8ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{6}" :db/id 17592186406638} {:answer/id #uuid "46c27bd0-b639-51d1-a04d-8098da45991e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186406642} {:answer/id #uuid "b3565871-fc75-5a3f-bb6e-506cbb0458f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186406644} {:answer/id #uuid "bfd57b0f-3965-5b70-833f-7fa36e06ae4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186406646} {:answer/id #uuid "e14e0ad1-a7b2-5023-b79c-bff39fbd35df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186406649}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186406644} :answer-field/id #uuid "491c6e1c-81dd-5170-b618-833ce2679d93" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186406651}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8a69da2c-f673-5e64-a265-9fe904a3c9ad" :question/math-academy-id "q-40514" :question/problem "Let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. :question/math-academy-id "q-178268" :question/problem "$$ {u}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] $$ Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true? I. ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0$ II. $\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})\}$ is orthogonal III. $\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})\}$ is orthonormal" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$ The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following: - The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal. - $||Q(x)||=||x||.$ - If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors. - $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set. With that in mind, let's examine our statements. - Statement I is false. Indeed, $$ {u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=2+2\ne 0. $$ - Statement II is false. Notice that, $Q({u}_{1})⊥̸Q({u}_{2})$ since $$ Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}\ne 0. $$ - Statement III is false since the set is not even orthogonal. Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true.""} :step/id #uuid "eef50253-8c08-55c7-bab7-bc37bdee6bfe" :step/next {:db/id 17592186526149}} {:db/id 17592186526149 :step/content where $\mathbf F$ is the resultant force, measured in **Newtons** $(\text N),$ $m$ is the mass, measured in $\textrm{kg},$ and $\mathbf a$ is the acceleration, measured in $\textrm{m/s}^2.$ Note the following: - Force, like acceleration, is a *vector* quantity. - The term "resultant force" means the (vector) sum of forces acting on the particle. - When considering forces acting in one dimension, we usually write $$F = ma.$$ From this equation, we see that a $1\,\textrm{N}$ is the total force required to accelerate a mass of $m = 1\,\textrm{kg}$ at a rate of $a = 1\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$ Let's see One such method is the trapezoidal method, which takes the *average slope in the interval between $x$ and $x_\text{new} = x + \Delta x.$* More formally, the **trapezoidal method** with step size $\Delta x$ is given by $$ \Delta y = \dfrac12(y' + y'_\text{new}) \cdot \Delta x, $$ with $y'_\text{new} = f(x_\text{new},y_\text{new})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values. Like the implicit Euler method, the trapezoidal method is an implicit numerical method. To apply the method, we substitute the formula for $\Delta y$ into the update formula $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{2}({y}^{'}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{'})\cdot Δx \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{2}(f(x,y)+f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}}))\cdot Δx,\end{aligned} $$ and solve the resulting implicit equation for $y_\text{new}$ directly, rather than explicitly calculating the value of $\Delta y$ beforehand. In this lesson, we'll focus on IVPs whose slope function is linear in $y,$ i.e., of the form $$ f(x,y) = a(x)y + b(x). $$ In such cases, we can simply solve the implicit equation for $y_\text{new},$ as demonstrated in the following worked example. For more complex slope functions, we require a root-finding method, such as Newton's method, to solve the implicit equation iteratively. Since the step size $\Delta x = 1$ remains the same, the update formula derived in the previous step still applies. From the previous step, we have $x=1$ and $y=9.$ Hence, the new $x$-value is $x_\text{new} = 1+1=2,$ and the new $y$-value is $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =1+2+3\cdot 9+2 \\ & =32.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we conclude that $y(2) \approx 32.$ We can visualize this second step as follows: ![](images/cd/cd9752c16b15ebcfcfa214c775e99fb68139a1dfa9364a5f552fbf676d7953f7.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "31f14503-26a9-5e09-b9cf-10a636f52db7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14898 :tutorial/title "Multiple Iterations of the Trapezoidal Method"} :step/id #uuid "b71ca947-77a6-59f8-9d4b-6ed77ec28832" :step/math-academy-id 608074 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222369}}] :activity/title "The Trapezoidal Method" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186221465} {:db/id 17592186222365 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222492 :tutorial/content "We have seen how, for an initial value problem $$ y' = f(x,y), \qquad y(a) = c, $$ Euler's method approximates a solution by evaluating the slope at the current point, $$ \Delta y = y' \cdot \Delta x, $$ while the implicit Euler method approximates a solution by evaluating the slope at the next point, $$ \Delta y = y'_\text{new} \cdot \Delta x. $$ Both have their advantages, but is there a way to combine them into one numerical method, applying the slope at both the current point and next point to update $y?$ Yes, there is! One such method is the trapezoidal method, which takes the *average slope in the interval between $x$ and $x_\text{new} = x + \Delta x.$* More formally, the **trapezoidal method** with step size $\Delta x$ is given by $$ \Delta y = \dfrac12(y' + y'_\text{new}) \cdot \Delta x, $$ with $y'_\text{new} = f(x_\text{new},y_\text{new})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values. Like the implicit Euler method, the trapezoidal method is an implicit numerical method. To apply the method, we substitute the formula for $\Delta y$ into the update formula $$ \begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{2}({y}^{'}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{'})\cdot Δx \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{2}(f(x,y)+f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}}))\cdot Δx,\end{aligned} $$ and solve the resulting implicit equation for $y_\text{new}$ directly, rather than explicitly calculating the value of $\Delta y$ beforehand. In this lesson, we'll focus on IVPs whose slope function is linear in $y,$ i.e., of the form $$ f(x,y) = a(x)y + b(x). $$ In such cases, we can simply solve the implicit equation for $y_\text{new},$ as demonstrated in the following worked example. For more complex slope functions, we require a root-finding method, such as Newton's method, to solve the implicit equation iteratively. The system is called **almost linear** at an equilibrium point $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ if the Jacobian determinant at this point is nonzero there, i.e. $$ \det\!\bigl(\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}^\ast)\bigr)\neq 0. $$ For example, let ![](images/e6/e640b7ca9ddc8252223ec70f011147a702cd25bca0ee8a20314693695c1bec40.svg) First, notice that $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}^\ast)=\mathbf{0},$ so $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ is an equilibrium. =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y)=1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)=1\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have ![](images/93/93058061ca42daa7114b615bcb77a8f9ccbc9cdccec98559db3eb288a7208940.svg) Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](images/72/72feeca197610c24c70b01f4c1075c75eebe89ae29f1aced83caeb252c275cce.svg) to get $$ \begin{aligned}J(0,0) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1+2(0) \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, since the Jacobian is $0,$ the system is *not* almost linear at $\mathbf{x}^\ast$." :tutorial/id #uuid 17592186222326 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222496 :tutorial/content "Suppose the system $$ \mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}), $$ is almost linear at an equilibrium $\mathbf{x}^\ast.$ In this case, the system's behavior near $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ can be approximated by a linear system. First, we define the deviation from equilibrium by $$ \mathbf{u}=\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^\ast. $$ Small values of $\mathbf{u}$ correspond to points close to the equilibrium. Next, assuming $\mathbf{x} = [x, y]^T,$ we compute the Jacobian matrix ![](images/7a/7a0ff677dae0e51e34aed63faadfcb31f277f060c03488fdc1828cf8a2a5a0ec.svg) and evaluate it at $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ to obtain the constant matrix $J = \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}^\ast).$ Finally, since $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}^\ast)=\mathbf{0},$ the nonlinear system can be approximated by the **linearized system** $$ \mathbf{u}'= J \mathbf{u}. $$ This linear system captures the leading-order behavior of solutions close to the equilibrium. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "9356e91f-f080-5827-a567-781aedac309a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14494 :tutorial/title "Linear Approximations Near Equilibria"} :step/id #uuid "c10be260-d12b-595c-b241-523d377180f4" :step/math-academy-id 591484 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222327}} {:db/id 17592186222327 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221418 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221181 :question/id #uuid "87b69a53-94f5-51e6-9c3a-e403abbf1fa3" :question/math-academy-id "e-21674"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a9aeac73-8ee3-5fef-a47c-a96e3545d89c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049962} {:db/id 17592186050780}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221965} {:db/id 17592186221966} {:db/id 17592186368134} {:db/id 17592186368143} {:db/id 17592186368152} {:db/id 17592186368175} {:db/id 17592186368184} {:db/id 17592186444533} {:db/id 17592186444536} {:db/id 17592186444541} {:db/id 17592186444542} {:db/id 17592186510396}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Linear Approximations Near Equilibria"} :step/id #uuid "264a8b35-ed46-5392-a8ec-e88ead83801a" :step/math-academy-id 591485 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222328}} {:db/id 17592186222328 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222495 :tutorial/content "Again, suppose $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ is an equilibrium of the nonlinear system $$ \mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}), $$ and assume the system is *almost linear* at $\mathbf{x}^\ast$. This information can be summarized in the following table. | **Eigenvalues of the Jacobian** | **Behavior** | **Stability** | | --- | --- | --- | | real and both positive | source / unstable node | 17592186222330}} {:db/id 17592186222330 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222497 :tutorial/content "In the classification above, we intentionally skipped one case: The eigenvalues $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ of the Jacobian at the equilibrium are purely imaginary. In this situation, the corresponding linearized system has a *center* at the origin, meaning that solutions neither grow nor decay, but instead circulate around the equilibrium. For the original nonlinear system, however, this case is *inconclusive*. While the linearized system predicts closed orbits, the nonlinear system *may* exhibit a stable center, an unstable spiral, or other nearby behavior. Therefore, when the Jacobian has purely imaginary eigenvalues, linearization alone is not sufficient to classify the equilibrium. In such cases, further analysis beyond linear approximation is required." :tutorial/id #uuid "5d168b25-7771-5e55-8be8-2eb16080b9b0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14496 :tutorial/title "A Note About Stable Centers"} :step/id #uuid "d039d8e2-81e7-5160-bcfd-7765a694f63a" :step/math-academy-id 591492}] :activity/title "Linear Approximations Near Equilibria" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186221470} {:db/id 17592186222324 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222494 :tutorial/content "Consider an autonomous system written as $$ \mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}), $$ where ![](images/60/60be83e58a72728b03ebfa2de6999ec80f17ee29e3f2ab3060d8ca43bbf45de8.svg) and ![](images/98/98bb67f212fa8deee63da1b69ae93086b9eb56a3ec64d70ba36e6a94dff1527b.svg). The system is called **almost linear** at an equilibrium point $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ if the Jacobian determinant at this point is nonzero there, i.e. $$ \det\!\bigl(\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}^\ast)\bigr)\neq 0. $$ For example, let ![](images/e6/e640b7ca9ddc8252223ec70f011147a702cd25bca0ee8a20314693695c1bec40.svg) First, notice that $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}^\ast)=\mathbf{0},$ so $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ is an equilibrium. Now, we compute the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y+{y}^{2})=1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y+{y}^{2})=1+2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y)=1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)=1\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have ![](images/93/93058061ca42daa7114b615bcb77a8f9ccbc9cdccec98559db3eb288a7208940.svg) Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](images/72/72feeca197610c24c70b01f4c1075c75eebe89ae29f1aced83caeb252c275cce.svg) to get $$ \begin{aligned}J(0,0) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1+2(0) \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, since the Jacobian is $0,$ the system is *not* almost linear at $\mathbf{x}^\ast$." :tutorial/id #uuid "fbbe8bd0-4cef-54d0-9803-a59eee727c6d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14492 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6570665c-9c0e-5698-9c44-79ef60fe6401" :step/math-academy-id 591480 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222325}} {:db/id 17592186222494 :tutorial/content "Consider an autonomous system written as $$ \mathbf{x}'=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}), $$ where ![](images/60/60be83e58a72728b03ebfa2de6999ec80f17ee29e3f2ab3060d8ca43bbf45de8.svg) and ![](images/98/98bb67f212fa8deee63da1b69ae93086b9eb56a3ec64d70ba36e6a94dff1527b.svg). &=-3x(t)+{y}^{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}?$ | ${u}^{′}=\,\,$ | | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} | | $\,\,u,\,$ where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} | | | |" :question/worked-solution "The system can be rewritten in matrix form as $$ {x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x) $$ where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+2y \\ -3x+{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.$ We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ In -5\end{aligned}]. $$ Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by $$ {u}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}]u, $$ where the deviation vector is $$ What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[2,\text{ }1]^{T}?$ | ${u}^{′}=\,\,$ | | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} | | $\,\,u,\,$ where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} | | | |" :question/worked-solution "The system can be rewritten in matrix form as $$ {x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x) $$ where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+2y-6 \\ x-3y+{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.$ We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ In our case, we have the following: $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix} $$ First, we compute the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2y-6)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2y-6)=2 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x-3y+{y}^{2})=1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-3y+{y}^{2})=-3+2y\end{aligned} $$ Thus, we have $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2x & 2 \\ 1 & 2y-3\end{bmatrix}. $$ Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ to get $$ \text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}2(2) & 2 \\ 1 & 2(1)-3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}. $$ Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by $$ {u}^{′}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}u, $$ where the deviation vector is $$ u=x-{x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y-1\end{bmatrix}. $$"} :step/id #uuid
