In general, if $f$ is a differentiable real-valued function of $n$ variables, $\mathbf y$ is a point in the domain of $f,$ and if the gradient vector is nonzero, i.e., $$ \nabla f (\mathbf y)= \left \langle f_{x_1}(\mathbf y), f_{x_2}(\mathbf y), \cdots, f_{x_n}(\mathbf y)\right \rangle \neq \mathbf 0, $$ then we have the following result: *$\nabla f (\mathbf y)$ is a normal vector to the level $z=f(x,y)$, if both partial derivatives $f_x,$ $f_y$ exist and are continuous in a neighborhood of a point $P(x_0,y_0)$ in the domain of the function, and if $\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0) \neq \mathbf 0,$ then we have the following result: *$\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $C$ that passes through the point $P.$ * This property is one of the most important facts in multivariable calculus since it gives a fundamental link between calculus and geometry! Let's illustrate this property with a concrete example. Consider the paraboloid $z = f (x, y)= x^2 + y^2$ and the level curve $\color{red}C$ of $f(x,y)$ corresponding to the point $P(1,-1).$ It is easy to see that $\color{red}C$ is a circle of radius $\sqrt{2}$ with equation $x^2+y^2 = 2.$ ![](images/f2/f2461dbfcde2403e6ed7de9d6288d33a4deb52319d35b7036628c3fa8b3789dc.png) In this particular instance, the property says that *$\nabla \! f(1,-1)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $\color{red}C$ that passes through the point $P(1,-1).$ * ![](images/48/481b68af522b9144e232d9c775f734cd998b31a21571cbfd983c23d0f68c3688.png) Looking at the situation in the $xy$-plane, we see the following: ![](images/ce/ceb353d5164d6aa089a37e77c9469d747ef4430e363e42f9d35ee6d769d9a4e4.png) Let's verify that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is a normal line to the level curve $C$ at the point $P(1,-1).$ - First, computing the gradient, we find that $\nabla f = \langle 2x, 2y \rangle.$ Therefore, $$ \nabla f(1,-1) = \langle 2, -2 \rangle. $$ - Then, using elementary calculus, we can show that the equation of the tangent to $C$ at $P$ is $y=x-2.$ Since this line has slope $m=1,$ it follows that the vector $\langle 1,1 \rangle$ is parallel to the level curve. - Finally, taking the dot product between the gradient and the tangent vector, we obtain $$ \nabla f(1,-1)\cdot \langle 1,1 \rangle = \langle 2, -2\rangle \cdot \langle 1,1 \rangle = 0. $$ This means that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is *perpendicular* to the tangent line to $C$ at $(1,-1).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "68a96106-e224-5989-af04-8d464b6e58d5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2499 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "35b375f8-a01b-56db-97b7-ac88f2a7883a" :step/math-academy-id 11200 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125306}} {:db/id 17592186125735 :tutorial/content "Given a function $z=f(x,y)$, if both partial derivatives $f_x,$ $f_y$ exist and are continuous in a neighborhood of a point $P(x_0,y_0)$ in the domain of the function, and if $\nabla \! $f(x,y,z)=2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1).$" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-2,-3,1).$ So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1):$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\ & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy)\,k \\ & =(4x-y)\text{ }i-x\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-2,-3,1) & =(4(-2)-(-3))\,i-(-2)\,j+2(1)\,k \\ & =-5\,i+2\,j+2\,k\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $-5\,i+2\,j+2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1).$"} "ef115c0b-3981-5c8f-8e9d-f41c20799c2d" :question/math-academy-id "q-130719" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $2y-x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y}).$ Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side: $$ \begin{aligned}2y-x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x & =0\end{aligned} $$ If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,1).$ So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,1):$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\ & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x)j \\ & =(\frac{2y}{x}\cdot \frac{1}{2y}+1)i+(\frac{2y}{x}\cdot (-\frac{x}{2{y}^{2}})-2)j \\ & =(\frac{1}{x}+1)i+(-\frac{1}{y}-2)j \\ ∇f(2,1) & =(\frac{1}{2}+1)i+(-\frac{1}{1}-2)j \\ & =\frac{3}{2}\,i-3\,j \\ & =⟨\frac{3}{2},-3⟩\end{aligned} $$ Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨\frac{3}{2},-3⟩$ is a normal =2(-1)\text{ }i+2(-1)\text{ }j+2(1)\text{ }k \\ & =-2\,i-2\,j+2\,k \\ & =⟨-2,-2,2⟩\end{aligned} $$ Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $xy={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7.$ Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side: $$ \begin{aligned}xy & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7 \\ 0 & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7\end{aligned} $$ If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\ & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,j \\ & =(2x-y)\,i+(2y-x)\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(2(2)-(-1))\,i+(2(-1)-2)\,j \\ & =5\,i-4\,j \\ & =⟨5,-4⟩\end{aligned} $$ Hence, $∇f(2,-1)=⟨5,-4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,-1).$ Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{5} & =\frac{y-(-1)}{-4} \\ -4(x-2) & =5(y+1) \\ -4x-5y+8-5 & =0 \\ -4x-5y+3 & =0 \\ 4x+5y-3 & =0\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid "053dd984-66f7-5e60-a777-6ca3631e9fa4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186497423}} {:db/id 17592186497423 :step/content :question/worked-solution "If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-3{y}^{2},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=6.$ A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(3,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,1).$ So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,1):$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\ & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,j \\ & =2x\,i-6y\,j \\ ∇f(3,1) & =2(3)\,i-6(1)\,j \\ & =6\,i-6\,j \\ & =⟨6,-6⟩\end{aligned} $$ Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨6,-6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(3,1).$ Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-3}{6} & =\frac{y-1}{(-6)} \\ -6(x-3) & =6(y-1) \\ -(x-3) & =y-1 \\ -x+3 & =y-1 \\ x+y-4 & =0\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id :question/math-academy-id "q-71406" :question/problem "Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz$ at the point $(1,0,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side: $$ \begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned} $$ If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0,1).$ So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,1):$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\ & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)k \\ & =(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+yz)\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xz)\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,0,1) & =(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(0)(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(1))\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(0))\,k \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{3}{2}\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k \\ & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned} $$ Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be written as $$ \begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,∇f(1,0,1)=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩,\end{aligned} $$ where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$"} :step/id #uuid point $(3,1).$" :question/worked-solution "If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-3{y}^{2},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=6.$ A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(3,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,1).$ So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,1):$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\ & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,j \\ & =2x\,i-6y\,j \\ ∇f(3,1) & =2(3)\,i-6(1)\,j \\ & =6\,i-6\,j \\ & =⟨6,-6⟩\end{aligned} $$ Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨6,-6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(3,1).$ Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-3}{6} & =\frac{y-1}{(-6)} \\ -6(x-3) & =6(y-1) \\ -(x-3) & =y-1 \\ -x+3 & =y-1 \\ x+y-4 & =0\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{u}^{2}+{v}^{2} \\ uv\end{bmatrix}. $$" :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation $$ T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}, $$ the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve $$ \frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0. $$ Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=uv.$ First, we find the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =v\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\ & =\begin{vmatrix}2u & 2v \\ v & u\end{vmatrix} \\ & =2u\cdot u-2v\cdot v \\ & =2{u}^{2}-2{v}^{2}.\end{aligned} $$ The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ 2{u}^{2}-2{v}^{2} & =0 \\ {v}^{2} & ={u}^{2}.\end{aligned} $$ The equation ${v}^{2}={u}^{2}$ defines a pair of intersecting lines $v=u$ and $v=-u$ in the $uv$-plane."} {:db/id 17592186199001 :question/id #uuid "1a6af403-e6c8-5c17-8e90-e6cdab8d3462" :question/math-academy-id "q-81169"} {:db/id 17592186278306 :question/id #uuid $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve $$ \frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0. $$ Here, we have $x(u,v)=v(u-1)^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=v{u}^{2}.$ First, we find the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2(u-1)v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =(u-1)^{2} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2uv & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & ={u}^{2}\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\ & =\begin{vmatrix}2(u-1)v & (u-1)^{2} \\ 2uv & {u}^{2}\end{vmatrix} \\ & =2(u-1)v\cdot {u}^{2}-(u-1)^{2}\cdot 2uv \\ & =2{u}^{2}(u-1)v-2u(u-1)^{2}v.\end{aligned} $$ The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ 2{u}^{2}(u-1)v-2u(u-1)^{2}v & =0 \\ 2u(u-1)v(u-(u-1)) & =0 \\ 2u(u-1)v & =0.\end{aligned} $$ The equation $2u(u-1)v=0$ defines the lines $u=0,$ $u=1,$ and $v=0$ in the $uv$-plane."} {:db/id 17592186383522 :question/id #uuid "9f0fb416-ba54-5520-a3cd-23b891dc09c2" :question/math-academy-id "q-160477" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}, $$ the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve $$ \frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0. $$ Here, we have $x(u,v)=u{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)={u}^{2}+2v.$ First, we find the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={v}^{2} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2uv \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =2\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\ & =\begin{vmatrix}{v}^{2} & 2uv \\ 2u & 2\end{vmatrix} \\ & ={v}^{2}\cdot 2-2uv\cdot 2u \\ & =2{v}^{2}-4{u}^{2}v.\end{aligned} $$ The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ 2{v}^{2}-4{u}^{2}v & =0 \\ v(2v-4{u}^{2}) & =0.\end{aligned} $$ The equation $v(2v-4{u}^{2})=0$ defines the line $v=0,$ i.e., the $u$-axis, and the parabola $v=2{u}^{2}$ in the $uv$-plane."} {:db/id 17592186401179 :question/id #uuid "6940edb0-4ff9-5079-afa0-d099bcae85dd" :question/math-academy-id \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve $$ \frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0. $$ Here, we have $x(u,v)=3{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=u+v.$ First, we find the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =6u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =4v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\ & =\begin{vmatrix}6u & 4v \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ & =6u\cdot 1-4v\cdot 1 \\ & =6u-4v.\end{aligned} $$ The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ 6u-4v & =0 \\ v & =\frac{3}{2}u.\end{aligned} $$ The equation $v=\frac{3}{2}u$ defines a line in the $uv$-plane."} {:db/id 17592186402616 \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\ & =\begin{vmatrix}3(u-1)^{2} & -3(v-2)^{2} \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ & =3(u-1)^{2}\cdot 1-(-3(v-2)^{2})\cdot 1 \\ & =3(u-1)^{2}+3(v-2)^{2}.\end{aligned} $$ The function compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation $$ \frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}. $$ Here, we have $u(x,y)=2xy$ and $v(x,y)=\frac{y}{x}.$ First, we compute the case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows: - First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$ - Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation $$ \frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}. $$ Here, we have $u(x,y)=xy$ and $v(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}.$ First, we compute the partial -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{vmatrix} \\ & =y\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}})-x\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\ & =-\frac{2x}{y} \\ & =-2v.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we take the reciprocal: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\ & =-\frac{1}{2v}\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186351292 :question/id #uuid "7c73b659-30f6-5b1c-afe8-2ef5c03763e0" true according to the inverse function theorem. - $f$ is invertible in some neighborhood of $x=1$ - ${f}^{-1}(y)$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $y=-2$ - The derivative of ${f}^{-1}(y)$ at $y=2.91$ equals $\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(3)}$ Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "The inverse function theorem for single-variable functions states the following: *If $f:U\to R$ is continuously differentiable on an open set $U⊆R,$ $f(a)=b$ and ${f}^{′}(a)\ne 0$ for $a\in U,$ then* - *$f$ is invertible in some neighborhood of $a,$* - *${f}^{-1},$ the inverse of $f,$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $b,$ and* - *the derivative of ${f}^{-1}$ is given by* $$ {({f}^{-1})}^{′}(b)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(a)}=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(b))}\,. $$ With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn. - Statement I is true. The function $f$ satisfies the conditions for the inverse function theorem at $x=1.$ Indeed, - $f$ is continuously differentiable on an open set containing $x=1,$ for example, $(0,2),$ and - the derivative of $f$ is nonzero at $x=1,$ i.e., ${f}^{′}(1)\ne 0.$ Therefore, by the inverse function theorem, $f$ is invertible in *some* neighborhood of $x=1.$ - Statement II is false. Notice that $y=-2=f(2).$ However, the function $f$ does *not* satisfy the conditions for the inverse function theorem at $x=2$ since ${f}^{′}(2)=0.$ So, the theorem can't be applied in this situation. - Statement III is false. Notice that $y=2.91=f(3),$ but $f$ is not continuous at $x=3.$ So, the theorem can't be applied in this situation. Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} {:db/id 17592186281362 :question/id #uuid "649157e5-32cb-5583-98fc-af0b21c39379" :question/math-academy-id "q-161858"} {:db/id 17592186281363 :question/id 17592186199314}} {:db/id 17592186199249 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199450 :tutorial/content "Consider a transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by ![](images/fe/fefb7b82a6da1421bb96798fe6377e66199b50b8630dc396518927a0f3fe204b.svg) The points in the $(u,v)$ plane where $\mathbf T$ is *locally* non-invertible are known as **critical points**. We've already seen that $\mathbf T$ is locally non-invertible when the Jacobian determinant is zero. Therefore, the critical points of $\mathbf T$ are the solutions to the equation $$ \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}=0. $$ Let's compute the critical points of the following transformation: ![](images/8e/8e55b2da9a0c1fcf1ab901d361c50b652c906b92f0fcd4b158793f7782cfe5f4.svg) First, we find the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =4u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-6v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\ & =|\begin{aligned}4u & -6v \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ & =4u\cdot 1-(-6v)\cdot (-1) \\ & =4u-6v.\end{aligned} $$ The function has critical points when the Jacobian equals zero. So, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ 4u-6v & =0 \\ 2u-3v & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the critical points of $\mathbf{T}$ consist of those points that lie on the line $2u-3v=0$ in the $uv$-plane, shown below. ![](images/5c/5c544e3d3ecbdeaf7dc372b40ee0f37cb14e3ba292b8180a263c91103a9efe61.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "5f47e688-774b-5c89-a90d-ead52a871598" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4312 :tutorial/title "Critical Points of Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "16b2c818-03e6-5801-97b2-0ce8d225c3d5" :step/math-academy-id 26206 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199248}} {:db/id 17592186199266 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199460 :tutorial/content "Let's now state the so-called **inverse function theorem** for single-variable functions: *If $f: U \to \Bbb R$ is continuously differentiable on an open set $U\subseteq \mathbb R,$ $f(a) = b$ and $f'(a)\neq 0$ for $a\in U,$ then* - *$f$ is invertible in some neighborhood of $a,$* - *$f^{-1},$ the inverse of $f,$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $b,$ and* - *the derivative of $f^{-1}$ is given by* $$ \left(f^{-1}\right)'(b) = \dfrac{1}{f'(a)} =\dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(b))}\,. $$ To explain this concretely, consider the graph below: ![](images/4d/4dfd8b142b594a2ca4f0e39f9b8ca1e04018bf0efd63f9dc2235bd61e9f9d70e.png) In this example, the function $f$ is continuously differentiable at $x=a$ and has a nonzero derivative. As a result, $f^{-1}$ exists in a neighborhood of $x=b$ and is continuously differentiable at this point. On the other hand, if $f$ is continuously differentiable at $x=a$ but $f'(a) = 0,$ then one of two things can happen: - **Case 1**: The function $f$ does not have a local inverse at $a.$ ![](images/04/04ee310e6068e517aec42a67fa83837986f8807e1250b89b52e7a62e3975bb38.png) In the example above, $f$ is not one-to-one in a neighborhood of $a,$ so it's not invertible there. - **Case 2**: The function $f$ has a local inverse at $a,$ but its inverse is not continuously differentiable at $b.$ ![](images/3e/3e2738a16f999d503fb295f4fd6535a854884468a4d190ffa537a4ec9295490c.png) In the example above, $f$ is invertible in a neighborhood of $a,$ but $f^{-1}$ is not differentiable at $x=b$ since it has a vertical tangent at this point." :tutorial/id #uuid "c45037f7-31c7-5911-a00d-edaa4c5b86e4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7036 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "54cb06ef-1ffc-5b15-9147-a1baf70b985c" :step/math-academy-id 42404 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199315}} {:db/id 17592186199268 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198370 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198012 :question/id #uuid "f794d50a-cb44-5a6f-a922-8438a6192d46" :question/math-academy-id "e-11157"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2fe16334-8f63-56ed-bd58-95e095993b9f" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186199002} {:db/id 17592186199003} {:db/id 17592186278312} {:db/id 17592186278313} {:db/id 17592186278314} {:db/id 17592186278315} {:db/id 17592186278316} {:db/id 17592186351292} {:db/id 17592186351297} {:db/id 17592186479853} {:db/id 17592186486385}] :knowledge-point/title "Jacobian Determinants of Inverse Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "1b07afe2-9993-5d3c-bfe7-b98917224b3b" :step/math-academy-id 42423} {:db/id 17592186199314 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199477 :tutorial/content "The inverse function theorem can be generalized to transformations too. We state it below: *Let $\mathbf T:U \to \Bbb R^2$ be a $C^1$ (continuously differentiable) transformation on an open set $U\subseteq \mathbb R^2,$ where * ![](images/82/829c083606df36014d5b5b078b80c1c0ff1edb72f981880b4a1a6a16affb32dc.svg) *Further, suppose that $(u_0,v_0)$ is **not** a critical point of $\mathbf T.$* Then, - *$\mathbf T$ is locally invertible at $(u_0,v_0),$* - *$\mathbf T^{-1},$ the inverse of $\mathbf T,$ is a $C^1$ function in a neighborhood of $(x_0,y_0),$ and* - *the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T^{-1},$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} ,$ is given by* $$ \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right)^{-1}. $$" :tutorial/id #uuid We state it below: *Let $\mathbf T:U \to \Bbb R^2$ be a $C^1$ (continuously differentiable) transformation on an open set $U\subseteq \mathbb R^2,$ where * ![](images/82/829c083606df36014d5b5b078b80c1c0ff1edb72f981880b4a1a6a16affb32dc.svg) *Further, suppose that $(u_0,v_0)$ is **not** a critical point of $\mathbf T.$* Then, - *$\mathbf T$ is locally invertible at $(u_0,v_0),$* - *$\mathbf T^{-1},$ the inverse of $\mathbf T,$ is a $C^1$ function in a neighborhood of $(x_0,y_0),$ and* - *the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T^{-1},$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} ,$ is given by* $$ \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right)^{-1}. $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "04daa2a7-b824-543f-b8d6-79a5b54e4799" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7678 :tutorial/title "The Inverse Function Theorem for Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "63b8e23b-b4a6-5984-b37f-dab9c1ced3af" :step/math-academy-id 44589 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199268}} {:db/id 17592186199249 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199450 :tutorial/content "Consider a transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by ![](images/fe/fefb7b82a6da1421bb96798fe6377e66199b50b8630dc396518927a0f3fe204b.svg) The points in the $(u,v)$ plane where $\mathbf T$ is *locally* non-invertible are known as **critical points**. We've already seen that $\mathbf T$ is locally non-invertible when the Jacobian determinant is zero. Therefore, the critical points of $\mathbf T$ are the solutions to the equation $$ \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}=0. $$ Let's compute the critical points of the following transformation: ![](images/8e/8e55b2da9a0c1fcf1ab901d361c50b652c906b92f0fcd4b158793f7782cfe5f4.svg) First, we find the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =4u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-6v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\ & =|\begin{aligned}4u & -6v \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ & =4u\cdot 1-(-6v)\cdot (-1) \\ & =4u-6v.\end{aligned} $$ The function has critical points when the Jacobian equals zero. So, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ 4u-6v & =0 \\ 2u-3v & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the critical points of $\mathbf{T}$ consist of those points that lie on the line $2u-3v=0$ in the $uv$-plane, shown below. ![](images/5c/5c544e3d3ecbdeaf7dc372b40ee0f37cb14e3ba292b8180a263c91103a9efe61.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "5f47e688-774b-5c89-a90d-ead52a871598" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4312 :tutorial/title "Critical Points of Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "16b2c818-03e6-5801-97b2-0ce8d225c3d5" :step/math-academy-id 26206 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199248}} {:db/id 17592186199450 :tutorial/content "Consider a transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by ![](images/fe/fefb7b82a6da1421bb96798fe6377e66199b50b8630dc396518927a0f3fe204b.svg) The points in the $(u,v)$ plane where $\mathbf T$ is *locally* non-invertible are known as **critical points**. \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}, $$ the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve $$ \frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0. $$ Here, we have $x(u,v)=3{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=u+v.$ First, we find the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =6u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =4v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\ & =\begin{vmatrix}6u & 4v \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ & =6u\cdot 1-4v\cdot 1 \\ & =6u-4v.\end{aligned} $$ The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ 6u-4v & =0 \\ v & =\frac{3}{2}u.\end{aligned} $$ The equation $v=\frac{3}{2}u$ defines a line in the $uv$-plane."} :step/id #uuid locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve $$ \frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0. $$ Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=uv.$ First, we find the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-2v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\ & =\begin{vmatrix}2u & -2v \\ v & u\end{vmatrix} \\ & =2u\cdot u-(-2v)\cdot v \\ & =2{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}.\end{aligned} $$ The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ 2({u}^{2}+{v}^{2}) & =0 \\ {u}^{2}+{v}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned} $$ The equation ${u}^{2}+{v}^{2}=0$ defines the point $(0,0)$ in the $uv$-plane."} :step/id #uuid "85b72007-63eb-5d72-bd12-04d202f52103" The function $f$ satisfies the conditions for the inverse function theorem at $x=1.$ Indeed, - $f$ is continuously differentiable on an open set containing $x=1,$ for example, $(0,2),$ and - the derivative of $f$ is nonzero at $x=1,$ i.e., ${f}^{′}(1)\ne 0.$ Therefore, by the inverse function theorem, $f$ is invertible in *some* neighborhood of $x=1.$ - Statement II is false. Notice that $y=-2=f(2).$ However, the function $f$ does *not* satisfy the conditions for the inverse function theorem at $x=2$ since ${f}^{′}(2)=0.$ So, the theorem can't be applied in this situation. - Statement III is false. Notice that $y=2.91=f(3),$ but $f$ is not continuous at $x=3.$ So, the theorem can't be applied in this situation. transformation $$ T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}, $$ the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve $$ \frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0. $$ Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=uv.$ First, we find the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =v\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\ & =\begin{vmatrix}2u & 2v \\ v & u\end{vmatrix} \\ & =2u\cdot u-2v\cdot v \\ & =2{u}^{2}-2{v}^{2}.\end{aligned} $$ The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ 2{u}^{2}-2{v}^{2} & =0 \\ {v}^{2} & ={u}^{2}.\end{aligned} $$ The equation ${v}^{2}={u}^{2}$ defines a pair of intersecting lines $v=u$ and $v=-u$ in the $uv$-plane."} :step/id #uuid "4da312bf-59b4-5062-8ec0-dbcdcb029a0e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186486481}} {:db/id locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve $$ \frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0. $$ Here, we have $x(u,v)=u{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)={u}^{2}+2v.$ First, we find the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={v}^{2} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2uv \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =2\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\ & =\begin{vmatrix}{v}^{2} & 2uv \\ 2u & 2\end{vmatrix} \\ & ={v}^{2}\cdot 2-2uv\cdot 2u \\ & =2{v}^{2}-4{u}^{2}v.\end{aligned} $$ The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ The function $f$ satisfies the conditions for the inverse function theorem at $x=1.$ Indeed, - $f$ is continuously differentiable on an open set containing $x=1,$ for example, $(0,2),$ and - the derivative of $f$ is nonzero at $x=1,$ i.e., ${f}^{′}(1)\ne 0.$ Therefore, by the inverse function theorem, $f$ is invertible in *some* neighborhood of $x=1.$ - Statement II is false. Notice that $y=-2=f(2).$ However, the function $f$ does *not* satisfy the conditions for the inverse function theorem at $x=2$ since ${f}^{′}(2)=0.$ So, the theorem can't be applied in this situation. - Statement III is false. Notice that $y=2.91=f(3),$ but $f$ is not continuous at $x=3.$ So, the theorem can't be applied in this situation. \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows: - First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$ - Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation $$ \frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}. $$ Here, we have $u(x,y)=2x+3y$ and $v(x,y)=2x+y.$ First, we compute the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =3 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =2 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =1\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\ & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ & =2\cdot 1-3\cdot 2 \\ & =-4.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we take the reciprocal: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\ & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned} $$"} :step/id #uuid "4f3a2d34-0995-5368-905a-f5f4b05fda88" :step/next $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve $$ \frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0. $$ Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=uv.$ First, we find the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-2v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{vmatrix} \\ & =\begin{vmatrix}2u & -2v \\ v & u\end{vmatrix} \\ & =2u\cdot u-(-2v)\cdot v \\ & =2{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}.\end{aligned} $$ The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ 2({u}^{2}+{v}^{2}) & =0 \\ {u}^{2}+{v}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned} $$ The equation ${u}^{2}+{v}^{2}=0$ defines the point $(0,0)$ in the $uv$-plane."} :step/id #uuid "a476947a-9128-5e05-b499-9b539dccc98c" $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, and $F.$ These line segments form a loop. ![](images/25/259bfd166a7870bd1a057b28d4b3324f3b98d05222596f1426afa01d6573e3d8.png) A chain of straight line segments that form a loop is called a **polygon**. The line segments are the **sides** of the polygon, and the endpoints of the sides are the **vertices**. For this polygon: - The $6$ vertices are $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, and $F.$ - The $6$ sides are $\overline{AB}$, $\overline{BC}$, $\overline{CD}$, $\overline{DE}$, $\overline{EF}$, and $\overline{AF}.$ To denote a particular polygon, we start at one vertex and loop around the polygon, reading off the vertices in order. So, the polygon above can be denoted $ABCDEF.$ The singular form of the word *vertices* is **vertex**. So, $A$ is a vertex, $B$ is a vertex, etc." :tutorial/id #uuid "342100ff-c1a7-531c-90a6-e07a80e83fda" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9674 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "5fbe01e1-2066-5d27-b53a-a2fa74fc43e6" :step/math-academy-id 188116 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106652}} {:db/id 17592186106652 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107179 :tutorial/content "The name of a polygon is determined by the number of sides it has. A polygon is **simple** if its boundary does not intersect itself. 3680} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186180626 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180777 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to solve the following subtraction problem: $$ 2 - 4.5 $$ We can solve this problem using a number line. To subtract $4.5$ from $2,$ we break up $4.5$ into its whole number part ($4$) and its decimal part ($0.5$) and proceed in two steps. - First, we subtract the whole number part. We start at $2$ on the number line and move $4$ places to the left, which brings us to $-2.$ - Then, we subtract the decimal part. We move the remaining $0.5$ places to the left, leaving us at $-2.5.$ ![](images/e7/e79d6ec2413d47e2b2b67237194a057d802746d1b9b016dcf118ca91b2bf31df.png) Therefore, we conclude that $$ 2 - 4.5 = -2.5. $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1e60ed87-2f30-5d4d-9d0b-990a5f1b8e1f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8384 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "8566447b-d96f-5adc-9b6e-c089a3f423a4" :step/math-academy-id 75114 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180627}} {:db/id 17592186180627 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179812 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179458 :question/id #uuid "0e9e4dd1-3161-5d3c-afab-5514e1c2d0d4" :question/math-academy-id "e-13383"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "44b96053-1ffa-56d3-8129-15ada765b9a7" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048549} {:db/id 17592186048911} {:db/id 17592186049097}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180189} {:db/id 17592186180191} {:db/id 17592186444435} {:db/id 17592186444436} {:db/id 17592186444438} {:db/id 17592186444439} {:db/id 17592186444440}] :knowledge-point/title "Subtracting Positive Decimals From Decimals With Halves"} :step/id #uuid "6c4541f7-07d8-51f6-b705-9bb2d82f1069" :step/math-academy-id 75115 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180628}} {:db/id 17592186180628 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180778 :tutorial/content "We can use the same methods that we learned to subtract whole numbers in more complicated situations. As an example, let's consider the following problem: $$ {\color{red}{3.5}} - {\color{blue}{9.8}} $$ We're subtracting a *positive* decimal from a smaller *positive* decimal. So the final answer must be negative. We start by solving the following easier problem, which is to carry out the subtraction *in the reverse order*: $$ {\color{blue}{9.8}} - {\color{red}{3.5}} = 6.3 $$ However, since our final answer must be negative, we conclude that $$ {\color{red}{3.5}} - {\color{blue}{9.8}} = -6.3 $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b35021fd-095a-5cca-9a9e-24ce11a93ae2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8385 :tutorial/title "Subtracting Positive Decimals From Positive Decimals"} :step/id #uuid "56a03151-c084-5924-9eca-03e11afc4c98" :step/math-academy-id 75118 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180629}} {:db/id 17592186180629 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180779 :tutorial/content "Now suppose we have the following problem: $$ -3.2 - 6.4 $$ In this case, we're subtracting a *positive* decimal from a *negative* decimal. So the final answer must be negative. We start by solving the following easier problem, which is to *add their absolute values*: $$ 3.2+6.4 = 9.6 $$ However, since our final answer must be negative, we conclude that $$ -3.2 - 6.4 = -9.6 $$ **Remember** - When we subtract a *positive* number from a smaller *positive* number, we carry out the subtraction *in the reverse order* and then make the final answer negative. - When we subtract a *positive* number from a *negative* number, we *add their absolute values* and then make the final answer negative." :tutorial/id #uuid "93e4bd99-076c-5ac9-9c1b-362ae1e66e8f" [{:db/id 17592186153002 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153465 :tutorial/content "The **natural numbers** are the positive whole numbers: ${\color{blue}1},\: {\color{blue}2},\: {\color{blue}3},\: There's some debate among mathematicians about whether zero should be considered a natural number. In other words, *every* natural number is also an integer." :tutorial/id #uuid "4109da7f-f9b5-5c94-8215-06f5ea408038" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9070 :tutorial/title "The Integers"} :step/id #uuid "bfd8720b-23e8-55fe-8c02-ac787976007a" :step/math-academy-id 172684 :step/next {:db/id 17592186153005}} {:db/id 17592186153005 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152125 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151860 :question/id #uuid "30b0a464-f903-5ee1-b649-97bfb366a73b" :question/math-academy-id "e-14643"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ebf3f930-2768-5399-8470-48ac430065a3" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152400} {:db/id 17592186152870} {:db/id 17592186433609} {:db/id 17592186433610} {:db/id 17592186524970}] :knowledge-point/title "Classifying Numbers as Integers"} :step/id #uuid "34d04639-2557-5679-9ab1-fa22b4733ce3" :step/math-academy-id 172685 :step/next {:db/id 17592186153006}} {:db/id 17592186153006 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153467 :tutorial/content "The **rational numbers** consist of all numbers that can be written as the ratio of two integers. For example: $$ {\color{purple}-\dfrac{1}{2}}, \quad {\color{purple}\dfrac{1}{2}}, \quad {\color{purple}\dfrac{1}{3}}, \quad {\color{purple}-\dfrac{2}{3}}, \quad {\color{purple}\dfrac{2}{3}} $$ Every integer is also a rational number because every integer can be expressed as a ratio of two integers. For example, $$ {\color{blue}2} = {\color{black}\dfrac{2}{1}}, \qquad {\color{red}-9} = {\color{black}\dfrac{(-9)}{\phantom{-}1}} $$ Likewise, any mixed number is a rational number because it can be written as an improper fraction. For example, $$ 2 \, \dfrac{1}{3} $$ is a rational number because $$ 2 \, \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{2 \times 3 + 1}{3} = \dfrac{7}{3} $$ We can now add the rational numbers to our inclusion diagram. ![](images/12/124ced6b317bdd2df4f967e6ea45e613b89d9fa136acb5edf8f7ed86fa8a4c06.png) Notice that the integers (and therefore the natural numbers) are contained within the rational numbers." :tutorial/id #uuid "3563ca37-8d82-5742-92b2-bb3918a71477" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9071 :tutorial/title "The Rational Numbers"} :step/id #uuid "cc715ab1-8b8b-555b-bd73-97d8d33107c0" :step/math-academy-id 172688 :step/next {:db/id 17592186153007}} {:db/id 17592186153007 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152126 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151861 :question/id #uuid "471f680f-5a51-5dac-aa3c-834610690f0e" :question/math-academy-id "e-14644"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f7063140-eebe-598c-b530-3c13509d359b" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152877} {:db/id 17592186152878} {:db/id 17592186424829} {:db/id 17592186433607} {:db/id 17592186433608} {:db/id 17592186518173}] :knowledge-point/title "Classifying Numbers as Rational"} :step/id #uuid "ba79c281-b939-528f-8605-0a6cd2aa6abd" :step/math-academy-id 172689 :step/next {:db/id 17592186153008}} {:db/id 17592186153008 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153468 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following rational number: $$ \dfrac13 $$ We can find the decimal representation of this rational number by dividing $1$ by $3$ using long division, as follows: | $\,\,0 \,. 3 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 3 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 3$$\:\ldots$$3$$\!\require{enclose}\enclose{longdiv}{1 {\,. \,} 0 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 0 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 0}$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$9$$1$$0$$-\!\!\!\!\!$$9$$1$$0$$-\!\!\!\!\!$$9$$1$$\,\ldots$ | | --- | Note that, in this case - the long division process never ends, and - the digit $3$ after the decimal point repeats *forever*. Therefore, we have that $$ \dfrac13 = 0.333\,333\ldots $$ This is an example of a **repeating decimal**. A repeating decimal is a decimal where the digits after the decimal point continue forever but in a repeating pattern. It's convenient to use the following special notation to indicate decimals that repeat indefinitely. $$ 0.\overline{3} = 0.333\,333\ldots $$ Some decimals have two or more digits that repeat indefinitely. For example: $$ \begin{aligned} 0.78^(―) &= 0.78787878… \\ 0.675^(―) &= 0.675675675… \end{aligned} $$ Some repeating decimals have non-repeating digits before the repeating part. For example: $$ 0.333\overline{67} = 0.333\,67\,67\,67\,67\ldots $$ The key takeaway for this section is that every repeating decimal is rational! In other words, every repeating decimal can be expressed as a ratio of two integers. For example: $$ \begin{aligned} 0.3^(―) &= \frac{1}{3} \\ 0.78^(―) &= \frac{26}{33} \\ 0.33367^(―) &= \frac{16517}{49500} \end{aligned} $$ In a future lesson, we'll learn how to express a repeating decimal as a fraction. For now, you can verify these results using a calculator." :tutorial/id #uuid "28ff4afd-e8c7-511c-86a4-14d547e6c6d2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9072 :tutorial/title "Repeating Decimals"} :step/id #uuid "8cd64bc9-e39e-5f5c-9c0d-618b3294cff3" :step/math-academy-id 172692 :step/next {:db/id 17592186153009}} {:db/id 17592186153009 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152127 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151862 :question/id #uuid "f0bf7717-e639-5889-92fe-7cdcce737a55" :question/math-academy-id "e-14645"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "be826645-6351-54ab-b57d-2c2a83a1b68d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050724}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152519} {:db/id 17592186152676}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Rational Decimals"} :step/id #uuid "7c946365-2b4a-5987-84b7-84cce8c8a6f4" :step/math-academy-id 172693}] :activity/title "Natural Numbers, Integers, and Rational Numbers" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186152314} {:db/id 17592186153002 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153465 :tutorial/content "The **natural numbers** are the positive whole numbers: ${\color{blue}1},\: {\color{blue}2},\: {\color{blue}3},\: {\color{blue}4},\: {\color{blue}5},\ldots$ We also refer to them as the **counting numbers**. Therefore, we have that $$ \dfrac13 = 0.333\,333\ldots $$ This is an example of a **repeating decimal**. A repeating decimal is a decimal where the digits after the decimal point continue forever but in a repeating pattern. It's convenient to use the following special notation to indicate decimals that repeat indefinitely. $$ 0.\overline{3} = 0.333\,333\ldots $$ Some decimals have two or more digits that repeat indefinitely. For example: $$ \begin{aligned} 0.78^(―) &= 0.78787878… \\ 0.675^(―) &= 0.675675675… \end{aligned} $$ Some repeating decimals have non-repeating digits before the repeating part. For example: $$ 0.333\overline{67} = 0.333\,67\,67\,67\,67\ldots $$ The key takeaway for this section is that every repeating decimal is rational! In other words, every repeating decimal can be expressed as a ratio of two integers. For example: $$ \begin{aligned} 0.3^(―) &= \frac{1}{3} \\ 0.78^(―) &= \frac{26}{33} \\ 0.33367^(―) &= \frac{16517}{49500} \end{aligned} $$ In a future lesson, we'll learn how to express a repeating decimal as a fraction. :tutorial/content "The squares of negative numbers are always positive because a negative times a negative is positive: $$ \begin{aligned}(-)\,\cdot \,(-)\,=\,(+)\end{aligned} $$ Some squares of negative numbers are as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}(-1)^{2}\,=\,(-1)\cdot (-1) & \,=\,1 \\ (-2)^{2}\,=\,(-2)\cdot (-2) & \,=\,4 \\ (-3)^{2}\,=\,(-3)\cdot (-3) & \,=\,9 \\ (-4)^{2}\,=\,(-4)\cdot (-4) & \,=\,16 \\ (-5)^{2}\,=\,(-5)\cdot (-5) & \,=\,25\end{aligned} $$ **Watch Out!** When squaring negative numbers, the parentheses are important! Consider the following squared quantity: $$ -3^2 $$ This is *not* the same as $(-3)^2$. Instead, this is a shorthand way of writing $$ (-1) \cdot 3^2. $$ According to the order of operations, we should square $3$ *first* and *then* multiply by $-1.$ Therefore: $$ \begin{aligned}-{3}^{2} & =(-1)\cdot {3}^{2} \\ & =(-1)\cdot 9 \\ & =-9\end{aligned} $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "38064eee-d6b6-5557-881a-ed03baadeed7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8103 :tutorial/title "Squaring Negative Numbers"} :question/worked-solution "We need to calculate the product of $-5.5$ with itself: $$ (-5.5)^{2}=(-5.5)\cdot (-5.5)=(5.5)\cdot (5.5) $$ First, we ignore the decimal points and multiply as if both numbers were whole numbers: $$ \begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} & & & \,\,\,\,\begin{aligned}\boxed{2} \\ \boxed{2}\end{aligned}\,\,\,\, & \\ & & & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,\times \,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, \\ & & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,7\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,+\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,7\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, \\ & \,\,\,\,3\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\,\end{aligned}\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $55\times 55=3\,025.$ We now count the total number of decimal places in the two factors. There is $1$ decimal place in the first factor ($5.5$) and $1$ decimal place in the second factor ($5.5$), so their product will have $1+1=2$ decimal places. 17592186045485} :question/problem "The joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given in the table below. Find $\text{E}[X{e}^{Y}].$ | $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ | | --- | --- | --- | | $X=1$ | $0.3$ | $0.1$ | | $X=2$ | $0.5$ | $0.1$ |" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables with supports ${S}_{X}$ and ${S}_{Y},$ respectively, and $f(x,y)$ is their joint probability mass function with support $S={S}_{X}\times {S}_{Y}.$ If $r:{R}^{2}\to R$ is a function of two variables, then the rule of the lazy statistician states that $$ \text{E}[r(X,Y)]={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}r(x,y)\,f(x,y). $$ In our case, we have $$ r(x,y)=x{e}^{y}. $$ Therefore, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[X{e}^{Y}] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}r(x,y)\,f(x,y) \\ & =(1\cdot {e}^{0})\cdot f(1,0)+(1\cdot {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3})\cdot f(1,\operatorname{ln}⁡3)+(2\cdot {e}^{0})\cdot f(2,0)+(2\cdot {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3})\cdot f(2,\operatorname{ln}⁡3) \\ & =1\cdot f(1,0)+3\cdot f(1,\operatorname{ln}⁡3)+2\cdot f(2,0)+6\cdot f(2,\operatorname{ln}⁡3) \\ & =1\cdot 0.3+3\cdot 0.1+2\cdot 0.5+6\cdot 0.1 \\ & =0.3+0.3+1+0.6 \\ & =2.2.\end{aligned} $$"} {:db/id 17592186476876 normal vector on $C$ can be expressed as $$ n=\frac{a(t)\,i+b(t)\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}. $$ Find the function $a(t).$" :question/worked-solution "For convenience, we express $r(t)$ in column vector notation: $$ r(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} $$ To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps: **Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$ Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ **Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector. The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation is $$ \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}. $$ Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise, we get $$ \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}. $$ **Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2. Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation). Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we conclude that $a(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$"} {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "The closed, positively oriented curve $C$ is defined as $r(t)=10\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+10\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector on $C$ can be expressed as $$ n=\frac{a(t)\,i+b(t)\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}. $$ Find the function $a(t).$" :question/worked-solution "For convenience, we express $r(t)$ in column vector notation: $$ r(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}10\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 10\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} $$ To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps: **Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$ Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-10\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 10\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ **Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector. The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation is $$ R=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}. $$ Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise, we get $$ \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-10\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 10\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}10\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 10\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}. $$ **Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2. Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation). Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}\begin{bmatrix}10\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 10\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\frac{10\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+10\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we conclude that $a(t)=10\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$"} {:db/id :tutorial/content "When $C$ is a closed curve, there is always a well-defined notion of "inside" and "outside" $C.$ It is usually easy to determine which region is inside or outside an arbitrary closed curve using our natural intuition. One important quantity that we often need when dealing with closed, oriented curves is the **outward-pointing unit normal vector,** usually denoted $\mathbf n$. As the name suggests: - $\mathbf n$ is normal (i.e., perpendicular) to the curve $C$ at *every* point, - it is a unit vector (i.e., its magnitude equals $1$), and - it always points in the outward direction. Since $\mathbf n$ must be normal to $C$ at *every* point, it must vary as we move around $C.$ Therefore, it is usually written either as a function of the parameter space (i.e., $\mathbf n(t)$) or as a function of the coordinates of the points on $C$ (i.e., $\mathbf n(x,y)$). As a concrete example, let's consider the closed, positively oriented ellipse $C,$ parameterized as $$ \mathbf r(t) = 3\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 2\sin t\,\mathbf{j}, \qquad t \in [0,2\pi). $$ ![](images/fe/fea4c20453e9c80493f5c5431859fd7918d75cbaa494ad0b3deeccacfae24019.png) For convenience, we first express $\mathbf r(t)$ in column vector notation: ![](images/c7/c7d514dbfdb746d94487a7ebca6b239173b854010eeccb80b4afc06cd09a9c0e.svg) Let's calculate the vector $\mathbf n$ for this curve. To do this, we follow three steps. **Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector $\mathbf r'(t).$ Differentiating the expression for $\mathbf r(t),$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ A typical tangent vector for our curve is shown below. ![](images/10/10ae867f682158bce2098234210206d4d7eb811be780505ca1984fb9e9516a27.png) **Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate $\mathbf r'(t)$ by $90^\circ$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector. The rotation matrix that corresponds to a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation is ![](images/27/27e11f86245d4331e33cec34742a7b6c395ff22fe95bcf465ec569f7168b4c0f.svg) Rotating the vector $\mathbf r'(t)$ by $90^\circ$ clockwise, we get the vector $\tilde{\mathbf n}(t),$ given by ![](images/00/006458079641036b283371fb36a94b39b11dcb09d796175a555539287218d8a7.svg) The vector $\tilde{\mathbf n}(t)$ is shown below: ![](images/7c/7ca9a18d78783a923b63fcc41a8bc41ccab5c4a12bb00f5c305e35e2e1bc40e5.png) **Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2. The vector $\tilde{\mathbf n}(t)$ in an outward-pointing normal vector, but it is not a unit vector. Therefore, we need to normalize it. Notice that $$ ||\mathbf r'(t)|| = \sqrt{(3\sin t)^2 + (2\cos t)^2} = \sqrt{9\sin^2 t + 4\cos^2 t}. $$ Furthermore, the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of $\mathbf r'(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation). Therefore, we can calculate our outward-pointing unit vector $\mathbf n$ as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}(t)}{||{r}^{′}(t)||} \\ & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||} \\ & =\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j}{\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t}}\end{aligned} $$ In conclusion, the vector $$ \mathbf n = \dfrac{2\cos t\,\mathbf i + 3\sin t\,\mathbf j}{\sqrt{9\sin^2 t + 4\cos^2 t}} $$ gives us an outward-pointing unit normal vector to every point on our ellipse." :tutorial/id #uuid "f96a7b70-f713-5ac8-afbe-0bc9a8caf7b8" :tutorial/math-academy-id y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}6\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix} $$ To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, *negatively* oriented curve, we follow three steps: **Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$ Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}6\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ **Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented clockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *counterclockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector. The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ counterclockwise rotation is $$ R=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}. $$ Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ counterclockwise, we get $$ \begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}6\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}6\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}. $$ **Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2. 6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\frac{6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we conclude that $b(t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$"} :step/id #uuid is defined as $r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector on $C$ can be expressed as $$ n=\frac{a(t)\,i+b(t)\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}. $$ Find the function $a(t).$" :question/worked-solution "For convenience, we express $r(t)$ in column vector notation: $$ r(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} $$ To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps: **Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$ Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ **Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector. The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation is $$ \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}. $$ Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise, we get $$ \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}. $$ **Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2. Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation). Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we conclude that $a(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$"} :step/id #uuid ${90}^{∘}$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector. The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation is $$ \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}. $$ Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise, we get $$ \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-8\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}. $$ **Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2. "q-149679" :question/problem "The closed, positively oriented curve $C$ is defined as $r(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector on $C$ can be expressed as $$ n=\frac{a(t)\,i+b(t)\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}. $$ Find the function $a(t).$" :question/worked-solution "For convenience, we express $r(t)$ in column vector notation: $$ r(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] $$ To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps: **Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$ Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$ **Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector. The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation is $$ [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]. $$ Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise, we get $$ [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]. $$ **Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2. Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation). Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]=\frac{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we conclude that $a(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$"} :step/id #uuid cubes**. Both of these polynomials follow a similar factor pattern: $$ \begin{aligned} a^{3}+b^{3} &= (a+b)(a^{2}-ab + b^{2}) \\ a^{3}-b^{3} &= (a-b)(a^{2}+ab + b^{2}) \end{aligned} $$ One trick to memorizing the signs in these patterns is to use the mnemonic **SOAP**, which stands for **S**ame, **O**pposite, **A**lways **P**ositive. - The sign of the linear factor is the **S**ame as that of the original polynomial, - the first sign of the quadratic factor is the **O**pposite sign, and - the last sign of the quadratic factor is **A**lways **P**ositive." :tutorial/id #uuid 17592186069844 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069923 :tutorial/content "To verify the identity $$ a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)(a^2 - ab + b^2) $$ we begin by expanding the right-hand side: $$ (a + b)(a^2 - ab + b^2) = a(a^2 - ab + b^2) + b(a^2 - ab + b^2) $$ Now, we apply the distributive law to each term: - For the first term, we have $a(a^2 - ab + b^2) = a^3 - a^2b + ab^2$. - For the second term, we have $b(a^2 - ab + b^2) = a^2b - ab^2 + b^3$. 17592186046941 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1005 17592186046975 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1007 "Mathematics for Machine Learning" 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1008 "Our Mathematics for Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning. This course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals. On completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network. Students then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms. As part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process. Students will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data. The course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data. A solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks. Students also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning. Students work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions. On the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail. Students extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling. The course concludes with parametric inference, focusing on point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals, which form the statistical foundation for many machine learning strength of the (linear) dependence between two random variables. One measure that we use for this purpose is covariance. The **covariance** between two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as $$ \textrm{Cov}[X, Y] = \textrm{E}\Big[\left(X - \textrm{E}[X]\right)\left(Y - \textrm{E}[Y]\right) \Big]. $$ Let's break this formula down a bit: - $\left(X - \textrm{E}[X]\right)$ is the deviation of $X$ from its mean - $\left(Y - \textrm{E}[Y]\right)$ is the deviation of $Y$ from its mean Therefore, the covariance measures the expected value of the product of these deviations. The covariance can also be expressed as $$ \textrm{Cov}[X, Y] =\sum_{(x,y)\in S}(x − \textrm E[X])(y − \textrm E[Y])f(x,y) $$ where $f(x,y)$ is the joint PMF of $X$ and $Y,$ and $S$ is the joint support. Let's sketch a few diagrams to get a feel for what the covariance tells us. - A *positive* covariance means that if $X$ increases, then $Y$ is likely to increase. We say that $X$ and $Y$ are **positively correlated**. ![](images/bb/bbfae3f0fb38bc8652cd26716e4b0b128cf1f2039350267034d97161d7f5dac4.png) - A *negative* covariance means that if $X$ increases, then $Y$ is likely to decrease. We say that $X$ and $Y$ are **negatively correlated**. ![](images/fd/fd45053fdc39f070e3438c3b8c61fe01613201595cfe00bd4cc6c6e481bf73ab.png) Note the following: - If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $$ \textrm{Cov}[X, Y] = 0. $$ The reverse implication does not always hold! For example, two random variables can have zero covariance yet be dependent. This is because covariance measures *linear* dependence only. - The covariance of a random variable with itself is its variance: $$ \begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,X] & =\text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])(X-\text{E}[X])] \\ & =\text{E}[{(X-\text{E}[X])}^{2}] \\ & =\text{Var}[X]\end{aligned} $$ - Aside from indicating whether two random variables are positively or negatively correlated, the covariance *by itself* does not tell us very much. For example, if $$ \textrm{Cov}[X_1, Y_1] > \textrm{Cov}[X_2, Y_2] > 0 $$ this does not necessarily mean that the dependence between $X_1$ and $Y_1$ is somehow "stronger" than the dependence between $X_2$ and $Y_2.$ This is because the covariance does not take the variance of the individual random variables into account. In a future lesson, we'll use the covariance to define the so-called **correlation coefficient,** which *does* consider the variance of the individual random variables and so *can* be used to compare the relative strength of the linear dependence between two pairs of random variables." 17592186045417] [17592186163290 1065 5624 17592186045417] [17592186163290 1066 #uuid [17592186046659 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I develops the core mathematical structures and analytical tools used throughout theoretical and applied physics. Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems. Students learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability. Students then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields. The course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems. The course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism. Students then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density. The final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating strings, mechanical systems, and electromagnetic circuits." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1012 154 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1013 "PS1" 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1014 #uuid work with bivariate distributions for *discrete* random variables. This lesson will examine the case where the random variables are *continuous.* A function $f(x,y)$ is a **joint probability density function** (or **joint PDF**) for the two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ if the following three conditions are satisfied: - $f(x,y) \geq 0$ for all $(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ - $\displaystyle \iint_{\mathbb R^2} f(x,y) \,\textrm{d}x\textrm{d}y = 1$ - $P\left((X,Y)\in A\right) = \displaystyle \iint_{A} f(x,y) \,\textrm{d}x\textrm{d}y,$ where $A$ is a subset of $\mathbb R^2.$ There is some nice intuition to these conditions. - The first condition states that $f$ must be nonnegative everywhere. - The second condition states that the sum (integral) of $f$ over possible values of $X$ and $Y$ must add up to $1.$ - The third condition states that we compute the probability of an event $A$ by summing (integrating) $f$ over all regions associated with $A.$ It's worth taking a minute to compare these conditions with those we've seen previously. Firstly, they are the continuous analog of those for the joint PMF of two discrete random variables. Secondly, they are the two-dimensional analog of those for the PDF $f(x)$ of a (single) continuous random variable $X.$ It's also worth noting that these conditions can be generalized to multivariate distributions $(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n)$ of $n$ continuous random variables. Let's now take a look at a concrete example." 17592186045417] [17592186163282 1065 5472 17592186045417] [17592186163282 1066 #uuid "5efc289c-9713-5098-ba27-c3f5e5e11dc6" 17592186045417] [17592186163282 1067 "Introduction" 17592186045417] [17592186163329 1064 "Suppose that $f(x,y)$ is a joint probability density function for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y.$ As previously discussed, for any subset $A$ of $\mathbb{R}^2,$ we have $$ P\big( (X,Y) \in A \big) = \iint_A f(x, y) \;\textrm{d}x\textrm{d}y. $$ In particular, if $A$ is the event defined as $$ A = \big\{ (X,Y) \:|\: a \leq X \leq b, \, c \leq Y \leq d \big\}, $$ then the corresponding probability can be computed as $$ P(a \leq X \leq b, c \leq Y \leq d) = \int^{d}_{c} \int^{b}_{a} f(x,y) \;\textrm{d}x \: \textrm{d}y = \int^{b}_{a} \int^{d}_{c} f(x,y) \;\textrm{d}y \: \textrm{d}x. $$ Finally, analogously to the case of a single continuous random variable, the probability that $(X,Y)$ takes on any particular value $(x,y)$ is zero, i.e., $$ P(X = x, Y=y) = 0. $$ Let's see an example of how to compute a probability in practice." 17592186045417] [17592186163329 1065 6285 17592186045417] [17592186163329 1066 #uuid "48e7fa44-96c7-5c63-a119-8ef92feda964" 17592186045417] [17592186163329 1067 "Finding Probabilities Using Joint PDFs" 17592186045417] [17592186163330 1064 "Let's show that the following function is a valid joint PDF: ![](images/2f/2fcc03e45f23018485c2aff1ff3c6804899928e37bedaa05d9dafc5e02780179.svg) We only need to check the first two conditions to show that this is a valid joint PDF for *some* pair of random variables.
